title: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience

questions.subtopic: OSI vs TCP/IP Reference Model. Layer Mapping
questions.question: An IS auditor maps controls documented in TCP/IP terms to the OSI model. Which OSI layers does the TCP/IP application layer MOST closely cover?

options.A: Transport, session and application layers together
options.B: Physical and data link layers of the model
options.C: Session, presentation and application layers
options.D: Network and transport layers of the model

questions.key_concept: The TCP/IP application layer combines the OSI session, presentation and application layers; transport remains a separate layer in both models.
questions.pre_read: Count the layers in each model. Ask which OSI layers have no separate TCP/IP counterpart.
questions.correct_explanation: The TCP/IP model folds the top three OSI layers (session, presentation and application) into its single application layer. Transport is a separate layer in both models, which is why the runner-up fails: it pulls the OSI transport layer into the application layer, although TCP and UDP sit in a TCP/IP transport layer of their own.

wrong_explanations.A: Transport is its own layer in both models. TCP and UDP sit in the TCP/IP transport layer, not inside the application layer.
wrong_explanations.B: Physical and data link functions map to the TCP/IP link layer at the bottom of the stack, not the application layer.
wrong_explanations.D: Network and transport functions map to the TCP/IP internet and transport layers, which sit below the application layer.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe lower layers that map to the TCP/IP link, internet and transport layers.
Final two: C beats A because transport stays a separate layer in both models; only the top three OSI layers merge.
Exam cue: TCP/IP has four layers, and its application layer absorbs OSI layers 5 to 7, nothing below.
questions.framework_ref: OSI Reference Model (ISO/IEC 7498-1); RFC 1122 (Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers); RFC 791 (Internet Protocol); RFC 9293 (Transmission Control Protocol)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'OSI 7-layer vs TCP/IP 4-layer model comparison per ISO/IEC 7498-1 and RFC 791/793'. Public sources: ISO/IEC 7498-1, IETF RFCs. First D4 question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IT operations manager plans to replace manual batch submission with job scheduling software. Which benefit is the PRIMARY reason to adopt it?

options.A: Automated job runs in dependency order, cutting keying errors
options.B: Nightly backups verified by automated restore tests
options.C: Rerouting of traffic when bandwidth thresholds are hit
options.D: Automatic restarts of failed jobs, skipping operator review steps

questions.key_concept: Job scheduling software automates production jobs in dependency order and reports outcomes, reducing manual errors while keeping exceptions under operator review.
questions.pre_read: Separate the tool's core purpose from features it may offer. Ask what manual submission does badly.
questions.correct_explanation: Job scheduling software exists to run production jobs automatically, in the right order and at the right time, and to report outcomes. Removing manual submission cuts sequencing and keying errors, which is the core control benefit. Automatic restarts are a useful feature, but restarting failed jobs with no operator review can hide data problems and rerun jobs that should be investigated first.

wrong_explanations.B: Backup and restore verification belong to backup tooling, not job scheduling, although a scheduler may trigger the backup job.
wrong_explanations.C: Traffic rerouting is a network management function. Job scheduling software controls job execution, not bandwidth.
wrong_explanations.D: Restarts are a feature, not the purpose. Rerunning failed jobs without review can duplicate postings or mask the error that caused the failure.

tips: Eliminate: B describes backup tooling and C describes network management, not job scheduling.
Final two: A beats D because controlled, ordered execution is the purpose; unreviewed restarts weaken oversight of failures.
Exam cue: automation adds value when exceptions still get human review; options that remove that review are rarely BEST.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations); ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 (Service Management System)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Job scheduling PRIMARY function per ISACA Job Scheduling Audit guidance and ITIL 4'. Public sources: ISACA, ITIL 4. Common examples: cron, Windows Task Scheduler, Control-M, Autosys. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A service level manager is drafting an SLA for a payroll service. Which element is MOST essential for the SLA to serve its purpose?

options.A: An informal promise to resolve escalated issues quickly
options.B: Financial penalties payable to the customer for each missed target
options.C: Technical design documents for each service component
options.D: Numeric service targets with agreed performance reporting

questions.key_concept: An SLA documents agreed, measurable service targets and reporting; penalties and remedies only work once performance can be measured.
questions.pre_read: Ask what must exist before anyone can show the provider failed. Remedies follow measurement.
questions.correct_explanation: An SLA is only as useful as what it can measure. Agreed, quantified targets with regular reporting of actual performance let both parties see whether the service met its commitment. Financial penalties give the agreement teeth, but without measurable targets nobody can prove a breach occurred, so penalties depend on the targets and cannot replace them.

wrong_explanations.A: An informal promise has no measurable target or reporting. ITIL service level management requires documented, agreed and measurable commitments.
wrong_explanations.B: Penalties only work once a breach can be shown. Without quantified targets and reporting, a breach cannot be proven, so penalties are secondary.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal design documents describe how the provider builds the service. They do not state what the customer receives or how it is measured.

tips: Eliminate: C is internal design detail and A is informal, with nothing to measure.
Final two: D beats B because a breach must be measurable before any penalty can apply.
Exam cue: for agreements and contracts, measurable targets come first; remedies and penalties depend on them.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Service Level Management practice; ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 (Service Management System); COBIT 2019 APO09 (Managed Service Agreements)

questions.question: A business continuity manager is starting a new continuity program. What is the PRIMARY output the business impact analysis should provide?

options.A: A ranked list of threats most likely to disrupt operations
options.B: Recovery priorities and time objectives for critical processes
options.C: A complete inventory of IT assets and vendor contracts
options.D: A review of IT budget spending and savings opportunities

questions.key_concept: The BIA identifies critical processes, measures disruption impact over time and sets recovery priorities and objectives (RTO, RPO) that drive strategy.
questions.pre_read: Separate impact from likelihood. Ask which output the recovery strategy is built on.
questions.correct_explanation: A business impact analysis identifies critical business processes and measures how disruption harms them over time. Its output is recovery priorities and objectives such as RTO and RPO, which drive the continuity and recovery strategy. Ranking threats by likelihood belongs to the risk assessment: the BIA asks what happens if a process stops, whatever the cause.

wrong_explanations.A: Ranking threats by likelihood is a risk assessment output. The BIA focuses on the impact of disruption over time, regardless of cause.
wrong_explanations.C: An asset inventory supports recovery planning but says nothing about which business processes matter most or how fast they must return.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget review is a financial activity. It does not establish which processes are critical or what their recovery objectives are.

tips: Eliminate: C is an asset inventory and D is a budget review; neither sets recovery priorities.
Final two: B beats A because the BIA measures impact over time; threat likelihood belongs to the risk assessment.
Exam cue: the BIA answers what hurts most and how fast it must return, and it comes before any recovery strategy.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 Clause 8.2.2 (Business Impact Analysis); NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems; ISACA Business Continuity Management Audit/Assurance Program
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'BIA PRIMARY purpose per ISO 22301 and NIST SP 800-34'. Public sources: ISO 22301, NIST SP 800-34. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that visitors can plug laptops into open wall ports in meeting rooms. Which measure would BEST prevent unauthorized connections?

options.A: WPA3 encryption enabled on each wireless access point
options.B: Badge-controlled entry points at the main building lobby
options.C: IEEE 802.1X authentication before a port allows access
options.D: MAC address filtering configured on each switch port

questions.key_concept: Port-based network access control (IEEE 802.1X) authenticates devices before any wired or wireless port grants access; MAC filtering is easily spoofed.
questions.pre_read: Note where the visitors are and what they plug into. Ask which control proves identity rather than trusting it.
questions.correct_explanation: IEEE 802.1X makes every port, wired or wireless, demand authentication before it passes traffic, so an unknown laptop gets no network access even when plugged in. MAC filtering looks similar but trusts an identifier anyone can read and copy; a visitor can spoof an approved MAC address and pass the filter.

wrong_explanations.A: WPA3 protects wireless access. The exposure here is open wired ports, which wireless encryption does not touch.
wrong_explanations.B: Visitors are already legitimately inside the building, so lobby entry control does nothing to stop them using a meeting-room port.
wrong_explanations.D: MAC addresses are easy to observe and spoof, so filtering identifies hardware weakly and offers little resistance to a deliberate attacker.

tips: Eliminate: A covers wireless access, and B fails because the visitors are already inside.
Final two: C beats D because authentication proves identity, while a MAC address can be spoofed.
Exam cue: prefer controls that authenticate before access over controls that trust identifiers an attacker can copy.
questions.framework_ref: IEEE 802.1X (Network Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-3 (Device Identification and Authentication); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.20 (Networks Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'LAN/WAN edge security via 802.1X per IEEE 802.1X and ISACA Network Management guidance'. Public sources: IEEE, ISACA. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: HR asks for evidence of one employee's web misuse, and the IS auditor reviews the forward proxy. Which proxy configuration is MOST important to support that request?

options.A: Authenticated users with every web request logged
options.B: Transparent proxying with anonymous, unlogged sessions
options.C: Category-based URL filtering applied to outbound traffic
options.D: Direct internet access allowed when the proxy is slow

questions.key_concept: Proxy authentication plus request logging gives accountability for web use; filtering prevents misuse but cannot attribute activity to a user.
questions.pre_read: Note the objective: evidence about one employee. Ask which configuration records who did what.
questions.correct_explanation: Investigating misuse needs attribution: the proxy must authenticate users and log each request so activity can be tied to a person. URL filtering is a valuable preventive control, but it blocks categories rather than recording who did what, so it cannot answer the evidence request. When the objective is investigation, accountable logging outranks prevention.

wrong_explanations.B: Anonymous, unlogged sessions remove accountability entirely. No activity could be attributed to the employee.
wrong_explanations.C: Filtering prevents some misuse but records nothing tying activity to a named user, so it cannot supply the evidence requested.
wrong_explanations.D: Letting traffic bypass the proxy creates unlogged, unfiltered access and destroys the evidence trail the request depends on.

tips: Eliminate: D and B both remove the logging and identity the investigation depends on.
Final two: A beats C because the objective is evidence of who did what; filtering prevents but does not attribute.
Exam cue: match the control to the objective; an investigation needs identity plus logs, not just prevention.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.15 (Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Forward proxy controls per ISACA Proxy Server guidance and NIST SP 800-53'. Public sources: ISACA, NIST. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: USB Mass Storage Devices. Risk Management
questions.question: An organization's data loss review shows staff copying client files to personal USB drives. Which control BEST addresses this risk while preserving legitimate business use?

options.A: An annual signed policy acknowledgement banning personal drives
options.B: Antivirus scanning of each drive when it is connected
options.C: Epoxy sealing of the USB ports on every endpoint
options.D: Device control allowing approved encrypted drives, with logging

questions.key_concept: Device-control policies enforce removable media rules technically: approved encrypted drives allowed, others blocked, and all use logged.
questions.pre_read: Note that staff already broke the expectation. Ask which option enforces the rule rather than restating it.
questions.correct_explanation: Endpoint device control enforces the rule technically: approved, encrypted drives work, unapproved drives are blocked, and transfers are logged for review. That stops copies to personal drives yet keeps business use. A signed policy sets expectations and supports discipline, but it is a directive control that relies on staff choosing to comply, which is exactly what failed here.

wrong_explanations.A: A policy states the rule but does not enforce it. Staff already ignored expectations, so a directive control alone leaves the copying possible.
wrong_explanations.B: Antivirus addresses malware on the drive, not data leaving the organization. Clean drives can still carry client files out.
wrong_explanations.C: Sealing ports stops the copying but also blocks legitimate business use, which the stem requires the control to preserve.

tips: Eliminate: B targets malware rather than data leaving, and C blocks the legitimate use the stem says to preserve.
Final two: D beats A because a technical preventive control enforces the rule; a signed policy only asks for compliance.
Exam cue: when a directive control has already failed, the BEST answer usually enforces the rule technically.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 MP-7 (Media Use); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.10 (Storage Media)

questions.question: A network security manager must secure a new corporate wireless network for employee laptops. Which configuration provides the STRONGEST protection against unauthorized access?

options.A: WEP encryption combined with a hidden network name
options.B: WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and certificate-based EAP-TLS
options.C: An open network restricted by MAC address filtering
options.D: WPA3-Personal with a long, regularly rotated passphrase

questions.key_concept: Enterprise wireless should use WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and EAP-TLS so access is authenticated and revocable per user, not shared.
questions.pre_read: Two options use modern encryption. Ask how each one decides who may connect.
questions.correct_explanation: WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X to authenticate each user or device individually, and EAP-TLS adds certificates, so access ties to corporate identity and can be revoked per person. WPA3-Personal encrypts well, but everyone shares one passphrase: anyone who learns it gets in, and removing one leaver means changing it for every user.

wrong_explanations.A: WEP is broken and can be cracked in minutes. Hiding the network name adds little because it still appears in wireless traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: An open network has no encryption, and MAC addresses are easily spoofed, so access control is trivial to bypass.
wrong_explanations.D: A shared passphrase gives no individual accountability. Once leaked or known by a leaver, anyone can connect until it is changed for everyone.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on broken WEP, and C leaves traffic unencrypted behind spoofable MAC filtering.
Final two: B beats D because per-user certificate authentication is revocable and accountable; a shared passphrase is not.
Exam cue: for enterprise access, individual authentication tied to the directory beats any shared secret, however strong.
questions.framework_ref: WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3); IEEE 802.11 (Wireless LAN Standards); IEEE 802.1X (Network Access Control); NIST SP 800-97 (Wireless Network Security)

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the IT asset register is built solely from purchase orders. Which enhancement would MOST improve lifecycle control?

options.A: Depreciation tags applied to assets at purchase
options.B: An annual spreadsheet stock count performed by the finance team
options.C: Ongoing discovery reconciled to the register through disposal
options.D: Separate inventories kept by each business unit

questions.key_concept: IT asset management covers the full lifecycle (acquisition, assignment, change and secure disposal), kept accurate by ongoing discovery and reconciliation.
questions.pre_read: Ask which lifecycle stages a purchase-fed register never sees. Pick the option that covers them continuously.
questions.correct_explanation: A register fed only by purchasing sees assets arrive but not move, change or leave. Ongoing discovery reconciled to the register catches in-use changes and unrecorded devices, and tracking through disposal confirms data is destroyed. An annual count by finance adds a check, but it is a once-a-year snapshot that misses most movements and does not verify sanitization.

wrong_explanations.A: Depreciation tagging is still a purchase-time finance step. It adds nothing about in-use changes or disposal.
wrong_explanations.B: A yearly count is a stale snapshot. Assets move, change hands and leave between counts, and finance does not verify media sanitization.
wrong_explanations.D: Decentralized inventories create inconsistent records and gaps, worsening enterprise visibility rather than closing the lifecycle gap.

tips: Eliminate: D fragments the records, and A is another purchase-time step.
Final two: C beats B because ongoing reconciliation covers the whole lifecycle; a yearly count is a stale snapshot.
Exam cue: asset management runs from acquisition to secure disposal; prefer ongoing reconciliation over point-in-time counts.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets); ITIL 4 IT Asset Management practice; NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2 (Guidelines for Media Sanitization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ITAM full-lifecycle per ISACA IT Asset Management guidance and ITIL 4 Service Configuration Management'. Public sources: ISACA, ITIL 4. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a nightly interface that sends payment files from the ERP to the bank. Which control BEST ensures the data arrive complete and accurate?

options.A: Input validation edits run in the ERP before export
options.B: Encryption of the payment file while in transit
options.C: Weekly rather than nightly runs of the interface
options.D: Record counts and control totals reconciled on receipt

questions.key_concept: Interface controls reconcile record counts and control totals at the receiving end, with exceptions followed up, to prove completeness and accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in the flow loss or change could happen. Pick the check that sees the data after it arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness and accuracy across an interface are proven at the receiving end: record counts, control totals or hash totals are compared with what was sent, and mismatches raise exceptions. Validation edits in the ERP confirm the data were correct when they left, but they cannot detect records lost, duplicated or altered after export.

wrong_explanations.A: Source edits confirm data quality at export. They cannot show that every record arrived at the bank unchanged.
wrong_explanations.B: Encryption protects confidentiality in transit. It does not prove that every record was sent or that totals agree.
wrong_explanations.C: Running less often changes the volume per run, not accuracy. Weekly batches can still lose or duplicate records undetected.

tips: Eliminate: B addresses confidentiality, and C changes frequency without adding any check.
Final two: D beats A because only reconciliation on receipt detects loss or change after export.
Exam cue: for interfaces, completeness and accuracy are proven by reconciling totals at the receiving end.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls); COBIT 2019 BAI03 (Managed Solutions Identification and Build)

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a material spreadsheet that calculates loan loss reserves is edited by several analysts. Which control MOST reduces the risk of undetected formula errors?

options.A: Independent review and approval of each formula change
options.B: Password protection required to open the spreadsheet
options.C: A daily backup copy saved to a network drive
options.D: Monthly reasonableness review of the final reserve figure

questions.key_concept: Material spreadsheets need change control: independent review and approval of formula changes, plus versioning, access restriction and testing.
questions.pre_read: Ask where formula errors enter. Prefer the control acting at that point over one that checks the result.
questions.correct_explanation: Formula errors enter when someone edits the logic. Requiring independent review and approval of each change stops errors before they reach the reported reserve, as change control does for formal systems. A monthly reasonableness review is a useful detective check, but it only catches errors large enough to distort the total; a wrong formula can still produce a plausible figure.

wrong_explanations.B: Password protection limits who opens the file, but the analysts making edits are already authorized, so their errors pass unchecked.
wrong_explanations.C: Backups support recovery of the file. They preserve wrong formulas just as faithfully as correct ones.
wrong_explanations.D: A reasonableness check catches errors big enough to look wrong. A flawed formula can still produce a plausible but misstated reserve.

tips: Eliminate: B restricts access the editors already have, and C supports recovery, not accuracy.
Final two: A beats D because change review stops formula errors at source; a total-level check misses plausible errors.
Exam cue: for material end-user computing, look for change control on the logic, not just checks on the output.

questions.question: An IT governance manager suspects business teams use unsanctioned cloud services. Which approach would BEST reveal the extent of shadow IT?

options.A: A review of the sanctioned IT services catalog
options.B: Analysis of CASB and proxy logs for cloud traffic
options.C: A survey asking each department to declare its tools
options.D: Blocking every unrecognized domain at the firewall

questions.key_concept: Shadow IT discovery relies on independent telemetry such as CASB and proxy logs; surveys and catalogs miss unsanctioned services.
questions.pre_read: Ask which source of evidence does not depend on teams' honesty or memory.
questions.correct_explanation: Discovery should rest on independent evidence. Cloud access security broker and proxy logs record actual traffic to cloud services, so they show what is used, by whom and how much, regardless of what teams admit. A departmental survey is a reasonable supplement, but self-reporting is incomplete: teams forget tools or omit ones they expect to lose.

wrong_explanations.A: The sanctioned catalog lists approved services. By definition it cannot reveal unsanctioned ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Self-reported surveys are incomplete and biased; teams may forget tools or hide ones they fear losing. They supplement telemetry rather than replace it.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking is a response, not discovery. It disrupts the business before the organization knows what is used or how valuable it is.

tips: Eliminate: D is a blunt response rather than discovery, and A lists what is already approved.
Final two: B beats C because observed traffic is independent evidence; self-reported surveys miss what teams forget or hide.
Exam cue: for discovery, evidence from systems outranks evidence from the people being assessed.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds production servers were hardened at deployment but never reviewed since. Which periodic activity would BEST address this gap?

options.A: Confirming automatic security updates are enabled on every server
options.B: Measuring CPU and memory utilization trends over time
options.C: Checking settings for drift from the secure configuration standard
options.D: Checking operating system license compliance each year

questions.key_concept: Periodic OS reviews compare current configuration, patches, privileged accounts and logging against an approved baseline to detect drift.
questions.pre_read: Ask what can change on a server after deployment besides missing patches.
questions.correct_explanation: Hardening decays: settings drift, accounts are added and services are switched on after deployment. Periodically comparing each server's current configuration with the approved baseline detects that drift, including privileged access and logging changes. Confirming automatic updates are on covers patching alone; a fully patched server can still carry weakened settings or excess administrator accounts.

wrong_explanations.A: Automatic updates address patch levels. They do not detect configuration drift, new privileged accounts or disabled logging.
wrong_explanations.B: Utilization measurement is a capacity activity. It says nothing about security settings or system integrity.
wrong_explanations.D: License compliance is a legal and cost concern. It does not test whether servers remain securely configured.

tips: Eliminate: B measures capacity and D checks license compliance; neither tests security.
Final two: C beats A because baseline comparison detects drift; update settings cover patching alone.
Exam cue: when hardening was set once and never checked, look for a periodic comparison against the approved baseline.

questions.question: A capacity manager sees storage use on a core system growing 4 percent a month. Which action BEST reflects proactive capacity management?

options.A: Add storage after users report slow performance
options.B: Run storage at full use to maximize hardware return
options.C: Alert at 95 percent use, then expand storage when the alert fires
options.D: Forecast demand and plan additions before thresholds are reached

questions.key_concept: Proactive capacity management forecasts demand from utilization trends and plans additions before thresholds are reached, preserving lead time.
questions.pre_read: Growth is steady and known. Ask which option uses that knowledge before a threshold is hit.
questions.correct_explanation: Proactive capacity management uses trend data to forecast demand and plans additions so capacity arrives before service degrades. With steady growth, the date of saturation can be predicted. A 95 percent alert is better than nothing, but it reacts at the last moment, leaving too little time for procurement, testing and change approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting for user complaints accepts service impact before acting. That is the reactive pattern proactive management avoids.
wrong_explanations.B: Running at full use removes the headroom needed for peaks and growth, making degradation certain.
wrong_explanations.C: A late threshold alert is reactive. At 95 percent there may be too little time to procure, test and approve the expansion.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for user impact, and B removes all headroom.
Final two: D beats C because forecasting gives lead time; a 95 percent alert fires too late to plan.
Exam cue: proactive means acting on forecasts before thresholds; alerts and complaints are reactive signals.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Capacity and Performance Management; COBIT 2019 BAI04 (Managed Availability and Capacity)

questions.question: During a major outage, the incident manager has a workaround that restores service, but the root cause is unknown. What should the incident manager do FIRST?

options.A: Apply the workaround and open a problem record
options.B: Pass the ticket to whichever developer is available
options.C: Confirm the root cause before applying any workaround
options.D: Wait for further user reports to confirm the impact

questions.key_concept: ITIL 4 incident management restores service first, using workarounds; root cause is pursued separately through problem management, never skipped.
questions.pre_read: Separate restoring service from preventing recurrence. Ask which practice owns each.
questions.correct_explanation: Incident management aims to restore normal service as quickly as possible, so a proven workaround should be applied at once. The unknown cause is not ignored: it passes to problem management through a problem record. Confirming the root cause first sounds rigorous, but it prolongs a major outage for an investigation that problem management can run after service returns.

wrong_explanations.B: Ad hoc assignment bypasses categorization, prioritization and escalation, so the outage may reach someone without the right skills.
wrong_explanations.C: Root-cause analysis belongs to problem management and can run after restoration. Holding a working fix during a major outage extends business impact.
wrong_explanations.D: A major outage is already confirmed. Waiting for more reports delays restoration and ignores priority-based incident handling.

tips: Eliminate: D delays a confirmed major outage, and B skips prioritization and proper escalation.
Final two: A beats C because incident management restores service first; problem management then finds the cause.
Exam cue: restore service first, but never skip root cause; look for the hand-off to problem management.

questions.question: An IS auditor suspects service desk agents close tickets quickly to meet targets. Which metric BEST shows whether issues are truly resolved?

options.A: Satisfaction scores from post-closure user surveys
options.B: Percentage of tickets reopened after their closure
options.C: Average elapsed time taken to close each ticket
options.D: Number of tickets handled per agent each day

questions.key_concept: Help desk effectiveness is shown by outcome measures such as reopen rates and first-contact resolution, not by speed or volume alone.
questions.pre_read: Note the suspected behaviour. Ask which metric would rise if tickets were closed without a fix.
questions.correct_explanation: If agents close tickets quickly to hit targets, unresolved issues come back. The reopen rate measures that directly: a ticket closed without a real fix returns. Satisfaction surveys add a useful perception view, but response rates are low and users rate courtesy and speed as much as resolution, so scores can stay high while fixes fail.

wrong_explanations.A: Surveys reflect perception, have low response rates and often reward courtesy and speed, so they can hide tickets closed without a real fix.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing time is the metric being gamed. Fast closure is exactly what the auditor suspects is masking unresolved issues.
wrong_explanations.D: Throughput per agent rewards volume, which encourages premature closure rather than showing resolution quality.

tips: Eliminate: C is the gamed speed metric, and D rewards volume over quality.
Final two: B beats A because reopen rates measure failed fixes directly; surveys measure perception.
Exam cue: when a metric may be gamed, look for an outcome measure that the gaming would expose.

questions.subtopic: Major Outage with Multiple Incident Overlap
questions.question: During a major outage, three concurrent incidents, including suspected lateral movement, are handled by separate teams with no shared lead. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Let each team continue independently on its own incident
options.B: Pause the response until links between incidents are analyzed
options.C: Appoint one incident commander over coordinated workstreams
options.D: Prioritize the database failure per the BIA and defer the others

questions.key_concept: Concurrent, possibly linked incidents need a single incident commander coordinating separate workstreams, priorities and communications.
questions.pre_read: Note the suspected intrusion. Ask which option keeps every incident moving under one set of decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Concurrent incidents that may be linked need one command structure: a single incident commander sets priorities, runs separate workstreams and coordinates communications and decisions. Focusing on the database failure reflects business impact, but deferring a suspected intrusion lets an attacker act unchecked and ignores the chance that the incidents share a cause. Coordination keeps every workstream moving.

wrong_explanations.A: Independent handling produces conflicting decisions and messages, and nobody sees links between incidents. This is the gap the auditor should close.
wrong_explanations.B: Halting response to analyze links during an outage extends impact. Links can be investigated in parallel within coordinated workstreams.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring a suspected intrusion risks data loss and spread, and ignores possible links to the outage. A commander can prioritize without stopping other workstreams.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the uncoordinated status quo, and B halts response mid-outage to analyze links.
Final two: C beats D because a single commander prioritizes without abandoning the suspected intrusion.
Exam cue: multiple concurrent incidents call for unified command, not choosing one and dropping the rest.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Multi-incident overlap response per ITIL 4 Incident Management and NIST SP 800-61'. Public sources: ITIL 4, NIST SP 800-61. Scenario specifics (B2B SaaS, 1.6M users, 90 minutes elapsed, 3 concurrent incidents — database + auth + lateral movement) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Shadow IT Discovery During Audit Engagement
questions.question: An IS audit found 73 unsanctioned SaaS services, some holding client data. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Risk-rank the services by data sensitivity and value
options.B: Document the services and accept the current state
options.C: Negotiate enterprise contracts for the most-used services
options.D: Disable every service until IT provides replacements

questions.key_concept: Shadow IT remediation starts with risk-ranking services by data sensitivity and value, then sanctioning, migrating or retiring each accordingly.
questions.pre_read: Note the mix of services. Ask what must be known before deciding which to keep, move or stop.
questions.correct_explanation: Before any remediation, the services need ranking by the sensitivity of the data they hold and the business value they deliver. That ranking decides which to sanction, which to migrate urgently and which to retire. Negotiating contracts for the most-used tools tackles cost and contract risk, but popularity is not risk; a little-used file-sharing service holding client data may matter most.

wrong_explanations.B: Accepting the current state leaves client data in unassessed services, ignoring the risk the audit has just surfaced.
wrong_explanations.C: Usage is not risk. Contracting by popularity can legitimize risky services and overlook low-use tools that store client data.
wrong_explanations.D: Blanket disablement disrupts legitimate business needs and ignores that some services may be low risk and worth sanctioning.

tips: Eliminate: D disrupts the business without assessment, and B accepts unassessed client-data risk.
Final two: A beats C because remediation should follow risk, not popularity or cost.
Exam cue: when many issues surface at once, risk-rank FIRST; sanctioning, migrating or retiring follows from the ranking.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (OCC/FRB/FDIC, 2023, superseding OCC Bulletin 2013-29); CSA Cloud Controls Matrix
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Shadow IT discovery remediation per ISACA Shadow IT Governance guidance'. Public sources: ISACA, OCC, CSA. Scenario specifics (4.5K-employee FS firm, 73 services, $2.1M annual cost, 28+12+8+25 split, CIO/CFO/business positions) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: After a quarter of repeated SLA availability breaches, four teams blame each other. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to establish the root cause?

options.A: Hold a joint workshop to agree on the main cause
options.B: Accept the operations team's capacity explanation
options.C: Have each team run a separate retrospective
options.D: Rebuild the outage timeline from monitoring telemetry

questions.key_concept: Structured root cause analysis starts from facts such as a telemetry-based timeline, then identifies multiple contributing factors and shared remediation.
questions.pre_read: Note that every team has a theory. Ask what evidence all four would have to accept.
questions.correct_explanation: Root cause analysis must start from facts. Rebuilding the outage timeline from monitoring telemetry gives every team the same evidence and usually reveals several contributing factors, which supports shared remediation. A joint workshop brings the teams together, but without an evidence base it settles the cause by negotiation or seniority, so the blame dispute simply moves into the room.

wrong_explanations.A: A workshop without shared evidence agrees a cause by negotiation. The loudest view wins, and real contributing factors may be missed.
wrong_explanations.B: Accepting one team's view closes on a single cause without evidence and ignores other contributing factors.
wrong_explanations.C: Separate retrospectives keep each team's view of events, so no shared timeline or cross-team factors emerge.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts one untested view, and C keeps the teams' analysis apart.
Final two: D beats A because cause must rest on evidence; a workshop without data negotiates it.
Exam cue: in blame disputes, the BEST first step establishes facts from independent evidence before anyone agrees a cause.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SLA breach structured RCA per ISACA SLA Breach Analysis guidance and ITIL 4 Problem Management'. Public sources: ISACA, ITIL 4, NIST. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A business line demands a 1-hour RTO costing $14 million more than current capability, and executives meet next week to approve targets. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Set the target to match current replication capability
options.B: Delay approval until impact and cost per option are compared
options.C: Let the CFO choose a target that fits the budget
options.D: Approve the 1-hour target and phase the spending over several years

questions.key_concept: RTO and RPO targets follow quantified business impact weighed against cost; management then approves the target and accepts residual risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether anyone has shown what an outage costs at each RTO. If not, what must happen before approval?
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery targets should come from quantified business impact weighed against cost, with management accepting the residual risk of the option chosen. Neither number has been tested yet, so the right move is to hold approval until each option's impact, regulatory exposure and cost are compared. Approving the 1-hour target and phasing spend sounds decisive, but it commits millions before showing the impact justifies it.

wrong_explanations.A: Matching current capability lets infrastructure set business targets, reversing the BIA logic in which business impact drives recovery objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Budget alone ignores business impact and regulatory exposure. Target-setting needs impact and cost weighed together, not one executive's constraint.
wrong_explanations.D: Phasing spend still commits to a target nobody has justified. The BIA must show the impact warrants a 1-hour RTO before funding follows.

tips: Eliminate: A lets current technology set the target, and C lets budget alone decide.
Final two: B beats D because impact must justify the target before money is committed.
Exam cue: waiting is BEST when a key input is missing; here the impact-versus-cost analysis must precede approval.

questions.question: An IS auditor notes that internal hosts use private IP addresses yet reach the internet through the firewall. Which function MOST likely makes this possible?

options.A: Compressing traffic to save outbound bandwidth
options.B: Routing the private subnets directly onto the internet
options.C: Translating private addresses to a public address
options.D: Encrypting packets so routers cannot read them

questions.key_concept: NAT rewrites addresses between private internal and public external address spaces at the boundary; private ranges are not internet-routable.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes private address ranges special. Ask what must happen to them at the boundary.
questions.correct_explanation: Private address ranges are not routable on the public internet, so the boundary device uses network address translation: it rewrites private source addresses to a public address and maps replies back. Routing alone sounds right, but internet routers drop packets from private ranges and would have no path back to them, so translation is what makes the connection work.

wrong_explanations.A: Compression reduces bandwidth. It has nothing to do with whether private addresses can communicate externally.
wrong_explanations.B: Private ranges are not routable on the internet. Without translation, replies have no path back, so routing alone cannot connect these hosts.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption protects confidentiality in transit. It does not change addresses, so it cannot let private addresses reach the internet.

tips: Eliminate: D is encryption and A is compression; neither changes addressing.
Final two: C beats B because private ranges are not routable on the internet and must be translated.
Exam cue: private addresses reaching the internet point to translation at the boundary; NAT hides internal addressing but is not encryption.
questions.framework_ref: RFC 3022 (Network Address Translation); RFC 1918 (Private Address Allocation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'NAT PRIMARY function per RFC 3022'. Public sources: IETF RFC 3022, ISACA guidance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor scoping a server hardware review has included processors, memory, storage and network interfaces. Which further hardware area is MOST important to add?

options.A: Attached peripherals such as printers and scanners
options.B: Operating system and application software
options.C: System users and administrator accounts
options.D: Power supply and cooling infrastructure

questions.key_concept: Core hardware groups are processing (CPU, memory), input/output (storage, network, peripherals) and supporting infrastructure (power, cooling).
questions.pre_read: Map the included items to the three hardware groups. Ask which group is missing entirely.
questions.correct_explanation: Hardware is commonly grouped into processing, input/output and the supporting infrastructure that keeps it running. The scope already covers processing and the main input/output paths, but omits power and cooling, without which every server fails at once. Peripherals are input/output hardware too, but printers and scanners matter little to server availability compared with the infrastructure everything depends on.

wrong_explanations.A: Peripherals are input/output hardware, but printers and scanners rarely affect server operation. Their failure is local, unlike a power or cooling failure.
wrong_explanations.B: Operating systems and applications are software. They belong to a different review, not a hardware component scope.
wrong_explanations.C: Users and administrator accounts are people and access matters, not hardware components.

tips: Eliminate: B is software and C concerns people and access, not hardware.
Final two: D beats A because power and cooling support every server; peripheral failures stay local.
Exam cue: hardware scope covers processing, input/output and supporting infrastructure; power and cooling are easy to forget.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets); ISACA CISA Review Manual, 28th Edition, Chapter 4 (Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hardware component categorization per ISACA Information Systems Audit and Assurance Standards'. Public sources: ISACA. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IT operations manager receives a critical vendor security patch for production database servers. Which action BEST reflects sound patch management?

options.A: Test it in staging, then deploy with a rollback plan
options.B: Upgrade to the next major database release instead
options.C: Hold it until the next annual hardware refresh
options.D: Install it on production at once to close the exposure

questions.key_concept: Patch management applies vendor fixes on a managed schedule with testing, change control and rollback; urgency shortens testing but never removes it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh speed against the risk of an untested change. Ask what an emergency process still requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Patch management applies vendor fixes on a managed basis: assess, test in a representative environment, deploy through change control and keep a rollback plan. Even critical patches can break production systems. Installing at once closes the exposure fastest, but an untested patch on a production database can cause an outage worse than the vulnerability; urgent patches get expedited testing, not none.

wrong_explanations.B: A major version upgrade is a separate project with its own risks. It does not apply the vendor's security fix in a controlled way.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a hardware refresh leaves a critical vulnerability open for months. Patching is unrelated to hardware replacement.
wrong_explanations.D: Untested patches can break production. Critical patches warrant expedited testing and emergency change control, not deployment with no testing or rollback.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps a fix for a risky upgrade, and C leaves the vulnerability open for months.
Final two: A beats D because even critical patches need testing and rollback; urgency shortens the process but does not skip it.
Exam cue: change control applies even in emergencies; prefer expedited testing over untested deployment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 (Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning); ITIL 4 Change Enablement practice; NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Patch management PRIMARY purpose per NIST SP 800-40 and ITIL 4'. Public sources: NIST, ITIL 4, ISACA. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A release manager is bundling twelve approved changes into a weekend deployment. Which activity is the release manager's PRIMARY responsibility?

options.A: Recording developer contributions for appraisals
options.B: Testing the combined package before go-live
options.C: Approving each individual change for production
options.D: Drafting customer marketing for the new features

questions.key_concept: Release management plans, builds, tests and deploys a coordinated package of approved changes; change management authorizes each change individually.
questions.pre_read: Note the changes are already approved. Separate authorizing a change from delivering a package.
questions.correct_explanation: Release management plans, builds, tests and deploys a coordinated package of changes with a defined scope and schedule. Testing the combined package matters because changes that pass alone can conflict together. Approving individual changes is a change management activity; here the changes are already approved, so the release manager's job is to make the bundle work as a whole.

wrong_explanations.A: Tracking individual contributions is a performance management activity unrelated to controlling what reaches production.
wrong_explanations.C: Approval of individual changes belongs to change management and has already happened. Release management integrates and tests the approved changes as one package.
wrong_explanations.D: Marketing announcements are a communications task. They do not plan, test or deploy the release.

tips: Eliminate: D is marketing and A is performance management; neither controls the release.
Final two: B beats C because the changes are already approved; release management tests them together as one package.
Exam cue: change management authorizes each change; release management plans, tests and deploys the bundle.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Release Management practice; ITIL 4 Deployment Management practice; COBIT 2019 BAI07 (Managed IT Change Acceptance and Transitioning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Release management PRIMARY purpose per ITIL 4 Release Management practice'. Public sources: ITIL 4, ISACA. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A data center manager wants to reduce unplanned server hardware failures. Which practice would BEST achieve this?

options.A: Hot spares that take over automatically when a server fails
options.B: Running hardware to failure, then replacing it promptly
options.C: Telemetry monitoring with trend analysis of early failure signs
options.D: Quarterly full shutdowns for manual visual inspection

questions.key_concept: Proactive hardware maintenance uses telemetry and failure trend analysis to replace degrading components in planned windows; redundancy reduces impact, not frequency.
questions.pre_read: Note the objective is fewer failures, not shorter outages. Ask which option acts before a failure.
questions.correct_explanation: Proactive maintenance uses hardware telemetry, such as disk health counters and environmental sensors, with trend analysis to spot degrading components and replace them in planned windows, cutting unplanned failures. Hot spares are valuable resilience, but they act after a failure: they limit its impact without making it any less likely, so the failure rate stays the same.

wrong_explanations.A: Hot spares reduce outage impact after a failure but do not reduce the number of failures, which is the stated objective.
wrong_explanations.B: Run-to-failure accepts every unplanned failure by design. It is the opposite of the stated objective.
wrong_explanations.D: Quarterly shutdowns cause planned outages, and visual checks miss most degradation signals that continuous telemetry detects.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts failures by design, and D adds outages while missing most warning signs.
Final two: C beats A because monitoring prevents failures; hot spares only soften their impact.
Exam cue: match the objective; reducing failures needs predictive, preventive controls, while reducing impact needs redundancy.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 MA-6 (Timely Maintenance); COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Proactive hardware maintenance per ISACA Hardware Lifecycle guidance and ITIL 4'. Public sources: ISACA, ITIL 4. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor is reviewing the production job scheduler. Which test provides the BEST evidence that scheduled jobs run as the business intends?

options.A: Check the schedule against agreed business requirements quarterly
options.B: Review the failed-job log for the past quarter's batch runs
options.C: Interview the scheduler administrator about job dependencies
options.D: Measure nightly jobs executed against the capacity plan

questions.key_concept: Scheduler reviews compare jobs with approved business requirements, catching unauthorized or mis-sequenced jobs that never appear in failure logs.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence compares actual jobs against an authoritative baseline, rather than showing only failures or opinions.
questions.correct_explanation: Comparing the schedule with approved business requirements tests whether the right jobs run, in the right order, at the right time, which is the scheduler's purpose. A failed-job log is useful operational evidence, but it shows only what broke; a job that runs successfully yet was never authorized, or runs in the wrong sequence, never appears there.

wrong_explanations.B: Failure logs show jobs that broke, not whether successful jobs were authorized or correctly sequenced against business needs.
wrong_explanations.C: An interview is testimonial evidence from the person who runs the scheduler, so it is weaker than comparing records with requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: Measuring jobs against the capacity plan addresses performance planning, not whether the jobs themselves are correct and authorized.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on testimony from the scheduler owner, and D measures capacity rather than job correctness.
Final two: A beats B because a baseline of approved requirements reveals unauthorized or mis-sequenced jobs that run without failing.
Exam cue: the best evidence compares what happens with an approved baseline; exception logs show only what broke.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Job scheduling reviews per ISACA Job Scheduling Audit guidance'. Public sources: ISACA. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that each application team grants access through its own local roles, with no common role definitions. Which recommendation is MOST effective?

options.A: Require the CISO to approve every individual access request
options.B: Track each application's user accounts in a shared spreadsheet
options.C: Enforce standard roles centrally through access control software
options.D: Have each application team recertify its own users every quarter

questions.key_concept: Access control software enforces standard roles consistently across applications; local recertification is detective and lacks independence.
questions.pre_read: Identify the root issue in the stem, then ask whether each option prevents it or merely detects it later.
questions.correct_explanation: Central access control software lets the organization define standard roles once and enforce them consistently, which supports least privilege and segregation-of-duties checks across applications. Quarterly recertification by each team is a useful detective step, but it leaves inconsistent local roles in place and has the granting team review its own decisions, so independence and consistency are both missing.

wrong_explanations.A: A single approver for every request creates a bottleneck and relies on personal judgment, not a consistent role-based policy that scales.
wrong_explanations.B: A spreadsheet records accounts but enforces nothing and quickly becomes stale, so it does not govern access.
wrong_explanations.D: Recertification detects errors after access is granted, and the team that granted access reviews itself, so inconsistent roles persist.

tips: Eliminate: A routes every grant through one person, and B documents accounts without enforcing any rule.
Final two: C beats D because centrally enforced roles prevent the inconsistency, while self-recertification only detects it later.
Exam cue: when the root issue is inconsistency across many systems, prefer a central preventive control over local detective reviews.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS05 (Managed Security Services); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.15 (Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Access control software governance per ISACA Access Control Software guidance and COBIT 2019 DSS05'. Public sources: ISACA, COBIT 2019, NIST SP 800-53. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Source Code Management. Production Code Custody
questions.question: A development manager keeps production source code only on developers' workstations, with no shared repository. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Back up each developer workstation nightly to a central file server
options.B: Move the code into a protected version-controlled repository
options.C: Email the latest source archive to every developer weekly
options.D: Recover source code from production binaries when needed

questions.key_concept: Production source code needs an authoritative, access-controlled repository with change history; backups of local copies protect availability only.
questions.pre_read: Separate integrity from availability. Ask which option gives one trusted version and a record of every change.
questions.correct_explanation: A version-controlled repository gives one authoritative copy of the code, a full change history and access controls, so integrity and availability are both protected and production builds can be traced to source. Nightly workstation backups help availability, but they copy unreviewed local versions, keep no reliable history of who changed what, and leave the code without access control.

wrong_explanations.A: Backups preserve copies but not an authoritative version, change history or access control, so code integrity remains unprotected.
wrong_explanations.C: Emailing archives spreads the code widely without access control and still provides no authoritative version or history.
wrong_explanations.D: Decompiled binaries lose comments and structure, and cannot be shown to match any approved source version.

tips: Eliminate: C spreads the code without access control, and D rebuilds source from binaries, which cannot prove integrity.
Final two: B beats A because a repository protects integrity and history, while backups only copy whatever each workstation holds.
Exam cue: for source code, look for one authoritative, access-controlled version with history; copies alone protect availability, not integrity.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.4 (Access to Source Code); SLSA v1.0 (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts); OWASP SAMM (Software Assurance Maturity Model)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Source code custody per ISACA Source Code Management guidance and SLSA framework'. Public sources: ISACA, SLSA, OWASP SAMM. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A vendor has announced a license audit, and the IT asset manager plans to rely on procurement records to show compliance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Present the procurement records to the vendor as proof of compliance
options.B: Buy an enterprise-wide license to cover any shortfall
options.C: Ask the vendor to postpone the audit until next year
options.D: Reconcile the software found installed with purchased entitlements

questions.key_concept: License compliance requires reconciling discovered installations with purchased entitlements; procurement records show only purchases.
questions.pre_read: Ask what compliance compares. Which option measures both what was bought and what is actually installed?
questions.correct_explanation: Compliance depends on what is actually installed and used compared with what the organization is entitled to run. Reconciling discovered installations to entitlements shows the true position and any gap before the vendor finds it. Procurement records are useful input, but they show only what was bought, not what was deployed, copied or left running after staff moved on.

wrong_explanations.A: Procurement shows purchases, not deployments, so unlicensed installations go unseen until the vendor finds them.
wrong_explanations.B: Blanket buying wastes money and is decided without knowing the actual shortfall, if any exists.
wrong_explanations.C: Postponing delays the exposure without measuring it, and contracts usually give the vendor audit rights.

tips: Eliminate: B spends money before the gap is known, and C delays the audit without measuring anything.
Final two: D beats A because compliance compares deployed software with entitlements, and purchase records show only one side.
Exam cue: license compliance reconciles two sides, what is installed and what is entitled; one side alone proves nothing.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 IT Asset Management practice; COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets); ISO/IEC 19770-1 (Software Asset Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Software license compliance per ISACA Software License Compliance guidance and ITIL 4'. Public sources: ISACA, ITIL 4. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that developers can run a raw-disk editing utility on production servers without approval. Which control is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Log each developer's utility sessions for monthly review
options.B: Uninstall administrative utilities from every production server
options.C: Limit the utility to named administrators via approved requests
options.D: Share one utility password with the support team for emergencies

questions.key_concept: Utilities that bypass application controls need preventive least-privilege access for named administrators, separate from developer roles.
questions.pre_read: Notice who has the access. Ask which option removes the risky access rather than watching it.
questions.correct_explanation: Powerful utilities can bypass application controls, so access should be preventive: limited to named administrators, granted through an approved request, and kept separate from developer roles. Logging developer sessions for monthly review is a sensible detective layer, but it still lets developers alter production data directly and finds misuse weeks after the damage is done.

wrong_explanations.A: Monthly log review detects misuse after it happens and leaves developers with direct production access, so segregation of duties is still broken.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing the tools blocks legitimate support and recovery work, so administrators would look for riskier workarounds.
wrong_explanations.D: A shared password removes individual accountability and widens access instead of restricting it.

tips: Eliminate: B blocks legitimate operations, and D shares one credential, destroying accountability.
Final two: C beats A because preventive restriction removes the developer access, while monthly log review only finds misuse afterwards.
Exam cue: for tools that bypass application controls, prefer named, approved, least-privilege access over detective review alone.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.18 (Use of Privileged Utility Programs); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); COBIT 2019 DSS01 (Managed Operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Utility program governance per ISACA Utility Programs guidance and NIST SP 800-53 AC-6'. Public sources: ISACA, NIST. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Service desk agents keep rediscovering the same workaround for a recurring fault whose permanent fix is months away. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep each related incident open until the permanent fix is deployed
options.B: Record a known error with its workaround for the service desk
options.C: Send every recurrence to the problem team for fresh analysis
options.D: Apply the permanent fix in production without change approval

questions.key_concept: When a root cause is known but unfixed, problem management records a known error and workaround so incidents are resolved quickly.
questions.pre_read: The cause is understood and a fix is planned. Ask what stops agents solving the same incident from scratch.
questions.correct_explanation: A recurring fault with a known workaround and a planned fix is a known error. Recording it with the workaround lets agents restore service quickly and consistently while problem management tracks the permanent fix. Sending each recurrence for fresh analysis sounds thorough, but the cause is already understood, so repeated investigation wastes effort and slows restoration.

wrong_explanations.A: Holding incidents open until the fix lands leaves users without service for months, although a working workaround already exists.
wrong_explanations.C: The root cause is already known; reanalysing each recurrence duplicates work and delays restoration without adding knowledge.
wrong_explanations.D: Even urgent fixes go through change control, using the emergency route if needed; bypassing approval risks a production failure.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves users down despite a workaround, and D bypasses change control.
Final two: B beats C because the cause is already known; a known error record reuses that knowledge instead of repeating analysis.
Exam cue: known cause plus workaround means a known error record; restore service first, fix permanently through change control.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the network team learns of outages only when users call the service desk. Which tool would MOST improve detection?

options.A: Performance monitoring with threshold-based alerts
options.B: Configuration management with nightly backups
options.C: Hourly manual ping checks logged in a spreadsheet
options.D: Quarterly user surveys on network quality

questions.key_concept: Network performance monitoring with alerts detects outages proactively; configuration management controls device settings, not live availability.
questions.pre_read: Name the gap in the stem first: detection. Then ask which tool actually watches the network in real time.
questions.correct_explanation: Network performance monitoring polls devices and links continuously and alerts operators when thresholds are breached, so issues are found before users call. Configuration management is valuable for controlling changes and restoring device settings, but it does not watch live performance or availability, so it would not have told the team about the outages any sooner.

wrong_explanations.B: Configuration backups help recovery and change control but do not watch live traffic or device health, so outages would still go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Manual hourly checks miss short outages, do not scale and still depend on a person noticing.
wrong_explanations.D: Surveys collect opinions long after events, which is still detection by users.

tips: Eliminate: C is manual and infrequent, and D still relies on users to report problems.
Final two: A beats B because monitoring with alerts detects live failures, while configuration management controls settings, not availability.
Exam cue: match the tool to the gap; a detection gap needs continuous monitoring and alerting, not configuration control.

questions.question: A monthly vendor patch release includes one critical flaw that attackers are actively exploiting. Which approach should the IT operations manager take as BEST?

options.A: Deploy every patch to production within 24 hours
options.B: Hold the patches for the annual maintenance window
options.C: Expedite the critical patch and test the rest as usual
options.D: Test the whole release together, then deploy it next month

questions.key_concept: Patch management is risk-tiered: actively exploited critical flaws are expedited, routine patches follow the standard tested cycle.
questions.pre_read: Notice that one flaw is actively exploited. Ask whether every patch deserves the same speed.
questions.correct_explanation: Patch handling should be risk-tiered. An actively exploited critical flaw justifies an expedited path with abbreviated testing, while routine patches follow the normal test-and-deploy cycle under change control. Testing the whole release together is orderly, but it leaves a known, exploited weakness open for another month, so the business carries an avoidable and immediate risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Rushing every patch skips testing for low-risk fixes and invites outages without any security benefit for them.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting up to a year leaves an actively exploited flaw open, an unacceptable exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Bundled testing is orderly, but it keeps an exploited flaw open for a month when an expedited path exists.

tips: Eliminate: A rushes low-risk patches without testing, and B leaves an exploited flaw open for up to a year.
Final two: C beats D because an actively exploited flaw needs the expedited path, while routine patches can follow normal testing.
Exam cue: in patching, risk sets the speed; active exploitation moves a patch to the emergency path, still under change control.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds each approved component of a payroll upgrade went live separately over three weeks, with no combined build, test or rollback plan. Which ITIL 4 practice is MOST clearly lacking?

options.A: Change enablement
options.B: Service continuity management
options.C: Service level management
options.D: Release management

questions.key_concept: Change enablement assesses and authorizes individual changes; release management coordinates packaging, testing and rollout of multiple changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice the changes were already approved. Ask which practice owns coordinating them into one release.
questions.correct_explanation: Release management plans and coordinates how a set of changes is packaged, tested and made available, including rollback. Here each change was approved, so change enablement worked as designed: it assessed risk and authorized each change individually. What was missing was the coordinated plan for deploying them together, which is the release management practice's job.

wrong_explanations.A: Each change was approved, so change enablement did its job. The gap is coordinating them as one package.
wrong_explanations.B: Service continuity management prepares for disaster recovery, not for how a set of changes is built, tested and rolled out.
wrong_explanations.C: Service level management agrees and tracks service targets; it does not plan deployments.

tips: Eliminate: B is about disaster recovery, and C is about agreed service targets, not deployments.
Final two: D beats A because the changes were already approved; packaging, testing and rolling them out together is release management's role.
Exam cue: change enablement authorizes individual changes; release management coordinates many changes into one planned, tested deployment.

questions.subtopic: Operational Log Management. Types and Coverage
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that application logs are retained, but operating system and database logs are overwritten daily. Which recommendation is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Forward the existing application logs to a write-once archive
options.B: Retain OS and database logs under a retention policy
options.C: Raise the verbosity level of application logging
options.D: Keep every log from every system indefinitely

questions.key_concept: Log management needs coverage across layers, including OS and database, retained under a defined policy before integrity measures matter.
questions.pre_read: Identify which logs are missing. Ask whether each option closes that gap or improves something already in place.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap is coverage: operating system and database logs record privileged actions and data changes that application logs never see, and daily overwriting destroys that evidence. Retaining them under a defined policy restores the trail. Write-once storage for application logs strengthens integrity, but it protects records the organization already keeps while the missing sources remain lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Write-once storage protects the integrity of application logs, but the OS and database evidence is still overwritten daily.
wrong_explanations.C: More application detail does not capture privileged OS or database activity, so the coverage gap remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Keeping everything forever ignores retention policy, cost and privacy limits, and makes review harder.

tips: Eliminate: C adds detail to a source already kept, and D drops any retention policy.
Final two: B beats A because the stated gap is missing log sources, and integrity protection for existing logs does not close it.
Exam cue: coverage gaps need more log sources, not stronger protection of the sources already kept.

questions.question: A security operations manager forwards raw logs from many sources to the SIEM, but alerts that rely on events from several sources rarely fire. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Log retention is set to ninety days
options.B: Logs stream in real time, not in batches
options.C: Events are not normalized to a common schema
options.D: No threat-intelligence feeds are integrated

questions.key_concept: SIEM correlation depends on normalizing events to a common schema so fields from different sources can be matched.
questions.pre_read: Focus on what fails: alerts that need several sources. Ask what a rule needs to link events together.
questions.correct_explanation: Correlation rules match fields such as user, host and address across sources. If raw events keep each vendor's own format, the same user or host appears under different field names, so multi-source rules cannot link them. Missing threat-intelligence feeds reduce matching against known indicators, but they would not stop correlation between the organization's own log sources.

wrong_explanations.A: Ninety days of retention still covers the short windows correlation rules use, so it does not explain missed alerts.
wrong_explanations.B: Real-time streaming helps detection; it does not prevent correlation across sources.
wrong_explanations.D: Threat feeds enrich alerts with known indicators, but internal cross-source correlation works without them.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns how long logs are kept, and B describes a benefit, not a fault.
Final two: C beats D because cross-source rules need a common field format, while threat feeds only add external indicators.
Exam cue: when correlation fails across sources, check normalization first; rules cannot match fields that are named differently.

questions.subtopic: Patch Deferral Decision in Regulated Context
questions.question: IT operations wants to defer a critical, exploitable Java patch on a legacy claims system because the vendor cannot confirm compatibility. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Defer with compensating controls and risk acceptance by the business owner
options.B: Deploy the patch at once with a tested rollback plan ready
options.C: Approve the deferral, since network segmentation already protects the system
options.D: Refer the patching decision to the audit committee to resolve

questions.key_concept: A patch deferral needs compensating controls and documented, time-bound risk acceptance by the accountable business owner.
questions.pre_read: Weigh both risks: exploitation and outage. Then ask who should own the decision to accept what remains.
questions.correct_explanation: When a critical patch cannot be applied safely yet, the accepted route is a time-limited deferral with compensating controls, such as isolation and heightened monitoring, plus documented risk acceptance by the accountable business owner while testing proceeds. Deploying at once honours the severity, but on a legacy system with unconfirmed compatibility it could halt claims processing, trading one serious risk for another.

wrong_explanations.B: A rollback plan helps, but untested compatibility on a critical legacy system risks a business outage that management has not weighed.
wrong_explanations.C: Relying on existing segmentation skips analysis of the new exposure and leaves no accountable owner accepting the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: The audit committee oversees; the business owner decides operational risk, and the auditor should advise rather than hand off.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes existing controls suffice with no accountable acceptance, and D hands an operational decision to an oversight body.
Final two: A beats B because management accepts a bounded, compensated risk instead of an untested change on a critical system.
Exam cue: when a fix cannot be applied safely, look for compensating controls plus documented acceptance by the risk owner.
