questions.question: Two days after a hospital network's DR failover test, threat hunters find attacker activity in the DR environment. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Preserve the DR snapshots and logs as forensic evidence
options.B: Rebuild the DR environment to restore recovery capability
options.C: Notify affected patients before any investigation begins
options.D: Proceed with the next scheduled DR test as planned

questions.key_concept: When an intrusion is found, preserve evidence before rebuilding; a rebuild can run in parallel on clean infrastructure, never on the compromised images.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a rebuild would destroy. Production is running, so check how urgent restoring DR really is.
questions.correct_explanation: The DR snapshots are the only record of what the attacker did, including whether patient data was taken. Preserving them first protects the forensic investigation and the breach-notification decision. Rebuilding DR is important, and can then proceed in parallel on clean infrastructure, but rebuilding first on the compromised environment destroys the evidence while production is still running normally.

wrong_explanations.B: Rebuilding first wipes the evidence needed to scope the intrusion and any PHI exposure, while production is still running.
wrong_explanations.C: Breach notification follows a reasonable investigation of what was accessed. Notifying before any investigation risks inaccurate notices.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing on a compromised environment ignores an active security incident and may spread or mask the intrusion.

tips: Eliminate: C notifies before knowing what was accessed, and D carries on as if no incident exists.
Final two: A beats B because evidence lost to a rebuild cannot be recovered, while DR can be rebuilt in parallel.
Exam cue: in incident response, preserve evidence before you change or rebuild the affected systems.

questions.question: An IT operations manager must return leased backup disks that held confidential data to the lessor. Which sanitization approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Quick-format the disks before handing them back
options.B: Physically destroy the disks and reimburse the lessor
options.C: Purge the disks with a verified, media-appropriate method
options.D: Delete the backup files through the operating system

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-88 matches Clear, Purge or Destroy to data sensitivity and whether media leaves organizational control, then verifies the result.
questions.pre_read: Note two facts: confidential data, and the disks leave your control. Ask which method fits both.
questions.correct_explanation: Media leaving organizational control after holding confidential data needs a Purge-level method suited to the medium, such as cryptographic erase or a firmware sanitize command, with the result verified and documented. Physical destruction is the strongest option and would protect the data, but it is more than the situation requires and breaches the lease, when a verified Purge already makes the data unrecoverable.

wrong_explanations.A: A quick format only rewrites file-system structures. The underlying data stays recoverable with common tools.
wrong_explanations.B: Destruction protects the data but exceeds what the case requires and breaks the lease, when a verified Purge suffices.
wrong_explanations.D: Operating-system deletion removes file references only. The data remains on the disk and can be recovered.

tips: Eliminate: A and D leave the data recoverable, since formatting and deletion do not sanitize media.
Final two: C beats B because a verified Purge protects data leaving your control without destroying leased assets.
Exam cue: choose the sanitization method by sensitivity and destination, not automatically the most extreme one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2 (Guidelines for Media Sanitization); ISO/IEC 27040 (Storage Security); LTO Consortium technical specifications
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Backup media types and sanitization per NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1'. Public sources: NIST, ISO/IEC, LTO Consortium. No legacy bank citation. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A business continuity manager excludes reputational damage from the BIA because it cannot be measured precisely. Which response from the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Agree, since reputational disruption mainly affects financial firms
options.B: Agree, since BIAs should cover quantifiable losses alone
options.C: Refer reputation to the PR team's crisis communications plan
options.D: Recommend assessing it through proxies such as customer attrition

questions.key_concept: Reputational damage is a real disruption impact; a BIA assesses it through measurable proxies such as customer attrition, revenue loss and regulator scrutiny.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether hard-to-measure means unmeasurable. Then ask where impacts must be captured to set recovery priorities.
questions.correct_explanation: Reputational damage drives real losses, such as customer attrition, lost revenue, partner withdrawal and regulatory scrutiny, so it belongs in the BIA, assessed through such proxies or qualitative scales. Leaving it out understates impact and can mis-rank recovery priorities. Crisis communications are an essential response, but they address how to react, not how severe the impact is, so they cannot replace its assessment in the BIA.

wrong_explanations.A: Every sector depends on customer and partner trust. Reputational impact is not confined to financial services.
wrong_explanations.B: BIAs routinely use qualitative scales alongside financial figures. Excluding hard-to-quantify impacts understates total business impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Crisis communications are a response measure. They do not assess the impact that sets recovery priorities in the BIA.

tips: Eliminate: A confines reputation to one sector, and B wrongly limits BIAs to quantified losses.
Final two: D beats C because impact must be assessed in the BIA, while communications are only the response.
Exam cue: hard to measure does not mean out of scope; BIAs use proxies and qualitative scales.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 Clause 8.2.2 (Business Impact Analysis); BCI Good Practice Guidelines 2023 PP3 (Analysis)

questions.question: An IS auditor finds backup tapes pass between operators, couriers and the offsite vault with no signed record at each handover. Which control is MOST important to add?

options.A: Itemized receipts acknowledged by both parties at transfer
options.B: Locked, tamper-evident cases for each tape shipment
options.C: Longer retention periods for tapes held at the vault
options.D: More frequent courier pickups from the data center

questions.key_concept: Chain of custody for backup media needs an itemized, acknowledged record at each transfer, so a loss can be traced to a point and party.
questions.pre_read: Picture a tape going missing. Ask which control shows where, and with whom, it was last seen.
questions.correct_explanation: Without an acknowledged record at each transfer, a missing tape cannot be traced to the point or party where it went astray, and nobody is accountable. Itemized receipts close that chain of custody. Locked, tamper-evident cases protect tapes in transit, but they show only whether a case was opened, not which tapes it held or who had it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tamper-evident cases deter interference in transit but record neither the tapes inside nor who held them, so custody stays unproven.
wrong_explanations.C: Retention length governs how long tapes are kept, not whether their movements are recorded.
wrong_explanations.D: More pickups move tapes offsite sooner but multiply undocumented handovers, widening the custody gap.

tips: Eliminate: C changes retention, and D adds more undocumented transfers.
Final two: A beats B because custody needs an accountable record per transfer; a sealed case proves nothing about who held which tape.
Exam cue: chain of custody means a documented, acknowledged record at every handover of evidence or media.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that IT set its recovery time objectives without input from business process owners. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: IT staff may be unaware of the plan's contents
options.B: Recovery priorities may not reflect business criticality
options.C: Plan documents may grow too long to maintain
options.D: IT may lack the budget to meet its own objectives

questions.key_concept: IT continuity derives from business continuity: the BIA sets what matters and how fast; IT plans how technology delivers it.
questions.pre_read: Ask where recovery time objectives should come from. Then ask what happens if that source is skipped.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery objectives should come from a business impact analysis owned by the business, because only process owners know what downtime the business can tolerate. Without their input, IT may restore the wrong systems first or too slowly. Budget shortfalls are a real feasibility concern, but they matter only after the right objectives exist; well-funded recovery of the wrong priorities still fails the business.

wrong_explanations.A: IT set the objectives itself, so it is likely aware of them. The gap is missing business input, not IT awareness.
wrong_explanations.C: Document length is a maintenance concern. It does not cause recovery to fail to meet business needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Funding matters for feasibility, but even fully funded objectives fail if they target the wrong business priorities.

tips: Eliminate: A contradicts the stem, since IT wrote the objectives, and C is a documentation concern.
Final two: B beats D because objectives must first match business needs; funding the wrong objectives still fails.
Exam cue: business impact analysis comes before IT strategy; IT recovery objectives without business input are the red flag.

questions.question: A firm retires a cloud object-storage bucket that held regulated backups encrypted with customer-managed keys. Which sanitization evidence should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: The backup schedule showing each data set's retention period
options.B: A provider certificate of physical drive shredding
options.C: Console logs showing every object was deleted
options.D: Logs confirming destruction of the customer-managed keys

questions.key_concept: In shared cloud storage, cryptographic erase by destroying customer-managed keys is the practical sanitization method; evidence is the logged key destruction.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the customer can reach the physical drives. Then ask what makes every copy unreadable, including replicas.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloud object storage spreads data across shared drives and replicas the customer cannot touch. Destroying the customer-managed keys is a cryptographic erase: every copy, including replicas and snapshots, becomes unreadable. Logs of key destruction are therefore the best evidence. Deleting objects in the console is a reasonable step, but it is a logical deletion and does not prove that replicas or provider-side copies are gone.

wrong_explanations.A: A schedule shows planned retention, not that sanitization happened. It is not evidence of disposal.
wrong_explanations.B: Drives in multi-tenant cloud storage are shared and not tied to one customer, so bucket-specific shredding is not feasible.
wrong_explanations.C: Console deletion is logical only. Replicas, versions or provider-side copies may remain readable.

tips: Eliminate: A is a plan rather than disposal evidence, and B is infeasible for shared multi-tenant drives.
Final two: D beats C because key destruction renders every copy unreadable, while console deletion is only logical.
Exam cue: for cloud data you cannot physically reach, cryptographic erase through key destruction is the sanitization answer.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the only periodic control over offsite backups is an annual review of the vendor contract. Which additional procedure would BEST show that backups remain usable?

options.A: Daily confirmation that each scheduled backup job completed
options.B: Annual renegotiation of the vendor's service levels
options.C: Quarterly restores from a sample of offsite media
options.D: Replacement of offsite tapes with continuous replication

questions.key_concept: Only a restore from the stored media proves a backup is usable; job logs and contracts show activity, not recoverability.
questions.pre_read: The stem asks what shows backups are usable. Separate evidence that a job ran from evidence that data comes back.
questions.correct_explanation: Restoring data from a sample of the media actually held offsite is the only procedure that proves the backups can be read and used in a recovery. Running it on a quarterly cadence gives ongoing assurance between contract reviews. Daily job-completion checks are valuable, but a job can finish successfully while writing unreadable or incomplete media, so they show activity rather than recoverability.

wrong_explanations.A: Job completion confirms the backup ran, not that the media can be restored. Corrupt or incomplete media still report a successful job.
wrong_explanations.B: Renegotiating service levels improves the contract but produces no evidence that any stored backup can be recovered.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing the architecture does not test anything, and continuous replication can copy corruption or ransomware straight to the second site.

tips: Eliminate: B only changes contract terms, and D swaps technology without producing any recovery evidence.
Final two: C beats A because a restore proves usability, while a completed job only proves the backup ran.
Exam cue: when asked what proves a backup works, pick the restore test over logs, contracts or monitoring.

questions.question: An IS auditor is planning an audit of a third-party offsite media storage vendor that provides a current SOC 2 report. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Assess the report's scope against our risks and test gaps
options.B: Rely on the report's unqualified opinion without any further testing
options.C: Limit the work to contract terms and insurance certificates
options.D: Photograph the facility during an unannounced site visit

questions.key_concept: Another assurer's report is usable evidence only after the auditor confirms its scope, period and controls cover the risks being audited.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the SOC 2 report was written for your risks. What must an auditor check before relying on someone else's work?
questions.correct_explanation: Before relying on a service auditor's report, the IS auditor must evaluate whether its scope, period and tested controls match the risks that matter to this engagement, such as chain of custody and environmental protection for the firm's media. Areas the report does not cover need the auditor's own testing. Accepting the opinion without that evaluation treats an unread scope as if it covered everything.

wrong_explanations.B: An unqualified opinion covers only the controls in the report's scope. Without checking that scope, the auditor cannot know whether key storage risks were tested.
wrong_explanations.C: Contracts and insurance show obligations and financial cover, not whether media are physically protected, tracked and recoverable.
wrong_explanations.D: Photographs capture appearance on one day. They do not test custody records, environmental controls or restore capability.

tips: Eliminate: C reviews paperwork rather than controls, and D gathers a single-day impression rather than control evidence.
Final two: A beats B because relying on another assurer's work first requires confirming its scope fits your risks.
Exam cue: when a SOC report is offered, the auditor's next step is to evaluate its scope and period, not accept it.

questions.question: During a business continuity audit, an IS auditor interviews recovery team members. Which interview approach would MOST effectively reveal gaps between the written plan and real readiness?

options.A: Asking whether the plan has been documented and tested
options.B: Interviewing the plan coordinator in place of team members
options.C: Walking members through their plan section for confirmation
options.D: Asking members to describe their duties without the plan

questions.key_concept: Unaided recall of roles, triggers and contacts tests real readiness; guided walkthroughs mostly test agreement with the document.
questions.pre_read: Think about what an interview can prove that the document cannot. Which question would expose a member who never read the plan?
questions.correct_explanation: Asking team members to explain their own duties, activation triggers and contacts without the document shows whether the plan lives in people's heads, which is what matters at 3 a.m. during a disaster. Walking them through their section looks thorough, but it invites people to nod along with text in front of them, so it confirms the document rather than their readiness.

wrong_explanations.A: Yes or no questions on documentation and testing produce self-attestation. They repeat what document review already shows and reveal nothing about readiness.
wrong_explanations.B: The coordinator knows the plan best, so interviewing only that person hides whether line managers and technical staff can perform their roles.
wrong_explanations.C: With the text in front of them, members tend to agree with it. The walkthrough tests the document, not whether they could act unaided.

tips: Eliminate: A gathers self-attestation that documents already show, and B samples only the person who wrote the plan.
Final two: D beats C because unaided recall tests readiness, while a guided walkthrough invites agreement with the text.
Exam cue: interviews add value when they test what people can do in practice, not what the paper says.

questions.question: A business continuity manager is building crisis communications capability into the continuity plan. Which element is MOST important to have in place before any incident occurs?

options.A: Statements drafted by legal once an incident is classified
options.B: Named, trained spokespersons using pre-approved message templates
options.C: A rule of no external comment until root cause is known
options.D: Permission for any employee to respond on social media

questions.key_concept: Crisis communication speed depends on pre-event preparation: named spokespersons and pre-approved templates allow a fast, single-voice response.
questions.pre_read: The stem stresses before an incident. Which element can only help if it was prepared in advance?
questions.correct_explanation: Named spokespersons and pre-approved templates let the organization speak quickly, consistently and with one voice in the first hours, when silence fuels speculation. Legal review matters, but drafting statements only after an incident is classified pushes the first message back by hours and leaves the organization improvising under pressure. Preparation done before the event is what makes rapid, accurate communication possible.

wrong_explanations.A: Legal input is valuable, but starting drafts after classification wastes the critical early hours. Templates should already be legally reviewed before any event.
wrong_explanations.C: Root cause can take days or weeks. Silence that long lets rumours define the story and damages stakeholder trust.
wrong_explanations.D: Uncoordinated posts create conflicting messages and may disclose sensitive details. Crisis communication needs a single, controlled voice.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves stakeholders without information for too long, and D destroys the single voice crisis communication needs.
Final two: B beats A because preparation before the event enables speed, while drafting after classification loses the first hours.
Exam cue: for crisis communication, the best answer prepares people and messages before the event, then speaks early with one voice.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22361 (Crisis Management — Guidelines); ISO 22301:2019 Clause 8.4.3 (Warning and Communication); BCI Good Practice Guidelines 2023 PP4 (Design); DRII Professional Practice 9 (Crisis Communications)

questions.question: A business continuity manager must prepare for severe disruptions that the risk assessment cannot foresee. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Build impact-based capabilities that work regardless of the cause
options.B: Write detailed response plans for each predicted extreme scenario
options.C: Increase insurance cover to offset losses from unforeseen events
options.D: Treat unforeseeable events as residual risk outside the plan

questions.key_concept: Plan for impacts, not causes: loss of people, sites, technology or suppliers can be recovered the same way whatever triggered it.
questions.pre_read: If you cannot predict the event, what can you still plan for? Think about the effect a disruption has, not its source.
questions.correct_explanation: Unforeseeable events cannot be listed in advance, but their impacts can: loss of a site, systems, staff or a key supplier. Capabilities built around those impacts, such as redundancy, delegated authority and flexible recovery options, work whatever the trigger. Writing a plan for each predicted extreme scenario sounds rigorous, but it only covers the events someone imagined, which is exactly what an unforeseeable event is not.

wrong_explanations.B: Scenario-specific plans cover only events someone predicted. The next severe disruption is likely to be one nobody listed.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance transfers part of the financial loss but restores no operations, customers or reputation during the outage.
wrong_explanations.D: Excluding the events most likely to cause severe damage leaves the organization with no prepared response when they happen.

tips: Eliminate: C funds losses without restoring operations, and D drops the most damaging events from planning entirely.
Final two: A beats B because impact-based capability covers any cause, while per-scenario plans only cover predicted events.
Exam cue: when the cause is unknown, choose the option that plans for the impact rather than the specific event.

questions.subtopic: BCI GPG PP1. Policy and Programme Management
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a CEO-signed continuity policy, but no steering group, assigned roles or management reviews. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: The policy wording may omit some critical business units
options.B: Staff may be unaware of where the policy is published
options.C: The policy file may be stored in an unsecured location
options.D: Policy commitments may never become a maintained programme

questions.key_concept: A policy sets intent; governance, roles and management review turn it into a maintained, improving continuity programme.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is missing in the stem: people, structure and review. What happens to a policy that nobody owns?
questions.correct_explanation: A signed policy states intent, but without a steering group, defined roles and periodic management review, nobody is accountable for turning it into plans, resources, tests and updates. The programme simply never happens or decays. A gap in the policy's scope is a real weakness, but it is the kind of issue the missing governance would normally catch and correct, so it is the narrower risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A scope gap is a fixable drafting issue. Without governance, even a perfectly scoped policy would not be implemented or reviewed.
wrong_explanations.B: Awareness of where the policy sits is a minor communication issue compared with having no one accountable for delivering the programme.
wrong_explanations.C: Storage security of a policy document is a low-impact housekeeping matter. It does not affect whether continuity capability exists.

tips: Eliminate: B is a minor awareness issue, and C is document housekeeping with little continuity impact.
Final two: D beats A because missing governance stops the whole programme, while a scope gap is one fixable flaw.
Exam cue: a policy without owners, roles and review is intent only; missing governance outranks a flaw in the wording.

questions.subtopic: BCI GPG PP2. Embedding BCM in Culture
questions.question: A business continuity manager wants continuity thinking to become part of routine decisions across the organization. Which initiative would be MOST effective?

options.A: Annual signed acknowledgment that staff have read the plan
options.B: Restricting plan details to the continuity team to avoid alarm
options.C: Continuity checks built into project and change approvals
options.D: An organization-wide awareness campaign with posters and e-learning

questions.key_concept: Continuity is embedded when it becomes a step in normal business processes, not a separate awareness activity.
questions.pre_read: The stem says routine decisions. Which option changes how work is approved rather than what people are told?
questions.correct_explanation: Building continuity checks into project and change approvals makes resilience a normal step in how the organization decides, so new systems, suppliers and processes are assessed before they go live. An awareness campaign is useful and common, but it raises recognition without changing how decisions are made. Embedding requires continuity to appear inside everyday processes, not alongside them.

wrong_explanations.A: A signed acknowledgment proves receipt of a document. It does not show understanding, and it changes no business decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Hiding the plan prevents the people who must act from knowing their roles, the opposite of embedding continuity.
wrong_explanations.D: Posters and e-learning raise general awareness, but they do not put continuity into the approvals where decisions are actually made.

tips: Eliminate: A tracks document receipt, and B keeps continuity away from the people who must act.
Final two: C beats D because a step inside approvals changes decisions, while a campaign only raises awareness.
Exam cue: to embed a discipline in culture, prefer the option that builds it into normal business processes.

questions.question: IT management proposes contracting a hot site now and completing the business impact analysis later to save time. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Perform a threat and vulnerability assessment of the primary data centre
options.B: Complete the business impact analysis before selecting a site
options.C: Select a warm site now as a lower-cost compromise
options.D: Negotiate hot-site terms with two competing vendors

questions.key_concept: The BIA sets recovery time and point objectives, and those objectives determine which recovery strategy and site are justified.
questions.pre_read: This item tests order. Ask which output tells you how fast recovery must be, and what depends on that answer.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery strategy depends on the recovery time and recovery point objectives that only the business impact analysis produces. Without them, a hot site could be wasted spend or still too slow. Waiting to finish the analysis is the right sequence here. A threat assessment is part of the same analysis phase, but it estimates what could happen, not how quickly each function must return, so it cannot size the site.

wrong_explanations.A: Threat assessment informs likelihood and mitigation, but it does not set recovery time objectives, so it cannot decide which site is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Choosing a cheaper site still selects a strategy before requirements are known. It may fail critical functions' recovery times.
wrong_explanations.D: Negotiating terms commits effort to a solution whose need and tier have not yet been established by the business.

tips: Eliminate: C and D both commit to a recovery site before the business requirements exist.
Final two: B beats A because the BIA sets recovery time objectives, while a threat assessment estimates likelihood, not urgency.
Exam cue: BIA comes before strategy. When a site or solution is chosen first, the BIA is the FIRST fix.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a continuity plan whose only recovery strategy is an IT hot site. Which gap is MOST significant?

options.A: No strategy for staff and suppliers the systems rely on
options.B: No insurance strategy to fund the cost of recovery
options.C: No documented procedure for failback to the primary site
options.D: No upgrade of the hot site to an active-active mirror

questions.key_concept: Continuity strategies must cover every resource a critical activity needs, including people and suppliers, not just technology.
questions.pre_read: Picture the hot site running perfectly. Who operates it, and who supplies the inputs the business still needs?
questions.correct_explanation: A recovered system is useless if no trained staff can operate it and key suppliers cannot deliver, so a technology-only strategy leaves critical activities unrecoverable. Strategies must cover all resources the business impact analysis identifies. A missing failback procedure is a genuine gap, but it matters only after recovery has succeeded, whereas the people and supplier gap stops recovery from working at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Insurance funds losses but restores no capability. Its absence does not prevent critical activities from resuming.
wrong_explanations.C: Failback must be planned, but it comes after recovery. The people and supplier gap prevents recovery from succeeding in the first place.
wrong_explanations.D: An active-active mirror is a technology upgrade that may not be justified by recovery objectives, and it fixes nothing outside IT.

tips: Eliminate: B funds losses without restoring service, and D adds more technology to a strategy that is already technology-only.
Final two: A beats C because missing people and suppliers stop recovery working, while failback matters only after recovery succeeds.
Exam cue: a strategy covering only IT is incomplete; look for the gap in people, premises or suppliers.

questions.question: Management has just approved a new business continuity plan and published it on the intranet. Which action should the business continuity manager take FIRST?

options.A: Schedule a full interruption test of the data centre
options.B: Outsource ongoing plan maintenance to a specialist consultancy
options.C: Run a tabletop exercise with the crisis management team
options.D: Train recovery team members on their assigned roles

questions.key_concept: Implementation comes before validation: people must be trained on their roles before exercises can meaningfully test the plan.
questions.pre_read: Publishing a plan is not implementing it. What must happen before an exercise can test anything useful?
questions.correct_explanation: A newly approved plan is only paper until the people named in it know their roles, so role-based training is the first implementation step. A tabletop exercise is the natural next step and is low risk, but running it before training mostly reveals that participants have not learned the plan, which training would have fixed. Exercises validate a plan that people have already been prepared to use.

wrong_explanations.A: A full interruption test on an untrained team and untried plan risks a real outage. It belongs late in a maturing test programme.
wrong_explanations.B: Outsourcing maintenance leaves the organization without internal ownership of its own plan and does nothing to prepare staff.
wrong_explanations.C: Exercising before training mainly shows that people do not yet know the plan. Training should come first so the exercise tests the plan.

tips: Eliminate: A risks a real outage with an untried plan, and B hands away ownership without preparing anyone.
Final two: D beats C because people must learn their roles before an exercise can test the plan.
Exam cue: the order is approve, train, exercise, then test more aggressively; pick the earliest missing step.

questions.subtopic: Plan Development. Other Issues (Dependencies + Supply Chain)
questions.question: An IS auditor notes that internal systems meet their recovery objectives, but a sole-source payment processor has no tested continuity arrangement. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add outage service credits to the processor's next contract
options.B: Accept the dependency because the vendor bears contractual liability
options.C: Require tested vendor continuity evidence or a second processor
options.D: Shorten internal recovery objectives to offset vendor downtime

questions.key_concept: Continuity planning extends to critical suppliers: the organization needs evidence of their tested recovery or an alternate source.
questions.pre_read: Recovering your own systems is not enough if a single supplier fails. What closes the dependency rather than compensating for it?
questions.correct_explanation: The organization's recovery is only as strong as its critical dependencies, so it needs evidence that the processor's continuity arrangements are tested, or an alternate processor if that assurance cannot be obtained. Service credits look like a sensible contractual control, but they only compensate after an outage and do nothing to keep payments flowing while the processor is down.

wrong_explanations.A: Service credits are a financial remedy. Customers still cannot pay during the outage, so the continuity gap remains.
wrong_explanations.B: Contractual liability does not transfer the operational impact. The organization still loses its payment capability and customer trust.
wrong_explanations.D: Faster internal recovery cannot help when the external processor is unavailable. The bottleneck is outside the organization.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses legal liability with continuity, and D speeds up the part that already works.
Final two: C beats A because assurance or an alternate keeps payments running, while credits only compensate after the outage.
Exam cue: for a critical supplier, prefer evidence of tested continuity or an alternate source over contractual penalties.

questions.question: Four months after an acquisition, the acquired unit is missing from the parent's continuity plan, and a quarterly exercise is due next month. What is the BEST recommendation by the IS auditor?

options.A: Postpone the exercise until a combined plan is completed
options.B: Run the exercise with added acquired-unit gap scenarios
options.C: Run the exercise unchanged using the parent's current plan
options.D: Hire consultants to write a combined plan within 30 days

questions.key_concept: A known integration gap is best surfaced by testing it: extend the scheduled exercise rather than pausing testing or ignoring the gap.
questions.pre_read: Two options keep the exercise and two do not. Which one uses next month's exercise to learn about the new risk?
questions.correct_explanation: Extending the scheduled exercise with scenarios involving the acquired unit keeps the testing cadence and turns the exercise into a way of documenting the integration gaps that the combined plan must close. Postponing until the combined plan exists seems prudent, but it leaves both businesses untested for months during the riskiest period of integration and gives the new plan no evidence to build on.

wrong_explanations.A: Postponing leaves the combined organization untested during integration, when risk is highest, and wastes a chance to gather evidence for the new plan.
wrong_explanations.C: Running the parent's plan unchanged ignores a known gap and could produce false assurance that the combined organization is recoverable.
wrong_explanations.D: A 30-day outsourced plan skips the joint business impact work and builds no internal ownership of the result.

tips: Eliminate: C tests the plan while ignoring the known gap, and D rushes an outsourced plan without the joint BIA.
Final two: B beats A because testing the gap now produces evidence, while postponing leaves months without any test.
Exam cue: when a plan has a known gap, prefer an action that tests and documents it over waiting for perfection.

questions.question: Eighteen hours into a ransomware outage, social media claims the firm is hiding a breach, while forensics is still incomplete. What should the IS auditor advise the CEO to do FIRST?

options.A: Issue a factual statement through the designated spokesperson
options.B: Withhold external comment until forensics confirms any exfiltration
options.C: Post a personal statement with estimated data-impact figures
options.D: Let customer-service agents answer queries in their own words

questions.key_concept: During a crisis, communicate early and factually with one coordinated voice, stating what is known and when updates will follow.
questions.pre_read: Rumours are already spreading. Which option fills the silence without saying more than the facts support?
questions.correct_explanation: A prompt, factual statement through the designated spokesperson, aligned with legal on what is known, fills the information gap and counters the rumour without speculating. It can confirm the outage, the response under way and when the next update will come. Waiting for forensics protects the legal position, but silence while accusations spread lets the rumour define the story and erodes trust.

wrong_explanations.B: Forensics may take days. Silence while accusations circulate looks like concealment, and a factual statement can be made without confirming exfiltration.
wrong_explanations.C: Estimated figures given before forensics may later prove wrong, and bypassing the spokesperson breaks the single coordinated voice.
wrong_explanations.D: Improvised answers produce inconsistent and possibly inaccurate messages that make the crisis worse.

tips: Eliminate: C speculates outside the agreed channel, and D creates many inconsistent voices.
Final two: A beats B because a factual statement counters rumour now, while silence until forensics lets the rumour win.
Exam cue: in a crisis, communicate early with verified facts through one voice; do not wait for full certainty.

questions.question: During a pandemic, a medical device maker's sole-source chip supplier is at 40% capacity, with three weeks of stock left. What is the BEST recommendation by the IS auditor?

options.A: Consolidate remaining chip stock through urgent air freight
options.B: Analyze the supplier's recovery plan before seeking alternatives
options.C: Allocate the remaining units evenly across hospital customers
options.D: Begin qualifying an alternate chip source in parallel

questions.key_concept: A sole-source dependency is a single point of failure; the durable response is to start the long-lead work of qualifying an alternate source.
questions.pre_read: Three weeks is short, but which option still matters after week three? Look for the action that removes the single point of failure.
questions.correct_explanation: The root exposure is a single supplier for a critical component, and qualifying an alternate source has the longest lead time, so it must start now alongside short-term measures. Air-freighting existing stock is a sensible tactical move, but it only buys a few weeks from the same constrained supplier and leaves the single point of failure in place when that stock runs out.

wrong_explanations.A: Air freight speeds delivery of a shrinking supply from the same source. It buys weeks but leaves the sole-source dependency unresolved.
wrong_explanations.B: Analysis spends scarce weeks of stock. With a sole source and three weeks left, alternate qualification must start now regardless of the plan.
wrong_explanations.C: Equal allocation ignores clinical criticality. Scarce units should go first to the uses where shortage would harm patients most.

tips: Eliminate: B spends scarce weeks analyzing before acting, and C ignores clinical priority in allocating scarce units.
Final two: D beats A because an alternate source removes the single point of failure, while air freight only buys weeks.
Exam cue: for a single point of failure, prefer the action that removes the dependency, started early because lead times are long.

questions.question: An IS auditor discovers the offsite backup vendor moved the firm's regulated media to an unaudited facility nine months ago without notice. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Terminate the contract and move the media to a new vendor
options.B: Assess the new site's controls and the media chain of custody
options.C: Accept the move because a recent restore test succeeded
options.D: Add stronger relocation-notice clauses at the next renewal

questions.key_concept: Before acting on a custody failure, establish the facts: whether media were protected and accounted for drives notification and vendor decisions.
questions.pre_read: Two options act decisively, two do not. What must the firm know before choosing between keeping and replacing the vendor?
questions.correct_explanation: The firm first needs to know whether its regulated media were protected and fully accounted for during and after the move, because that answer drives any breach notification, legal action and vendor decision. Terminating feels decisive, but it does not answer whether data was exposed, and moving the media again before the facts are known adds another custody risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Termination may follow, but it does not establish whether media were lost or exposed, and another move before assessment adds transit risk.
wrong_explanations.C: One successful restore shows that some media were readable. It says nothing about custody, physical security or unaudited controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Better clauses help in the future but ignore nine months of unknown exposure that may already require action.

tips: Eliminate: C treats one restore as proof of control, and D only addresses future contracts.
Final two: B beats A because the facts on custody drive every later decision, while termination answers none of them.
Exam cue: when exposure is unknown, the FIRST step is to establish the facts before choosing a remedy.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a Layer 3 switch routes traffic between cardholder-data and office networks without restriction. Which device would BEST enforce a security policy between the networks?

options.A: A load balancer spreading sessions across both networks
options.B: A separate Layer 2 switch for each of the networks
options.C: A firewall applying rule sets between the networks
options.D: A dedicated router forwarding packets between the networks

questions.key_concept: Routers and switches forward traffic; firewalls enforce security policy by permitting or denying flows according to rules.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each device is built to do. Which one decides whether traffic is allowed, not just where it goes?
questions.correct_explanation: A firewall's purpose is to enforce security policy, permitting only approved flows between zones and logging the rest, which is exactly what segmentation of cardholder data requires. A dedicated router looks like a reasonable boundary device, but its main job is forwarding packets between networks. Replacing one routing device with another would still let traffic pass without policy enforcement.

wrong_explanations.A: A load balancer distributes traffic across a server pool for availability. It is not designed to enforce access policy between zones.
wrong_explanations.B: Layer 2 switches forward frames within a network. Adding them does not control the routed traffic between the two networks.
wrong_explanations.D: A router's core role is forwarding between networks. Swapping the Layer 3 switch for a router still leaves traffic unfiltered.

tips: Eliminate: A is built for availability, and B works within a network rather than between networks.
Final two: C beats D because a firewall enforces policy, while a router's core job is forwarding packets.
Exam cue: forwarding devices move traffic; when the question asks to enforce policy between zones, choose the firewall.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing software inventory finds a GPL-licensed library embedded in a product the firm sells to customers. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Obligation to release the product's derived source code
options.B: Exceeding the number of licensed installation seats
options.C: Subscription fees rising at the next annual renewal
options.D: Missing attribution notices for the library's original authors

questions.key_concept: Copyleft licences such as the GPL can require distributed derivative works to be released under the same terms, exposing proprietary code.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes the GPL different from permissive and commercial licences. What happens when you distribute code built on it?
questions.correct_explanation: The GPL is a copyleft licence: distributing a product that incorporates GPL code can oblige the firm to release the derived source under the same terms, exposing proprietary intellectual property. Missing attribution notices are also a compliance gap, but they are cheap to correct by adding the notices, whereas forced source disclosure or withdrawal of the product strikes at the firm's commercial value.

wrong_explanations.B: Seat counts apply to commercial per-install licences. The GPL does not limit how many copies may be installed.
wrong_explanations.C: The GPL carries no subscription fees. Renewal pricing risk belongs to commercial subscription licences.
wrong_explanations.D: Attribution gaps are real but easily fixed by adding notices. They do not threaten the firm's proprietary code.

tips: Eliminate: B and C describe commercial licence risks that the GPL does not impose.
Final two: A beats D because forced source disclosure threatens the product itself, while missing attribution is easily corrected.
Exam cue: copyleft plus distribution means source-disclosure risk; that outranks notice and counting issues.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a network where iSCSI storage traffic and VoIP calls share the same Ethernet links. Which control is MOST important to verify?

options.A: Cable labelling and port-error counters on the shared switches
options.B: Vendor-reported uptime figures in the switch supplier's SOC report
options.C: Average link traffic kept below a defined monthly threshold
options.D: QoS and VLAN separation for each traffic class

questions.key_concept: On converged networks, QoS and segmentation stop one traffic class from starving another and limit cross-traffic exposure.
questions.pre_read: Two very different traffic types share one link. What stops a storage burst from ruining a voice call?
questions.correct_explanation: Storage and voice traffic have very different needs: iSCSI produces heavy bursts, while VoIP needs low latency and jitter. Quality of service and VLAN separation ensure each class gets its share of the link and is isolated from the other. Monitoring average utilization sounds like sound capacity management, but averages hide the short bursts that degrade calls and stall storage.

wrong_explanations.A: Labelling and error counters support maintenance, but they do not manage contention between storage and voice traffic.
wrong_explanations.B: A supplier's uptime figures say nothing about how this network's configuration prioritizes or separates traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: Monthly averages smooth out the brief congestion spikes that cause dropped calls and storage timeouts on converged links.

tips: Eliminate: A is cabling housekeeping, and B is vendor reporting unrelated to this configuration.
Final two: D beats C because QoS and separation handle bursts, while a monthly average hides them.
Exam cue: when different traffic types share a link, look for prioritization and segmentation, not average utilization.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds each site of a multi-site firm assigns private IP ranges independently, and the sites will soon be interconnected. What is the MOST important recommendation?

options.A: NAT at each site boundary to hide overlapping address ranges
options.B: Central IP address management with one allocation plan
options.C: Readdressing every site with public IPv4 address ranges
options.D: Larger DHCP scopes at each site to avoid exhaustion

questions.key_concept: Centrally governed IP address management prevents overlapping ranges at source, before interconnection makes conflicts costly.
questions.pre_read: The risk is overlapping private ranges once sites connect. Which option prevents the overlap rather than working around it?
questions.correct_explanation: Independent allocation will almost certainly produce overlapping private ranges, which break routing once sites connect. A central address management function with one allocation plan prevents the conflict at its source and gives a single record of who uses what. NAT at each boundary is a recognized workaround, but it masks the conflict, complicates routing, troubleshooting and logging, and leaves the root cause ungoverned.

wrong_explanations.A: NAT can make overlapping ranges work, but it adds complexity and hides the conflict rather than governing allocation.
wrong_explanations.C: Public IPv4 space is scarce and unnecessary for internal hosts. Private ranges are appropriate when centrally allocated.
wrong_explanations.D: Larger DHCP scopes address local exhaustion, not overlap between sites. They could even make conflicts more likely.

tips: Eliminate: C misuses scarce public addresses, and D solves local exhaustion rather than overlap.
Final two: B beats A because governance prevents the overlap at source, while NAT works around it and adds complexity.
Exam cue: prefer the option that fixes the cause through governance over a technical workaround that masks it.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds several critical servers past vendor end-of-support, kept in service to save capital. Which control would BEST govern such decisions?

options.A: Replacement of every server at the vendor-recommended age
options.B: An annual report of unsupported assets to IT finance
options.C: Risk-based exception approval by the business system owner
options.D: Extended hardware cover from a third-party maintainer

questions.key_concept: Running unsupported hardware is a risk decision that the accountable business owner must formally approve, based on criticality and cost.
questions.pre_read: The stem asks who governs the decision. Which option makes someone accountable for accepting the risk?
questions.correct_explanation: Keeping critical hardware past end-of-support can be justified, but only as an explicit risk decision. A risk-based exception, approved by the business owner and reviewed against criticality and cost, makes management accountable for the residual risk. An annual report gives useful visibility, but it only describes the situation to finance; nobody formally decides whether the risk is acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: Uniform replacement by age ignores criticality and cost. It wastes capital on low-risk assets and allows no justified extensions.
wrong_explanations.B: A report creates visibility but no decision. Without accountable approval, the risk is tolerated by default rather than accepted.
wrong_explanations.D: Third-party cover may supply parts, but it does not restore vendor patches or firmware updates, and it decides nothing about risk.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores criticality and cost, and D buys parts support without addressing the decision or patching.
Final two: C beats B because an owner's approval is a governed decision, while a report only gives visibility.
Exam cue: when a risk is knowingly kept, look for formal acceptance by the accountable owner, not just reporting.

questions.question: An IT operations manager finds storage capacity will saturate in 14 months, but warranties on the same arrays expire in six. What is the BEST approach?

options.A: Weigh early refresh against warranty extension in one cost view
options.B: Renew the warranties now and plan capacity separately next year
options.C: Run the arrays unsupported until the capacity is exhausted
options.D: Let the vendor account team set the refresh schedule

questions.key_concept: Capacity forecasts and warranty dates should feed one total-cost-of-ownership decision on when to refresh.
questions.pre_read: Two dates affect the same hardware. Should they be decided separately or together?
questions.correct_explanation: Because both dates concern the same arrays, the manager should compare refreshing early with extending warranty until the capacity point in one total-cost view, and choose the cheaper option that keeps the arrays supported. Renewing the warranty and planning capacity separately looks orderly, but it may pay for cover on hardware that will be replaced shortly afterward and misses the chance to align both events.

wrong_explanations.B: Treating the decisions separately may buy warranty for hardware due for replacement soon after. It forgoes the cheaper aligned option.
wrong_explanations.C: Unsupported critical storage risks long outages and data loss for eight months, a risk no cost saving justifies by default.
wrong_explanations.D: The vendor benefits from new sales. Refresh timing is the organization's decision, informed by its own capacity and cost analysis.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves critical storage unsupported, and D hands an internal decision to a party with a sales interest.
Final two: A beats B because one cost view aligns both dates, while separate decisions may pay for unneeded cover.
Exam cue: when two lifecycle dates affect the same asset, choose the option that decides them together on total cost.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a batch environment running about 14,000 scheduled jobs daily. Which approach would MOST effectively focus testing on failures with the highest business impact?

options.A: A random sample of 25 jobs tested for completion
options.B: The total count of failed jobs in the last month
options.C: A review of the scheduler's user interface settings
options.D: Dependency mapping to identify jobs on the critical path

questions.key_concept: In large schedules, dependency and critical-path analysis shows which job failures cascade into business impact, so testing can be risk-focused.
questions.pre_read: With thousands of jobs, which ones matter most? Think about failures that stop many later jobs.
questions.correct_explanation: Dependency mapping shows which jobs feed others and which lie on the critical path to business deadlines, so the auditor can concentrate testing where one failure cascades into many. A random sample of 25 is statistically respectable, but in 14,000 jobs it will probably miss most critical-path jobs, giving coverage of activity rather than of business risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A random sample treats all jobs as equal. In a population this large it will likely miss the few jobs whose failure matters most.
wrong_explanations.B: A failure count shows volume, not impact. Many minor failures can hide one failure that stalls critical processing.
wrong_explanations.C: Interface settings say little about which jobs depend on others or what their failure would do to the business.

tips: Eliminate: B measures volume, not impact, and C looks at interface settings rather than job risk.
Final two: D beats A because dependency mapping targets cascade risk, while a random sample treats every job as equal.
Exam cue: when asked to focus on business impact, prefer risk-based targeting over random or volume-based measures.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds operators changing production job schedules without change tickets to meet urgent business requests. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Monthly reconciliation of schedule changes to approved tickets
options.B: Formal change control with an expedited emergency route
options.C: A schedule freeze except within quarterly release windows
options.D: Acceptance of the practice because operators know the workload

questions.key_concept: Urgent changes still need change control; an expedited emergency route keeps speed while preserving authorization and later review.
questions.pre_read: The changes are urgent, so why did they bypass control? Look for an option that keeps both speed and authorization.
questions.correct_explanation: Operators bypassed change control because it offered no fast path, so the fix is formal change control that includes an expedited emergency route with authorization, logging and later review. Monthly reconciliation is a useful detective control, but it finds unauthorized changes weeks after they have already affected production, and it does nothing to remove the reason operators bypass the process.

wrong_explanations.A: Reconciliation detects unauthorized changes after the fact. It does not prevent them or give operators a legitimate fast route.
wrong_explanations.C: A freeze ignores real business urgency and would push operators to bypass control even more.
wrong_explanations.D: Operator knowledge does not replace authorization. Untracked schedule changes can break dependencies and hide errors or misuse.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores real urgency, and D replaces authorization with trust.
Final two: B beats A because a governed fast route prevents bypass, while reconciliation only detects it weeks later.
Exam cue: urgency never removes change control; look for an emergency path with authorization and later review.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that 23 spreadsheets feed regulatory reporting calculations, with no inventory or named owners. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Migrate the spreadsheets into an enterprise reporting application
options.B: Lock the formulas and freeze the current spreadsheet versions
options.C: Build an owned, criticality-ranked inventory of the spreadsheets
options.D: Leave the spreadsheets to the finance team's own discretion

questions.key_concept: End-user computing control starts with an owned, criticality-ranked inventory; validation, change control and migration decisions build on it.
questions.pre_read: The stem says FIRST and notes there is no inventory. What do all later controls depend on?
questions.correct_explanation: Controls cannot be targeted at spreadsheets nobody has listed or owns, so the first step is an inventory with named owners and a criticality rating. That ranking then drives validation, change control and any decision to migrate. Migrating into an enterprise application may be the right long-term answer for the most critical models, but choosing it before knowing what exists and how critical it is jumps ahead.

wrong_explanations.A: Migration may suit critical models later, but it is costly and slow, and without an inventory nobody knows which spreadsheets justify it.
wrong_explanations.B: Freezing formulas blocks legitimate updates such as regulatory changes and does not establish ownership or validation.
wrong_explanations.D: Spreadsheets feeding regulatory reports carry material risk. Leaving them ungoverned keeps the errors and ownership gap in place.

tips: Eliminate: B blocks needed updates, and D leaves material reporting risk ungoverned.
Final two: C beats A because you must know what exists and how critical it is before deciding what to migrate.
Exam cue: for end-user computing, the first control is an owned, risk-ranked inventory; everything else builds on it.

questions.subtopic: EUC Governance. End-User-Developed Tool Change Control
questions.question: A business owner asks how changes to user-built macros, scripts and small analyst tools should be controlled. What is the BEST approach for the IS auditor to advise?

options.A: Change controls scaled to each tool's assessed risk rating
options.B: Full development life cycle controls for every user-built tool
options.C: User discretion, since such tools sit outside IT governance
options.D: A ban on macros and scripts across the organization

questions.key_concept: Control effort over end-user tools should be proportional to risk: light controls for low-risk tools, rigorous change control for critical ones.
questions.pre_read: The tools range from trivial to critical. Should a personal macro face the same process as a model feeding financial reports?
questions.correct_explanation: End-user tools range from personal shortcuts to models that feed financial reporting, so change control should scale with risk: versioning for low-risk tools, peer review for medium ones and full testing, approval and rollback for high-risk ones. Applying full life cycle controls to every tool sounds rigorous, but the overhead drives users to bypass it and wastes effort on trivial tools.

wrong_explanations.B: Uniform heavy control wastes effort on trivial tools and encourages users to work around the process, weakening control over the critical ones.
wrong_explanations.C: User-built tools can drive material decisions and reports. Excluding them from governance leaves that risk uncontrolled.
wrong_explanations.D: A ban removes legitimate productivity and tends to push tool-building underground, where it is even less visible.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves material tools uncontrolled, and D bans useful tools and drives them out of sight.
Final two: A beats B because control proportional to risk is sustainable, while uniform heavy control invites bypass.
Exam cue: when assets vary widely in risk, prefer controls scaled to risk over one uniform level.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds network engineers sign in to core routers with one shared administrator account whose password is kept in a vault. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Issue named privileged accounts brokered through the PAM tool
options.B: Rotate the shared password automatically after each vault checkout
options.C: Grant every engineer standing full rights on each network device
options.D: Transfer router administration to a managed service provider

questions.key_concept: Privileged access to network devices needs named, individually attributable accounts; protecting a shared secret does not make actions traceable to a person.
questions.pre_read: Notice the account is shared. Ask which fix makes each router change traceable to one engineer.
questions.correct_explanation: The core weakness is accountability: with one shared account, no router change can be tied to a person. Named privileged accounts, brokered through privileged access management, make every session attributable and allow per-user revocation and review. Rotating the shared password after each checkout protects the secret better, but every action still appears under the same account, so attribution remains impossible.

wrong_explanations.B: Rotation limits password reuse, but all engineers still act under one identity, so changes cannot be traced to an individual.
wrong_explanations.C: Standing full rights for everyone breaks least privilege and widens the damage any compromised account can cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves the work but not the accountability; the firm still needs attributable access over its own infrastructure.

tips: Eliminate: C abandons least privilege, and D shifts the work without fixing who is accountable for each change.
Final two: A beats B because named accounts make actions attributable, while rotation only protects the shared secret.
Exam cue: when an account is shared, the fix is individual accountability, not a stronger shared password.

questions.question: An IS auditor notes that a firm relies on a strong perimeter firewall while its internal network is flat. Which control MOST reduces ransomware spreading between internal servers?

options.A: Tighten the inbound rule set on the internet-facing firewall
options.B: Monitor east-west traffic and alert the SOC on anomalies
options.C: Segment internal zones and block east-west traffic by policy
options.D: Place users in VLANs without any Layer 3 filtering between them

questions.key_concept: Internal segmentation with enforced east-west policy prevents lateral movement; perimeter rules and monitoring alone do not stop spread inside a flat network.
questions.pre_read: Notice the threat moves between internal servers. Ask which option actually stops that traffic rather than watching it.
questions.correct_explanation: Ransomware spreads laterally once inside, so the control must sit between internal systems. Segmenting the network into zones and enforcing east-west policy blocks unneeded server-to-server traffic and contains an outbreak. Monitoring east-west traffic is valuable, but it is detective: it raises alerts while the spread continues, and response may come too late to stop encryption across the flat network.

wrong_explanations.A: Perimeter rules address traffic entering from the internet, not movement between servers once an attacker is already inside.
wrong_explanations.B: Monitoring detects lateral movement but does not block it; a fast-moving outbreak can spread before analysts respond.
wrong_explanations.D: VLANs without Layer 3 filtering separate broadcast domains but still let traffic route freely between segments.

tips: Eliminate: A guards only the perimeter, and D creates segments with no enforcement between them.
Final two: C beats B because preventive segmentation stops lateral spread, while monitoring only reports it.
Exam cue: for lateral movement inside a network, prefer enforced internal segmentation over perimeter or detective controls.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds developers on a payments platform can merge code directly into the release branch. Which control is MOST important to recommend?

options.A: Recertify repository access quarterly with engineering leads
options.B: Require approved peer review before any merge to that branch
options.C: Back up the release branch nightly to a second region
options.D: Track commit volume per developer on a shared team dashboard

questions.key_concept: Branch protection with independent, approved review prevents unauthorized or unreviewed code from reaching release; access reviews and backups do not.
questions.pre_read: Notice developers can merge straight into the release branch. Ask which control stops unreviewed code at that point.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk is unreviewed or unauthorized code reaching the release branch for a payments system. Requiring an approved peer review before merge is a preventive, segregating control that stops a single developer from promoting code alone. Quarterly access recertification confirms who holds repository rights, but anyone legitimately on the list could still merge unreviewed code, so it does not address the stated weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Recertification keeps the access list current but does nothing to stop an authorized developer merging unreviewed code.
wrong_explanations.C: Backups protect availability of the code base, not the integrity of what is merged into release.
wrong_explanations.D: Commit volume is a productivity measure; it gives no assurance that changes were reviewed or authorized.

tips: Eliminate: C addresses availability, and D measures productivity rather than code integrity.
Final two: B beats A because review before merge stops unreviewed code, while access recertification only confirms who may merge.
Exam cue: when one person can push changes to release alone, look for a preventive second-person control at that step.

questions.question: An IT operations manager sets hardware maintenance policy for clustered web servers and a single, non-redundant core database server. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Repair each server when a failure is reported
options.B: Leave the maintenance mix to each vendor's contract terms
options.C: Run fixed-interval preventive maintenance on every server
options.D: Match the maintenance type to each server's criticality

questions.key_concept: Maintenance strategy is risk-based: preventive or condition-based care for critical single points of failure, reactive repair for redundant, low-impact assets.
questions.pre_read: Notice one server is clustered and one is not. Ask whether both deserve the same maintenance approach.
questions.correct_explanation: Maintenance effort should follow business impact. The non-redundant database is a single point of failure and warrants preventive or condition-based maintenance, while clustered web servers can tolerate reactive repair because a node failure does not stop service. Uniform fixed-interval maintenance looks disciplined, but it overspends on redundant assets and ignores condition, so it is not the best use of resources.

wrong_explanations.A: Run-to-failure on a non-redundant core database invites an outage of a critical service with no fallback.
wrong_explanations.B: Vendors set terms for their own interests; the firm must decide maintenance based on its own business impact.
wrong_explanations.C: Uniform scheduling ignores redundancy and condition, spending effort where failure is tolerable and missing early warning signs.

tips: Eliminate: A risks an outage of the single point of failure, and B hands a risk decision to the vendor.
Final two: D beats C because maintenance effort should follow criticality and redundancy, not one uniform schedule.
Exam cue: when assets differ in criticality, prefer the risk-based option over any one-size-fits-all policy.

questions.question: An IS auditor needs assurance that firewall and router configurations have not changed outside the change process. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: Automated drift alerts on running versus authorized configurations
options.B: Approved change tickets for every change recorded in the log
options.C: Successful test restores of saved device configuration backups
options.D: Device firmware versions compared with the vendor's latest release

questions.key_concept: Unauthorized configuration change is detected by comparing actual running configurations to approved baselines; ticket reviews only cover changes someone recorded.
questions.pre_read: Notice the risk is changes made outside the process. Ask which evidence would reveal a change nobody logged.
questions.correct_explanation: Changes made outside the process, by definition, leave no ticket. Comparing each device's running configuration with its approved baseline reveals any difference regardless of how it was introduced, so it directly tests the stated risk. Matching approved tickets to logged changes confirms that recorded changes were authorized, but it cannot reveal an undocumented change, which is exactly the population the auditor is concerned about.

wrong_explanations.B: Tickets matched to logged changes cover only recorded changes; an unrecorded edit never enters the sample.
wrong_explanations.C: Restore tests show configurations are recoverable, not that the running configuration matches what was approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Comparing firmware versions addresses patch currency, not whether configuration settings were changed without authorization.

tips: Eliminate: C tests recoverability, and D tests patch currency, neither of which detects unauthorized changes.
Final two: A beats B because drift alerts on the running state catch unlogged changes, while tickets cover only what was recorded.
Exam cue: to find changes made outside a process, test the actual state, not the process's own records.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that production DBAs can also disable and purge the database audit logs. Which recommendation BEST addresses this risk?

options.A: Have the DBA manager review audit log entries every month
options.B: Block application developers from production database access
options.C: Give audit log administration to a role independent of DBAs
options.D: Require DBAs to change their passwords more frequently

questions.key_concept: Those whose activity is logged must not control the logs; separating log administration from database administration preserves the integrity of the audit trail.
questions.pre_read: Notice DBAs control the logs that record their own actions. Ask which fix breaks that conflict.
questions.correct_explanation: The conflict is that DBAs can erase the evidence of their own actions. Moving audit log administration to an independent role, such as security operations, separates the duty of doing the work from the duty of keeping its record. A monthly manager review adds oversight, but it reads logs the DBAs could already have altered or purged, so the review may see an incomplete trail.

wrong_explanations.A: A review relies on the logs being complete; DBAs who can purge them can hide activity before the review happens.
wrong_explanations.B: Restricting developers is a sound control, but it does not address DBAs controlling their own audit trail.
wrong_explanations.D: Password frequency affects credential risk, not the conflict of DBAs administering their own activity logs.

tips: Eliminate: B fixes a different access issue, and D addresses credentials rather than the conflict of duties.
Final two: C beats A because independent log control protects the trail, while a review trusts logs DBAs can purge.
Exam cue: when people control the record of their own actions, separate the duty; a later review cannot fix it.

questions.subtopic: EUC Spreadsheet Failure During Regulatory Reporting
questions.question: Two days before a regulatory filing, the only analyst who maintains an undocumented reporting spreadsheet is hospitalized. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST immediate action?

options.A: Submit last quarter's figures with an explanatory cover note
options.B: Have backup analysts run the existing model under independent review
options.C: Rebuild the report overnight in a governed reporting tool
options.D: Delay the submission until the analyst is able to return

questions.key_concept: Under deadline pressure, run the proven existing model with independent review; untested rebuilds add risk. Fix the end-user computing weakness after the filing.
questions.pre_read: Notice the deadline and the missing owner. Ask which option is both timely and least likely to introduce new errors.
questions.correct_explanation: The spreadsheet has produced accepted filings before, so running it with backup analysts and independent review is the fastest way to a reliable submission. Its lack of documentation and single ownership should be fixed after the deadline. Rebuilding overnight in a governed tool sounds like the right long-term control, but an untested model built in hours is far more likely to misstate the filing.

wrong_explanations.A: Filing prior-period figures knowingly misstates the current report and creates regulatory exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: A rushed rebuild is untested; moving to a governed tool is the right remediation, but after the filing.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for an uncertain return risks missing a fixed regulatory deadline altogether.

tips: Eliminate: A knowingly files stale figures, and D risks missing the deadline altogether.
Final two: B beats C because a proven model under review is safer than an untested rebuild under time pressure.
Exam cue: in a crisis, prefer the tested, reviewed path now and schedule the structural fix afterward.

questions.question: A nightly batch overrun has blocked customer online access for 11 days, and adding compute has not helped. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Add further compute capacity to the batch servers
options.B: Notify customers and keep the current batch schedule
options.C: Start the planned 90-day re-architecture of the batch scheduler
options.D: Apply a parallel-run workaround and open a problem record

questions.key_concept: Restore service with a workaround first, and log a problem record so root cause is still investigated and fixed.
questions.pre_read: Notice customers are blocked now and extra compute already failed. Ask what restores service quickly without abandoning the root cause.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers are affected every day, so the first priority is a workaround that restores the online window, such as splitting the batch into parallel runs. Opening a problem record ensures the underlying causes are still analyzed and fixed. The 90-day re-architecture may be the right permanent fix, but starting it first leaves customers blocked for months while the structural work proceeds.

wrong_explanations.A: Extra compute has already failed to help, so more of it repeats an ineffective action.
wrong_explanations.B: Communication is useful, but keeping the schedule unchanged leaves customers blocked with no fix in sight.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-architecture may be the permanent fix, but it leaves the customer outage running for months.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats what already failed, and B communicates without fixing anything.
Final two: D beats C because service is restored first, while the problem record still drives the root-cause fix.
Exam cue: restore service before root cause, but look for the option that still commits to finding the root cause.

questions.subtopic: Hardware Refresh Budget Cut Affecting Resilience
questions.question: The CFO cuts a hardware refresh budget by 30% but allows reallocation; some DR equipment is past vendor support. What should the IS auditor recommend to the CIO as BEST?

options.A: Spread the cut evenly across every planned refresh category
options.B: Ask the audit committee to reinstate the original budget
options.C: Fund unsupported assets now and defer healthy equipment
options.D: Let the hardware vendor select the refresh mix within budget

questions.key_concept: Within a constrained budget, refresh by risk: replace unsupported and failing critical assets first, and defer healthy equipment with documented risk acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the CFO allows reallocation. Ask how to cover the highest risks within the budget management set.
questions.correct_explanation: Budget levels are management's decision, and the CFO has allowed reallocation. Funding unsupported DR equipment first and deferring refresh of healthy equipment reduces the greatest resilience risk within the approved budget, with the deferral documented for risk acceptance. Asking the audit committee to reinstate the budget sounds protective, but it bypasses management's decision when a risk-based reallocation already addresses the exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: An even cut treats unsupported DR equipment the same as healthy kit, leaving the highest risk underfunded.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor advises management; escalating to overturn a budget decision is premature when reallocation can cover the key risks.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor has a sales incentive; prioritization must reflect the firm's own risk assessment.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores relative risk, and D hands prioritization to a party with a conflict of interest.
Final two: C beats B because risk-based reallocation works within management's decision, while escalation tries to overturn it.
Exam cue: when resources are cut, prioritize by risk and document what is deferred; deferring low-risk items can be right.
