questions.subtopic: Network Segmentation Breach via Admin VLAN
questions.question: An attacker used misconfigured ACLs to reach the cardholder data zone, and the path is now blocked at the firewall. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Capture forensic images and logs of the affected segments
options.B: Rebuild the ACLs at once through an emergency change
options.C: Restore the cardholder systems from the latest backups
options.D: Tell customers that no card data was exposed

questions.key_concept: Once the threat is contained, preserve evidence before changing affected systems; rebuilding first can destroy what investigators and assessors need.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attacker's path is already blocked. Ask what would be lost if systems were changed before anything else.
questions.correct_explanation: With the path already blocked at the firewall, the immediate threat is contained, so the next step is to preserve evidence. Forensic images and logs show what the attacker accessed, which drives notification and assessor decisions. Rebuilding the ACLs through an emergency change is good practice, but doing it first overwrites the very configuration and traces that investigators need.

wrong_explanations.B: The rebuild is needed, but with containment in place it can wait briefly; changing first destroys evidence of the attacker's path.
wrong_explanations.C: Restoring overwrites compromised systems before evidence is taken, and the backups themselves may be affected.
wrong_explanations.D: Claiming no exposure before forensics finish is unsupported and could mislead customers and regulators.

tips: Eliminate: C overwrites evidence on possibly tainted backups, and D makes a claim with no evidence behind it.
Final two: A beats B because, once contained, evidence must be preserved before systems are changed.
Exam cue: after containment, preserve evidence first; eradication and rebuild come next.

questions.question: An IS auditor evaluates the catalog for a backup tape library stored partly with an offsite vendor. Which control BEST ensures the catalog stays complete and accurate?

options.A: Treat the offsite vendor's inventory list as the master record
options.B: Reconcile the catalog to physical and vendor counts monthly
options.C: Count the media held at the offsite vendor once each year
options.D: Label every cartridge with its content and retention date

questions.key_concept: A backup catalog stays accurate through frequent reconciliation across the backup software, physical media and vendor records, so lost or misfiled media surface quickly.
questions.pre_read: Notice records exist in more than one place. Ask which control detects differences between them soonest.
questions.correct_explanation: Media records live in the backup software, on site and at the vendor, so the catalog stays reliable only if these sources are regularly compared. A monthly three-way reconciliation detects missing, misplaced or mislabeled cartridges quickly. An annual count of offsite media is a real control, but a lost cartridge could go unnoticed for up to a year and it ignores media held on site.

wrong_explanations.A: Relying on the vendor's list cedes the record to a third party and provides no independent check.
wrong_explanations.C: An annual count detects discrepancies too late and covers only the offsite portion of the library.
wrong_explanations.D: Labels identify each cartridge but do not confirm that the catalog and actual holdings agree.

tips: Eliminate: A gives up independent control of the record, and D identifies media without checking the catalog.
Final two: B beats C because frequent reconciliation across all sources finds missing media sooner than a yearly offsite count.
Exam cue: when records sit in several places, look for regular reconciliation between them.

questions.question: An IT operations manager needs fast restores for daily operations and backup copies that ransomware cannot alter. Which backup design is BEST?

options.A: Tape for every backup tier to minimize storage costs
options.B: One network-attached deduplication appliance for every copy
options.C: Replication of every backup to a second cloud region
options.D: Disk backups for restores plus an immutable offline copy

questions.key_concept: Tier backup media by need: disk for fast operational restore, plus an immutable or offline copy that ransomware cannot encrypt or delete.
questions.pre_read: Notice two needs: speed and resistance to ransomware. Ask which design meets both.
questions.correct_explanation: Disk-based backup meets the need for fast operational restores, and an immutable or offline copy cannot be encrypted or deleted by ransomware that reaches the network. Replicating backups to a second cloud region adds geographic redundancy, but replication is usually online and synchronized, so encrypted or deleted data can be copied across too unless immutability is applied.

wrong_explanations.A: Tape-only is economical and can be offline, but restores are too slow to meet daily operational needs.
wrong_explanations.B: A single network-reachable appliance is fast, but ransomware that reaches the network can encrypt or delete every copy.
wrong_explanations.C: Online replication protects against site loss, but it can replicate encrypted or deleted backups without immutability.

tips: Eliminate: A fails the speed requirement, and B leaves every copy reachable by ransomware.
Final two: D beats C because only an immutable or offline copy resists ransomware; replication can copy the damage.
Exam cue: for ransomware resilience, look for immutability or an air gap, not just more copies.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the network monitoring tools that collect SNMP and NetFlow data. Which finding is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Dashboards refresh every five minutes rather than in real time
options.B: Alert thresholds in the tools have not been tuned since deployment
options.C: Several critical network segments send no data to the tools
options.D: The tool vendor's SOC 2 report notes one unrelated exception

questions.key_concept: Coverage comes first in monitoring: a segment sending no data is a total blind spot, worse than poorly tuned or displayed data.
questions.pre_read: Ask which finding means problems could occur with no chance of detection at all.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring can only detect what it sees. Critical segments that send no data are complete blind spots where outages and attacks go unnoticed, regardless of how well the tools are tuned. Untuned thresholds are a real weakness that cause noise or missed alerts, but the tools still receive the data and can be adjusted, whereas missing coverage provides no detection at all.

wrong_explanations.A: A five-minute refresh is a minor latency issue; data is still collected and alerts can still fire.
wrong_explanations.B: Untuned thresholds reduce alert quality, but the traffic is still collected and visible for analysis.
wrong_explanations.D: An exception unrelated to the monitoring service has little bearing on the firm's detection coverage.

tips: Eliminate: A is a small latency issue, and D concerns an exception outside the relevant service.
Final two: C beats B because a segment with no data is a total blind spot, while poor tuning still sees the traffic.
Exam cue: in monitoring audits, a coverage gap outranks problems with how collected data is analyzed.

questions.subtopic: Problem Management. Root Cause Analysis Methodology
questions.question: A problem manager finds the same storage outage has recurred three times, and each incident was closed after a restart. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Open a problem record to find the underlying cause
options.B: Automate the restart so service recovers faster next time
options.C: Close the incidents and measure recurrence risk over another quarter
options.D: Replace the storage array with a newer vendor model

questions.key_concept: Recurring incidents call for problem management: a structured root cause analysis with corrective action, not a faster workaround or an unproven replacement.
questions.pre_read: Notice the outage keeps recurring after restarts. Ask which option finds out why.
questions.correct_explanation: Three recurrences show the restart is a workaround, not a fix. Opening a problem record and applying a structured technique, such as 5-Whys or a fishbone analysis, identifies the underlying cause and drives a corrective action that prevents further outages. Automating the restart shortens each outage, which is helpful, but it institutionalizes the workaround and leaves the cause unknown and the outages continuing.

wrong_explanations.B: Faster recovery reduces impact, but the outage keeps happening because nobody has found out why.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring recurrence for another quarter accepts further business impact when the pattern is already clear.
wrong_explanations.D: Replacing hardware before diagnosis may spend money without fixing a cause that lies elsewhere.

tips: Eliminate: C waits a quarter for more harm, and D buys a solution before the cause is known.
Final two: A beats B because finding the root cause stops recurrence, while automation only speeds the workaround.
Exam cue: repeated incidents with the same symptom point to problem management and root cause analysis.

questions.question: Service desk reports show 99% of tickets resolved within SLA, yet business users rate the service poorly. Which change should the service level manager make FIRST?

options.A: Tighten resolution-time targets for every ticket priority
options.B: Report each technician's ticket count to management
options.C: Drop the targets the desk already meets consistently
options.D: Add satisfaction and repeat-incident measures to the SLA

questions.key_concept: Good SLA metrics balance speed with outcome and customer experience; when speed targets are met but users are unhappy, the metric set is incomplete.
questions.pre_read: Notice speed targets are met but users are unhappy. Ask what the current metrics are failing to measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Meeting speed targets while users are dissatisfied shows the metrics measure activity, not outcomes. Adding customer satisfaction and repeat-incident measures reveals whether tickets are truly resolved and whether users experience good service. Tightening resolution targets sounds rigorous, but it measures the same dimension more strictly and may push staff to close tickets faster without fixing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Stricter time targets reinforce the speed focus and can encourage premature closure rather than real resolution.
wrong_explanations.B: Per-technician volume is a productivity statistic that says nothing about whether users' issues are solved.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping met targets removes visibility of performance and does not explain the dissatisfaction.

tips: Eliminate: B measures individual output, and C removes visibility without explaining the gap.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is a missing outcome measure, not a speed target that is too loose.
Exam cue: when green metrics clash with unhappy users, the metric set is measuring the wrong thing.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviewing a help desk with strong SLA results has time for one more area. Which area presents the GREATEST risk to examine?

options.A: Accuracy of first-contact resolution figures in monthly desk reports
options.B: Escalation of security-related calls to the incident response team
options.C: Average handle time recorded for each desk agent
options.D: Formatting consistency of knowledge base articles

questions.key_concept: The help desk often hears of security incidents first; failing to escalate those calls lets attacks continue unnoticed.
questions.pre_read: Notice SLA results are already strong. Ask which area could let an active attack go unnoticed.
questions.correct_explanation: Security-related calls, such as reported phishing or suspicious account activity, that are handled as routine tickets can let an active incident run unnoticed. That is a direct risk to the firm. Accurate resolution figures matter because management relies on them, but an error distorts service reporting rather than leaving an attack uncontained, and the strong SLA results already give some comfort on service quality.

wrong_explanations.A: Overstated resolution figures mislead management about service quality, but they do not leave an active security incident uncontained.
wrong_explanations.C: Handle time is an efficiency metric with little bearing on control risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Article formatting is a usability matter, not a control weakness with meaningful risk.

tips: Eliminate: C is an efficiency metric, and D is a cosmetic usability issue.
Final two: B beats A because an unescalated security call can let an attack continue, while inaccurate figures only distort reporting.
Exam cue: at the help desk, check that security events leave the service queue quickly; that outranks service metrics.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds engineers make firewall rule changes directly in production and document them afterward. Which control is MOST important to recommend?

options.A: Back up firewall configurations to a secure repository
options.B: Document the full network topology in a current diagram
options.C: Approve and test firewall rule changes before they are made
options.D: Review the firewall change logs each week for unauthorized edits

questions.key_concept: Network change control is preventive: rule changes are approved and tested before implementation, not just documented or reviewed after the fact.
questions.pre_read: Notice changes are documented only afterward. Ask which control acts before a bad rule reaches production.
questions.correct_explanation: Changes made first and documented later mean a flawed or unauthorized firewall rule takes effect before anyone checks it. Requiring approval and testing before implementation stops bad rules from reaching production. A weekly review of change logs adds detection, but a harmful rule could expose systems for up to a week before anyone notices, and the review depends on logs being complete.

wrong_explanations.A: Backups help recover a configuration, but they do not stop unapproved rule changes going live.
wrong_explanations.B: A topology diagram supports understanding of the network, not authorization of rule changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Weekly log review detects issues after a harmful rule may already have exposed systems.

tips: Eliminate: A supports recovery, and B supports documentation; neither controls rule changes.
Final two: C beats D because approval before change prevents harm, while a weekly review finds it after the fact.
Exam cue: when changes are made first and recorded later, recommend the preventive approval step.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds powerful disk and registry utilities installed on all production servers and usable by any administrator. Which control BEST reduces the risk?

options.A: Restrict utilities to approved roles and log every use
options.B: Include utilities in the annual privileged access review
options.C: Remove every utility and rely on vendor diagnostic support
options.D: Keep open access since administrators are already vetted

questions.key_concept: Utility programs can bypass application controls, so access is limited to approved roles with logged use; outright bans or annual reviews alone are weaker.
questions.pre_read: Notice any administrator can use the tools. Ask which option limits who can use them and records what they do.
questions.correct_explanation: Utilities can bypass normal application controls, so the risk lies in who can run them and whether use is traceable. Restricting each utility to approved roles applies least privilege, and logging creates accountability for every use. Adding utilities to an annual access review is a sound detective step, but misuse could go unseen for up to a year and the tools stay open to every administrator meanwhile.

wrong_explanations.B: An annual review is detective and infrequent; it leaves broad access in place and misuse unseen for months.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing every tool impairs legitimate maintenance and incident response, and slows diagnosis when outages occur.
wrong_explanations.D: Vetting does not justify unrestricted access; least privilege still applies to trusted administrators.

tips: Eliminate: C harms operations, and D ignores least privilege for trusted staff.
Final two: A beats B because restricting and logging use prevents and records misuse, while an annual review finds it late.
Exam cue: for powerful tools, prefer restricted, logged access over both bans and after-the-fact reviews.

questions.subtopic: Problem Management Reporting. Cadence and Dashboards
questions.question: The IT steering committee wants oversight of problem management without operational detail. Which report BEST supports this need?

options.A: A year-end summary of the problems closed that year
options.B: Problem reports issued whenever executives request one
options.C: A real-time dashboard listing every open problem ticket
options.D: Monthly trends of recurring problems weighted by impact

questions.key_concept: Executive problem-management reporting is periodic, trend-based and weighted by business impact, giving oversight without ticket-level detail.
questions.pre_read: Notice the audience wants oversight, not detail. Ask which report shows direction and business impact at a regular pace.
questions.correct_explanation: A steering committee needs to see whether problems are recurring and which ones threaten the business. Monthly trends weighted by impact show direction and priority at a pace that allows timely decisions. A real-time dashboard of every open ticket looks transparent, but it gives operational detail the committee asked to avoid and leaves members to infer trends and business impact themselves.

wrong_explanations.A: A yearly summary arrives too late for the committee to act on emerging trends during the year.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting only on request leaves oversight to chance and misses issues executives do not know to ask about.
wrong_explanations.C: Ticket-level detail overwhelms an executive audience and does not show trend or business impact.

tips: Eliminate: A arrives too late to act on, and B depends on executives knowing what to ask.
Final two: D beats C because executives need impact-weighted trends, not ticket-level operational detail.
Exam cue: match the report to its audience: governance bodies get periodic trends tied to business impact.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm the incident response process works in practice, not just on paper. Which evidence is MOST persuasive?

options.A: An approved, current incident response policy and procedures
options.B: Timestamped records of recent incidents traced through each phase
options.C: Results of a tabletop exercise run by the response team
options.D: The response platform vendor's latest SOC 2 report

questions.key_concept: Operating effectiveness is shown by evidence of real execution: records of actual incidents traced through detection, containment, resolution and reporting.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words in practice. Ask which evidence shows the process actually ran on real events.
questions.correct_explanation: Operating effectiveness is best shown by what happened on real incidents. Tracing timestamped records of recent incidents through detection, containment, resolution and reporting shows whether each phase actually ran as designed and on time. A tabletop exercise is useful evidence of readiness, but it tests a simulated scenario in a discussion setting, so it is weaker than records of the process working under real conditions.

wrong_explanations.A: A policy shows design only; it gives no evidence that responders followed it on real incidents.
wrong_explanations.C: A tabletop shows readiness in simulation, which is weaker than evidence from real incidents handled end to end.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor report covers the platform's controls, not how the firm's own team responded to incidents.

tips: Eliminate: A shows design only, and D covers the vendor rather than the firm's response.
Final two: B beats C because records of real incidents prove operation, while a tabletop only simulates it.
Exam cue: for operating effectiveness, evidence of real execution outranks design documents and simulations.

questions.question: An outsourced provider reports SLA compliance from its own monitoring tool, and service credits depend on those figures. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the reports since the contract assigns measurement to the provider
options.B: Ask the provider to send its SLA compliance reports weekly
options.C: Measure key SLAs independently and reconcile to provider reports
options.D: Obtain the provider's SOC 2 report covering its monitoring tool

questions.key_concept: When a provider measures its own performance and money depends on it, the customer needs independent measurement reconciled to the provider's figures.
questions.pre_read: Notice the provider grades its own performance and credits depend on it. Ask which option gives the firm its own evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider has a financial interest in the figures it reports, so the firm needs its own evidence. Independently measuring key service levels and reconciling them to the provider's reports reveals methodology gaps and errors that affect service credits. A SOC 2 report gives some assurance over the provider's controls, but it rarely tests whether the measurement method matches the firm's SLA definitions.

wrong_explanations.A: Contract terms do not remove the conflict of interest; the firm still needs assurance over figures that drive credits.
wrong_explanations.B: More frequent reports from the same source add volume, not independence or accuracy.
wrong_explanations.D: A SOC 2 report covers general controls and seldom tests that metrics match the firm's specific SLA definitions.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts self-graded figures, and B adds frequency without adding independence.

questions.question: Management plans to consolidate two data centers to cut costs. Which governance step BEST keeps service levels aligned with this architecture change?

options.A: Review affected SLAs with service owners before design approval
options.B: Update the SLA documents to match performance after migration
options.C: Apply one uniform SLA target to every consolidated service
options.D: Let architects and service managers set targets separately

questions.key_concept: Service levels and architecture are aligned before decisions are approved: agreed SLAs shape the design, rather than being rewritten to fit what the design delivers.
questions.pre_read: Notice the change has not happened yet. Ask when service levels should influence the design.
questions.correct_explanation: Consolidation can change latency, capacity and recovery capability, so affected SLAs must shape the design before it is approved. Reviewing them with service owners at that stage lets the design meet committed service levels or forces an informed trade-off. Updating SLA documents after migration keeps records current, but it simply accepts whatever performance results, which can break commitments the business relies on.

wrong_explanations.B: Rewriting SLAs after migration lets the architecture dictate service levels instead of business needs shaping the design.
wrong_explanations.C: Uniform targets ignore differing criticality, overspending on minor services and underserving critical ones.
wrong_explanations.D: Separate target-setting invites designs that cannot meet agreed service levels.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores service criticality, and D keeps the two disciplines apart.
Final two: A beats B because service levels should shape the design before approval, not be rewritten to fit it afterward.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that backups held at an offsite facility can support recovery within the RTO. Which test provides the BEST evidence?

options.A: Review the storage vendor's SOC 2 report on the facility
options.B: Confirm the recovery plan is documented and approved
options.C: Reconcile offsite media inventory to backup catalog records
options.D: Restore sample backups from offsite and time the recovery

questions.key_concept: Recoverability is proven by restoring from offsite media and timing the result against the RTO; inventories and documents show existence, not usability.
questions.pre_read: Notice the objective names the RTO. Ask which test both proves the data is usable and measures time.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is recovery within the RTO, so the best evidence is an actual restore from offsite media, timed against that objective and checked for integrity. Reconciling the offsite inventory to the catalog confirms the right media are stored, which is necessary, but it shows existence, not that the data is readable or can be restored fast enough.

wrong_explanations.A: A facility SOC 2 report covers storage controls, not whether the firm's data can be restored in time.
wrong_explanations.B: Plan documentation shows design, not that recovery from offsite media actually works within the RTO.
wrong_explanations.C: Inventory reconciliation confirms media are present, not that they are readable or restorable within the RTO.

tips: Eliminate: A covers the facility, and B covers documents, not recovery itself.
Final two: D beats C because only a timed restore proves usability and speed, while reconciliation proves presence.
Exam cue: when the objective is recovery time, the best evidence is a timed recovery test.

questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing whether a business continuity plan is complete. Which check is MOST important?

options.A: Compare the plan's table of contents with last year's version
options.B: Check each critical BIA process has a recovery procedure
options.C: Confirm the plan was reviewed and approved within the last year
options.D: Rate the plan using the BCP coordinator's self-assessment

questions.key_concept: BCP completeness is tested by tracing critical processes from the BIA through strategy to a recovery procedure; currency and structure checks do not show coverage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the plan must cover, and where the list of critical processes comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan is complete only if every critical process identified in the BIA has a recovery strategy and procedure. Tracing from the BIA to the plan reveals gaps where a critical process has no recovery steps. Confirming an annual review and approval shows the plan is maintained, but a recently approved plan can still omit critical processes, so currency does not prove completeness.

wrong_explanations.A: Matching last year's structure only shows consistency; any gap in last year's plan is simply repeated.
wrong_explanations.C: Recent approval shows maintenance, not that every critical process from the BIA is covered.
wrong_explanations.D: A coordinator's self-assessment lacks independence and is not objective evidence of coverage.

tips: Eliminate: A only compares structure, and D relies on unverified self-assessment.
Final two: B beats C because checking every BIA process for a procedure proves coverage, while recent approval proves only currency.
Exam cue: BCP completeness starts from the BIA; check that every critical process traces to a recovery procedure.

questions.question: In hour 14 of a major outage, five executives are pushing conflicting recovery and communication actions. What should the IS auditor recommend the COO do FIRST?

options.A: Start a forensic review before any further recovery decisions
options.B: Let each executive run their own workstream in parallel
options.C: Appoint one incident commander with defined decision rights
options.D: Direct the CMO to brief customers and regulators right away

questions.key_concept: In a major incident with competing stakeholders, establish unified command and decision rights first; coordinated recovery and communication follow from it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem is conflicting direction, not a missing action. Ask what must exist before the actions can be coordinated.
questions.correct_explanation: The outage is prolonged because executives are pulling in different directions. Appointing one incident commander with clear decision rights creates a single point of coordination, so recovery, workarounds and communications are sequenced rather than contested. Briefing members and regulators is urgent and valuable, but launched before command is set, messages may contradict recovery decisions and need retracting later.

wrong_explanations.A: Halting recovery for a forensic review prolongs the outage when nothing points to malicious activity.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent workstreams are exactly what is causing the conflict; they need one point of coordination.
wrong_explanations.D: Communication matters, but without unified command messages may conflict with recovery decisions and need correction.

tips: Eliminate: A halts recovery without cause, and B keeps the conflict that is causing the delay.
Final two: C beats D because unified command must exist before communication and recovery can be coordinated.
Exam cue: when stakeholders conflict in a crisis, set up command and decision rights before choosing actions.

questions.question: Three vendors each report meeting their own SLAs, yet the firm's end-to-end monitoring shows its customer API SLA missed for three months. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Replace the database vendor as the most likely weak link
options.B: Trace end-to-end transactions to find where availability is lost
options.C: Escalate penalty claims to each vendor's executive sponsor at once
options.D: Lower customer SLA targets to match achieved availability

questions.key_concept: Component SLAs can all be met while the end-to-end service fails; trace the full transaction path before assigning accountability.
questions.pre_read: Notice that every vendor reports compliance. Ask what evidence would show where the customer-facing availability is actually lost.
questions.correct_explanation: Each vendor measures only its own layer, so component SLAs can all be met while the customer-facing service fails. End-to-end tracing shows where the time is lost and gives the evidence any later remedy needs. Penalty escalation is a legitimate lever, but without that evidence each vendor will simply cite its own compliant figures and the dispute stalls.

wrong_explanations.A: Choosing a vendor to replace by assumption skips root-cause analysis. The fault may sit between layers or in the firm's own architecture.
wrong_explanations.C: Escalation without evidence invites each vendor to repeat its compliant figures. Penalties come after tracing shows which layer, or which hand-off, is failing.
wrong_explanations.D: Lowering targets accepts the failure and shifts the cost to customers without finding or fixing the cause.

tips: Eliminate: A replaces a vendor on a guess, and D simply accepts the shortfall.
Final two: B beats C because penalties need evidence of where availability is lost, and only end-to-end tracing provides it.
Exam cue: when every party's own metric looks green but the service is red, measure end to end before assigning blame.

questions.subtopic: Network Outage Cascading to Critical Application
questions.question: A CAB-approved firewall rule change caused a 47-minute outage of a hospital's electronic health records before rollback restored service. What is the BEST next step for the IS auditor to recommend?

options.A: Freeze firewall changes until a production-like test lab exists
options.B: Discipline the engineer who authored the firewall rule change
options.C: Close the incident as routine because rollback restored service
options.D: Run a blameless post-incident review of the failed change

questions.key_concept: Once service is restored, a blameless post-incident review establishes root cause before any corrective action is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Rollback has already restored service. Ask what must happen before anyone can choose the right corrective action.
questions.correct_explanation: Service is already restored, so the next step is root cause. A blameless post-incident review examines why the change passed approval and testing, whether the gap was process, tooling or people, and produces lasting fixes. Freezing changes until a new test lab exists presumes the cause is tooling before anyone has looked, and blocks other needed changes on an assumption.

wrong_explanations.A: A change freeze tied to a new lab assumes tooling is the root cause before the review has found it, and halts other necessary changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Punishing one engineer ignores that approval and testing both missed the defect, and discourages honest reporting in future incidents.
wrong_explanations.C: A clinical system outage that slipped through two controls is not routine. Restoring service never removes the need for root-cause analysis.

tips: Eliminate: B blames one person for a two-control failure, and C skips root cause because service is back.
Final two: D beats A because the cause must be established before choosing the fix; a lab freeze assumes the answer.
Exam cue: after service is restored, find the root cause next; avoid answers that pick a remedy before the cause is known.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the business continuity plan lists five data centres where seven now operate, and its recovery objectives were set four years ago. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Refresh the business impact analysis against current operations
options.B: Rewrite the plan to cover every current site and vendor
options.C: Transfer the continuity programme to a specialist provider
options.D: Correct the site list during the next scheduled annual review

questions.key_concept: The business impact analysis drives recovery objectives and strategy, so a stale plan starts with a refreshed BIA, not a rewrite.
questions.pre_read: Notice the recovery objectives are four years old. Ask which document those objectives come from, and fix that first.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery objectives and strategies come from the business impact analysis. With four-year-old objectives and two unlisted sites, the BIA must be refreshed first so the rewritten plan reflects current priorities. Rewriting the plan straight away looks decisive, but it would copy stale recovery time objectives into a new document and need rework once the analysis is redone.

wrong_explanations.B: A rewrite without a fresh BIA carries stale recovery objectives into the new plan. The analysis must come first so the plan reflects current priorities.
wrong_explanations.C: Outsourcing delivery cannot transfer accountability for continuity. Management still owns the programme and its outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting a year leaves two sites and outdated objectives unprotected. A known gap of this size needs action now, not at the next cycle.

tips: Eliminate: C tries to outsource accountability, and D leaves a known gap open for a year.
Final two: A beats B because recovery priorities come from the BIA; rewriting first would carry stale objectives into the new plan.
Exam cue: BIA before strategy, and strategy before plan; when the analysis is stale, refresh it first.

questions.subtopic: Vendor Managed Service Unavailable During Ransomware
questions.question: Ransomware entered a bank through its managed service provider's remote tools, and the continuity plan names that provider as recovery lead. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Let the provider lead recovery as the continuity plan specifies
options.B: Restore core systems from the bank's own offline backups
options.C: Engage incident responders who are independent of the provider
options.D: Negotiate a ransom payment to shorten the core banking outage

questions.key_concept: When a supplier is the compromise path, independent incident responders must contain the attack before the firm restores from backup.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attack came through the very provider the plan relies on. Ask who can be trusted to contain it.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider is the attack path and may itself be compromised, so it cannot be trusted to investigate or contain the attack. Independent responders establish the scope, close the access path and protect evidence. Restoring from the bank's own backups is the right recovery source, but doing it before the intrusion is contained risks reinfection through the same remote tools.

wrong_explanations.A: The plan assumed an uncompromised provider. When the provider is the attack path, it cannot be the independent party that investigates and contains.
wrong_explanations.B: Clean backups are the right recovery source, but restoring before containment risks reinfection through the provider's still-open remote access.
wrong_explanations.D: Paying funds criminals, carries sanctions risk and does not guarantee decryption. Authorities advise against it.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts the compromised party, and D pays criminals with no guarantee of recovery.
Final two: C beats B because containment by an independent responder must precede restoration, or the attacker can reinfect restored systems.
Exam cue: when the recovery partner is the attack path, bring in an independent responder before restoring anything.

questions.question: A key customer's monitoring shows 99.2% availability, while the SaaS provider's own monitoring shows 99.93% against a 99.9% SLA. What should the IS auditor recommend the provider do FIRST?

options.A: Reject the claim because the provider's own monitoring shows compliance
options.B: Offer a goodwill service credit to preserve the relationship
options.C: Accept contract termination and focus on replacing the revenue
options.D: Reconcile both figures with the contract's availability definition

questions.key_concept: An SLA dispute starts with the contract's definition of the metric; reconcile both measurements to it before any commercial response.
questions.pre_read: Notice the two monitoring results disagree. Ask which document decides how availability is measured.
questions.correct_explanation: Two monitoring sources disagree, and the contract decides which measure counts: what is monitored, from where, and which outages are excluded. Reconciling both figures with that definition establishes the facts before any commercial response. A goodwill credit may follow, but offering it first concedes an unproven breach and sets a precedent for other customers with similar terms.

wrong_explanations.A: The provider's data is not automatically authoritative. The contract's measurement definition decides, and the customer's data may reveal a real gap.
wrong_explanations.B: A credit offered before the facts are known concedes an unproven breach and invites other customers with similar terms to claim the same.
wrong_explanations.C: Conceding termination abandons the account before anyone has checked whether the SLA was actually breached.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes the provider's data wins, and C gives up before the facts are known.
Final two: D beats B because the contract's measurement definition must settle the facts before any concession is offered.
Exam cue: when two parties' metrics disagree, go back to the agreed definition before taking a commercial position.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a firm's use of a cloud backup service under the shared responsibility model. Which finding is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Provider data-centre floor plans have not been shared with the firm
options.B: Restore testing is left to the provider's standard platform checks
options.C: Backup encryption keys are held and managed by the firm itself
options.D: Retention periods follow the provider's default backup settings

questions.key_concept: In cloud backup, the provider owns infrastructure while the customer owns its data, retention, keys and proof of restore.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option by which side of the shared responsibility model owns it, then weigh the firm's gaps.
questions.correct_explanation: Under shared responsibility the provider runs the infrastructure, but the firm owns its data, including proof that its backups can be restored. Platform checks show the service works, not that the firm's data comes back complete. Default retention is also the firm's to set and may breach its own rules, but untested recovery means the firm may not be able to recover at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Physical security of the facilities is the provider's responsibility and is covered by its assurance reports, not floor plans.
wrong_explanations.C: Customer-managed keys keep control of the data with the firm. This is good practice, not a weakness.
wrong_explanations.D: Retention is the firm's decision and defaults may conflict with policy, but an untested restore threatens whether any data can be recovered.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns the provider's side of the model, and C describes a good practice.
Final two: B beats D because untested recovery means the firm cannot show its data is recoverable, while default retention is a narrower policy gap.
Exam cue: in the cloud, the provider runs the platform but the customer still owns its data and must prove it can be restored.

questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing how a database team manages performance. Which evidence BEST shows that performance is managed proactively?

options.A: Monthly uptime percentages from the team's dashboard
options.B: Slow-query logs analyzed for root cause whenever users report delays
options.C: Trended metrics checked against agreed performance thresholds
options.D: The vendor's tuning guide stored on the team intranet

questions.key_concept: Proactive performance management compares trended metrics with an agreed baseline, so degradation is found before users report it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks for proactive management. Separate evidence gathered before users notice from evidence gathered after.
questions.correct_explanation: Proactive performance management needs a baseline of normal behaviour and trends compared against it, so degradation is spotted and capacity added before users notice. Slow-query review is useful tuning work, but triggered by user complaints it is reactive: it starts only after service has already suffered. Uptime and stored guidance say nothing about how performance is actually managed.

wrong_explanations.A: Uptime shows whether the database is available, not whether it performs well. A slow but running database still meets an uptime target.
wrong_explanations.B: Analyzing slow queries is useful, but triggering it from user complaints makes it reactive. Problems are found only after service has degraded.
wrong_explanations.D: A stored guide shows documentation exists, not that anyone follows it or measures the results.

tips: Eliminate: A measures availability rather than performance, and D shows documentation rather than practice.
Final two: C beats B because trends against agreed thresholds detect degradation before users do, while complaint-driven analysis reacts afterwards.
Exam cue: proactive management means a baseline plus trends; anything triggered by user complaints is reactive.

questions.question: A payments service keeps calling a failing fraud-check service, exhausting its threads and spreading the outage. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Circuit breakers that halt calls to the failing service
options.B: Retries with exponential backoff applied to every failed call
options.C: Higher service credits in the fraud-check vendor's contract
options.D: Redundant power feeds for the hosting data centre

questions.key_concept: A circuit breaker isolates a failing dependency so callers degrade gracefully instead of failing with it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the outage spreads through repeated calls. Ask which control stops the calls rather than spacing them out.
questions.correct_explanation: The outage spreads because the caller keeps waiting on a dependency that cannot answer. A circuit breaker stops those calls after a failure threshold, frees the threads and lets the payments service degrade gracefully. Backoff spaces out retries, but every failed call still holds resources and adds load to the struggling service, so the cascade continues more slowly.

wrong_explanations.B: Backoff spaces out retries, but the calls still tie up threads and add load to a failing service, so the cascade continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Service credits compensate after the outage. They do not stop one failing dependency from taking down the caller.
wrong_explanations.D: The failure is in an application dependency, not facility power. More power redundancy does not stop the cascade.

tips: Eliminate: C is a contractual remedy, and D addresses facility power rather than an application dependency.
Final two: A beats B because stopping calls to a failed dependency contains the cascade, while retries keep feeding it.
Exam cue: when one failing component drags others down, prefer the control that isolates it over one that keeps retrying.

questions.question: A critical system runs in two data centres 20 km apart that share a single metro fibre route. What is the GREATEST resilience concern for the IS auditor?

options.A: Replication between the two sites runs synchronously at this distance
options.B: DNS failover records use a long time-to-live setting
options.C: Each data centre runs its own uninterruptible power supply
options.D: One fibre cut or regional event could disable both sites

questions.key_concept: Geographic redundancy needs independent sites and network paths; a shared route or hazard zone is a single point of failure.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the two sites have in common. Ask whether one event could take out both.
questions.correct_explanation: Two sites only add resilience if they fail independently. A shared fibre route and the same regional hazard zone mean one cut, flood or power event can take both down together, so the second site gives little protection. A long DNS time-to-live slows failover, but failover still works; a common point of failure can defeat it entirely.

wrong_explanations.A: Synchronous replication is normal and practical at 20 km. It protects data rather than creating a resilience weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: A long time-to-live delays traffic moving to the surviving site, but failover still happens. A shared failure point can leave no surviving site.
wrong_explanations.C: Separate power protection at each site is good practice and supports their independence.

tips: Eliminate: A is normal at 20 km, and C is good practice.
Final two: D beats B because a shared failure point can defeat both sites at once, while a long time-to-live only slows failover.
Exam cue: redundancy is only as good as its independence; look for the dependency both copies share.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a procedure that lets on-call engineers deploy emergency fixes outside the change advisory board cycle. Which control is MOST important?

options.A: Engineer documentation of each change in its ticket after deployment
options.B: Independent review and approval of each change soon after deployment
options.C: Routing of every fix through the next scheduled CAB meeting
options.D: Tracking of engineer response times for each emergency fix

questions.key_concept: Emergency changes may bypass prior approval but must receive independent review and approval soon after implementation.
questions.pre_read: Notice who deploys the change. Ask who, other than the implementer, confirms afterwards that it was justified.
questions.correct_explanation: Emergency changes skip normal approval, so control must return through independent review soon afterwards: someone other than the implementer confirms the change was needed, authorised and correctly made. Engineer documentation creates a record, but a record written by the person who made the change is self-review and gives no independent assurance that the change was appropriate.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-documentation creates a record but no independent check. The implementer's own notes cannot confirm the change was justified or correct.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for the next scheduled meeting defeats the purpose of an emergency path when production is down.
wrong_explanations.D: Response time measures speed, not whether emergency changes were justified, authorised or correct.

tips: Eliminate: C defeats the purpose of an emergency path, and D measures speed rather than control.
Final two: B beats A because an independent reviewer gives assurance that the implementer's own record cannot.
Exam cue: emergency changes may skip prior approval but never skip control; look for independent review after the fact.

questions.question: Patch volume on a firm's internet-facing servers exceeds IT operations' capacity. Which factor should the IS auditor expect management to weight MOST when ordering patches?

options.A: The CVSS base score published for each vulnerability
options.B: The order in which vendors released each patch
options.C: Evidence that the flaw is being actively exploited
options.D: The download size and install time of each patch

questions.key_concept: Risk-based patching ranks known active exploitation on exposed assets above raw severity scores, vendor order or effort.
questions.pre_read: Notice the servers are internet-facing and capacity is short. Ask which factor shows the most immediate real-world threat.
questions.correct_explanation: When capacity is short, risk sets the order, and a flaw being exploited in the wild on exposed servers is the most immediate threat. Known-exploited catalogues exist for exactly this reason. The CVSS base score measures technical severity in isolation, so many high scores are never exploited while some lower-scored flaws are under active attack.

wrong_explanations.A: The base score rates technical severity in isolation. It ignores whether attackers are actually using the flaw, so it misorders many patches.
wrong_explanations.B: Release order reflects vendor schedules, not the risk each vulnerability poses to the firm.
wrong_explanations.D: Effort can help schedule work, but ordering by convenience leaves the most dangerous flaws open longest.

tips: Eliminate: B follows vendor timing, and D follows convenience rather than risk.
Final two: C beats A because active exploitation shows real, current threat, while a base score rates severity without that context.
Exam cue: in patch priority, known exploitation on exposed assets outranks a high score on paper.

questions.question: An IS auditor is reviewing a message queue platform that carries payment instructions between applications. Which test is MOST important?

options.A: Checking licence counts against installed broker nodes
options.B: Reading the software vendor's latest SOC 2 report
options.C: Reviewing queue-depth alert thresholds and their monitoring
options.D: Reconciling messages sent with messages received and processed

questions.key_concept: Middleware carrying financial transactions is tested first for completeness and integrity: every message sent is received and processed once.
questions.pre_read: Notice the platform carries payment instructions. Ask what would hurt most if a single message went missing.
questions.correct_explanation: For payment instructions, the key risk is a message that is lost, duplicated or altered in transit. Reconciling what was sent with what was received and processed tests completeness and integrity directly. Queue-depth alerts are a sound operational control that flags backlogs, but a queue can look healthy while individual messages are dropped or sent to a dead-letter queue unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.A: Licence compliance is a commercial matter. It says nothing about whether payment messages are complete or accurate.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor report covers the vendor's own controls, not how the firm configured and operates the platform for its payments.
wrong_explanations.C: Queue-depth monitoring shows backlogs and throughput, not whether each payment message arrived complete and was processed once.

tips: Eliminate: A is a licensing matter, and B covers the vendor rather than the firm's own platform.
Final two: D beats C because reconciliation proves each message arrived and was processed, while queue-depth alerts only show overall flow.
Exam cue: for data moving between systems, completeness and integrity tests outrank health monitoring.

questions.question: A disaster recovery plan requires the full executive committee to agree before the plan can be invoked. What is the GREATEST risk for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Invocation may be delayed beyond the recovery time objective
options.B: Members may rate system criticality inconsistently
options.C: The plan may be invoked too often for minor events
options.D: Recovery costs may exceed the approved business continuity budget

questions.key_concept: DR invocation needs a named authority and a backup; requiring consensus risks delaying recovery past the RTO.
questions.pre_read: Notice who must agree before invocation. Ask what happens to the recovery clock while they do.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery time objectives start counting at the disruption, not at the decision. Requiring every executive to agree means one absent or undecided member can delay invocation until the objective is already missed. Inconsistent criticality ratings are a real weakness, but documented triggers can fix them; the consensus requirement itself is what blocks a timely decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Inconsistent judgement is a weakness, but documented triggers can fix it. The consensus requirement is what blocks a timely decision.
wrong_explanations.C: A unanimous committee makes invocation harder, not easier, so over-invocation is the opposite of the real risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Cost overruns are a budget matter and are not created by the consensus requirement.

tips: Eliminate: C is the opposite of what consensus causes, and D is a budget matter.
Final two: A beats B because the consensus rule itself can block a timely decision, while inconsistent ratings can be fixed with defined triggers.
Exam cue: invocation needs a named decision-maker with a backup; any rule that needs everyone to agree risks missing the RTO.

questions.subtopic: Recovery Time Arithmetic. Parallel vs Serial
questions.question: A business continuity manager must estimate how long it will take to restore six interdependent systems after a disaster. Which method gives the MOST reliable estimate?

options.A: The single slowest system's own recovery time
options.B: The sum of every system's individual recovery time estimate
options.C: The longest dependency chain, given available staff
options.D: The duration of the last comparable recovery event

questions.key_concept: Total recovery time follows the critical path through system dependencies, adjusted for staff constraints, not the sum of all times.
questions.pre_read: Notice the systems depend on each other. Ask which ones can be restored at the same time.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent systems can be restored in parallel, while dependent ones must wait for what they rely on. The longest chain of dependencies, adjusted for how many staff can work at once, sets the real total. Adding every recovery time is safely conservative, but it assumes everything runs in series, overstates the total and can drive unnecessary spending on recovery strategy.

wrong_explanations.A: The slowest single system ignores dependencies: it may itself have to wait for others, so the real total can be longer.
wrong_explanations.B: Summing assumes everything is restored in series. It overstates the total and can lead to unnecessary investment in faster recovery options.
wrong_explanations.D: A past event had different systems, staff and conditions, so it cannot reliably predict this recovery.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores dependencies, and D relies on a different event.
Final two: C beats B because recovery runs in parallel where dependencies allow, so the dependency chain sets the total, not the sum.
Exam cue: total recovery time follows the critical path through dependencies, limited by the staff available.

questions.question: A newly formed crisis management team has never exercised the organization's continuity plan. Which exercise should the business continuity manager schedule FIRST?

options.A: A full-interruption test that shuts down production
options.B: A tabletop walkthrough of roles and key decisions
options.C: A parallel test that runs systems at the recovery site
options.D: A vendor-run drill that the crisis team watches as observers

questions.key_concept: BCM exercises progress from tabletop to simulation, parallel and full-interruption tests, each building capability for the next.
questions.pre_read: Notice the team has never exercised. Ask which exercise builds understanding without putting systems at risk.
questions.correct_explanation: A team that has never exercised needs to learn its roles and decision points before systems are moved. A tabletop walkthrough does this safely and exposes gaps in the plan cheaply. A parallel test is a valuable later step, but running recovery systems with a team unsure of its roles wastes the test and adds operational risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A full interruption of production is the riskiest test and is used only after lower-level exercises have succeeded.
wrong_explanations.C: Parallel tests come later in the progression. Running them before the team knows its roles wastes the test and adds operational risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching someone else's drill does not build the team's own decision-making or test its understanding of the plan.

tips: Eliminate: A risks production with an untrained team, and D leaves the team as spectators.
Final two: B beats C because exercises progress from discussion to live systems; the team must know its roles first.
Exam cue: build exercises step by step, tabletop before parallel and parallel before full interruption.

questions.subtopic: Vendor SOC Report Types and Audit Reliance
questions.question: An IS auditor plans to rely on a critical vendor's SOC 2 Type II report as audit evidence. Which check is MOST important before placing reliance?

options.A: Confirming the report's scope covers the services the firm uses
options.B: Confirming the service auditor issued an unmodified opinion
options.C: Requesting the vendor's SOC 3 report as a substitute
options.D: Re-performing a full set of the service auditor's control tests

questions.key_concept: Reliance on a SOC report starts with relevance: its scope and period must cover the services and period under audit.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the report is used as evidence. Ask whether it covers the services the firm actually uses.
questions.correct_explanation: A report gives assurance only over the systems and services it covers. If the services the firm uses are outside its scope, even a clean opinion provides no evidence for them. The opinion matters, and any qualifications must be weighed, but an unmodified opinion on the wrong scope is still irrelevant to the audit objective.

wrong_explanations.B: A clean opinion matters, but it applies only to what was in scope. An unmodified opinion on the wrong services gives no evidence for this audit.
wrong_explanations.C: A SOC 3 report is a brief public summary without test details, so it gives less evidence than the Type II report.
wrong_explanations.D: Re-performing everything defeats the purpose of relying on another auditor's work and is rarely justified.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps in a less detailed report, and D discards the reliance entirely.
Final two: A beats B because an opinion only means something for the scope it covers; relevance must be confirmed first.
Exam cue: before relying on another auditor's work, confirm it covers what you need, then judge its results.

questions.question: A manufacturer is adding its SCADA-controlled production lines to continuity planning. Which approach should the business continuity manager take as BEST practice?

options.A: Including OT in the enterprise plan with its own recovery sequences
options.B: Keeping a separate OT continuity plan owned solely by plant engineering
options.C: Applying existing IT recovery targets unchanged to OT systems
options.D: Adopting equipment vendors' playbooks as the OT recovery plan

questions.key_concept: OT continuity needs OT-specific recovery sequences and safety steps, integrated into the enterprise plan rather than run as a silo.
questions.pre_read: Notice the systems are industrial. Ask how to respect their differences while keeping them in the enterprise plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Operational technology needs its own recovery sequences, with safe start-up order and manual operation, but it must sit inside the enterprise plan so business impact sets priorities and IT and plant teams coordinate. A separate engineering-owned plan captures the technical detail, but it leaves OT outside enterprise priorities, testing and oversight, so gaps between the IT and OT recoveries go unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.B: An engineering-only plan captures technical detail but sits outside enterprise priorities and oversight, so IT and OT recoveries are not coordinated.
wrong_explanations.C: Industrial systems have physical safety and start-up order constraints that IT recovery targets and runbooks do not address.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor playbooks cover equipment, not the firm's own priorities, staff and dependencies. Accountability for continuity stays with the firm.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores OT's physical safety constraints, and D hands the plan to suppliers.
Final two: A beats B because OT needs its own sequences inside one enterprise plan, so business impact and coordination cover both IT and OT.
Exam cue: specialised systems need tailored procedures, but within one enterprise continuity programme, not a silo.

questions.question: Attackers have phoned a firm's help desk posing as executives to request MFA resets. Which control should the IT service manager implement as MOST effective?

options.A: Training agents to recognise social-engineering pressure tactics
options.B: Shortening reset times to reduce executive complaints
options.C: Requiring out-of-band identity verification before any MFA reset
options.D: Outsourcing the help desk to transfer the liability

questions.key_concept: Help-desk resets of privileged credentials need out-of-band identity verification, a process control that does not rely on agent judgement.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attackers impersonate executives by phone. Ask which control removes the voice as proof of identity.
questions.correct_explanation: The attack works because a convincing voice is accepted as proof of identity. Verifying the caller through a separate, pre-registered channel before any reset removes that weakness, however persuasive the caller is. Training raises awareness and helps, but it still depends on each agent spotting a skilled impostor under pressure, which attackers are practised at defeating.

wrong_explanations.A: Training helps, but it relies on each agent judging a skilled impostor under pressure. A verification step does not depend on that judgement.
wrong_explanations.B: Faster resets serve convenience and make the attacker's job easier, not harder.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability, and does nothing to verify callers.

tips: Eliminate: B helps the attacker, and D moves the work without fixing verification.
Final two: C beats A because a mandatory verification step works regardless of how convincing the caller is, while training relies on judgement.
Exam cue: prefer a control built into the process over one that relies on people noticing an attack.

questions.question: A firm relies on autoscaling for a cloud-native application but does not track the provider's service quotas. What is the GREATEST capacity risk for the IS auditor to report?

options.A: Developers may lose access to the provider's console
options.B: Autoscaling may stall at quota limits during peak demand
options.C: Unchecked scaling may cause unplanned cloud cost overruns each month
options.D: The provider may raise prices for reserved capacity

questions.key_concept: Cloud capacity planning must track provider service quotas, because autoscaling stops at those hard limits during peak demand.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the firm does not track. Ask what happens to autoscaling when it reaches that limit.
questions.correct_explanation: Autoscaling only works up to the account's service quotas. If nobody tracks them, the application can hit a hard limit at the busiest moment and fail to scale, causing an outage when demand is highest. Unexpected cost is a real risk of autoscaling, but it is a financial issue; the stem asks about capacity and availability.

wrong_explanations.A: Console access is an access management issue, unrelated to whether the application can scale under load.
wrong_explanations.C: Cost overruns are a real autoscaling risk, but they are a financial issue. They do not stop the application from serving users at peak.
wrong_explanations.D: Price changes affect budget, not whether capacity is available when demand rises.

tips: Eliminate: A is an access matter, and D is a pricing matter.
Final two: B beats C because a quota limit causes an outage at peak demand, while cost overruns are a financial rather than capacity risk.
Exam cue: elastic does not mean unlimited; cloud capacity planning includes tracking provider quotas.

questions.subtopic: Cloud Backup Ransomware. Object-Lock Bypass Attempt
questions.question: During a ransomware attack, Object Lock protected recent cloud backups, but attackers are now deleting older unlocked backups. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Pay the ransom because outage costs exceed the demand
options.B: Restore production immediately from the locked snapshots
options.C: Extend retention on the snapshots already under Object Lock
options.D: Revoke the attackers' access to the cloud backup account

questions.key_concept: During an active ransomware attack, contain the attacker's access first; restoring before containment risks re-encryption and further backup loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice the attackers are still active in the backup account. Ask what must stop before recovery can begin.
questions.correct_explanation: The attackers still hold access to the backup account and are destroying recovery options now. Revoking that access stops the deletion and is the containment step that must come before restoration. Restoring at once from the locked snapshots is tempting, but while the attackers remain inside, restored systems can be re-encrypted and the remaining backups lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Paying funds criminals, carries sanctions risk and does not guarantee recovery, especially when protected backups exist.
wrong_explanations.B: The locked snapshots are the right source, but restoring while the attackers still have access invites re-encryption and further backup loss.
wrong_explanations.C: The locked snapshots are already protected. Extending their retention does nothing to stop the deletion that is happening now.

tips: Eliminate: A pays criminals when clean backups exist, and C protects what is already safe.
Final two: D beats B because containment comes before recovery; restoring while attackers have access risks losing the restore too.
Exam cue: in an active attack, contain first, then restore; a restore into a live intrusion can be undone.

questions.question: A cloud region outage is two hours old with 6–12 hours to restore against a four-hour RTO, and the BCP names the CIO as invocation authority. What should the recovery manager do FIRST?

options.A: Fail over workloads for the customers who are demanding it
options.B: Invoke failover now and brief the CIO once it completes
options.C: Escalate to the CIO now for an immediate failover decision
options.D: Have the CIO wait for the provider's four-hour update

questions.key_concept: When an outage will exceed the RTO, the invocation decision must be made quickly by the authority the plan names.
questions.pre_read: Compare the provider's estimate with the RTO. Then check who the plan says makes the invocation decision.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider's estimate already exceeds the four-hour RTO, so a failover decision is needed now, but the BCP gives that decision to the CIO. Escalating immediately gets an authorized invocation within minutes. Invoking without the CIO feels decisive, but it bypasses the plan's named authority, and failover commits cost and data-loss trade-offs that the plan reserves for that executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Choosing by which customers complain replaces the plan's business-impact priorities with pressure from the loudest voices.
wrong_explanations.B: The plan reserves invocation for the CIO. Acting first and briefing later bypasses that authority when escalation takes only minutes.
wrong_explanations.D: By hour four the RTO has already passed, and failover still takes time. The current estimate is enough for the CIO to decide now.

tips: Eliminate: A lets customer pressure override the plan's priorities, and D waits until the RTO is already lost.
Final two: C beats B because the plan names the CIO as invocation authority, and escalating now costs minutes, not the RTO.
Exam cue: once the trigger is met, get the decision fast from the authority the plan names; neither wait nor bypass it.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds an emergency change that disabled an API authentication step was never reverted, and logs show an unknown IP accessed customer records. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Re-enable the authentication step on the API immediately
options.B: Begin a forensic review of the unknown IP's access
options.C: Wait for the on-call engineer to return and revert it
options.D: Record the event as a near miss in the change log

questions.key_concept: When a control gap is actively exposing data, contain it first while preserving evidence, then investigate and assess notification duties.
questions.pre_read: Notice the authentication step is still disabled. Ask what stops further access right now.
questions.correct_explanation: The open authentication gap is still exposing customer data, so containment comes first: re-enable the control, preserving logs as you do. A forensic review is essential and must follow quickly to scope the breach and support notification decisions, but investigating while the gap stays open lets further access continue.

wrong_explanations.B: Forensics is essential to scope the breach, but investigating while the authentication gap stays open allows further access to customer data.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for one person leaves the exposure open. Any authorised engineer can restore the control under the emergency process.
wrong_explanations.D: Customer records were accessed by an unknown party. This is a potential breach, not a near miss.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the exposure open, and D misclassifies a potential breach.
Final two: A beats B because containment stops further access; the investigation follows immediately but cannot come first.
Exam cue: in an active exposure, close the gap first, preserve evidence while doing so, then investigate.

questions.question: A binding directive requires a known-exploited vulnerability be patched within three days, but patching needs an outage before a fixed contract deliverable. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Defer the patch under a signed internal risk-acceptance memo
options.B: Seek a formal directive extension with compensating controls
options.C: Hold the patch for the next monthly maintenance cycle
options.D: Patch the test environment first and production after the deliverable

questions.key_concept: Internal risk acceptance cannot override an external mandate; use the mandate's formal exception process with compensating controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice the deadline is set by an external directive. Ask who has authority to grant a delay.
questions.correct_explanation: Management can accept risks it owns, but not waive an external mandate. The directive's formal exception route, with compensating controls in place meanwhile, keeps the firm compliant while protecting the deliverable. Internal risk acceptance is the normal tool for deferring patches, but here it would document a breach of the directive rather than authorise the delay.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal risk acceptance cannot waive an external directive. It would record a known violation instead of obtaining permission for the delay.
wrong_explanations.C: The monthly cycle ignores the three-day mandate and leaves an exploited flaw open.
wrong_explanations.D: Patching test systems leaves production exposed to a flaw already being exploited.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores the deadline, and D leaves production exposed.
Final two: B beats A because management can accept its own risks but cannot waive an external mandate; the formal exception route can.
Exam cue: when an external rule and a business need clash, use the rule's own exception process rather than internal sign-off.

options.B: Isolate the SCADA network to preserve forensic evidence

questions.subtopic: DR Test Reveals Ambiguous Invocation Criteria
questions.question: In a DR exercise, teams spent 47 minutes debating invocation because the plan's triggers said only “significant impact”. What is the BEST recommendation for the IS auditor to give the business continuity manager?

options.A: Retrain participants on the existing invocation wording
options.B: Commission a full rewrite of the continuity plan
options.C: Accept the debate as normal judgement under pressure
options.D: Define measurable invocation thresholds and re-test them

questions.key_concept: Ambiguous invocation triggers should be replaced with measurable thresholds and validated by a re-test, a targeted fix rather than a rewrite.
questions.pre_read: Notice the exercise exposed one specific problem. Ask which response fixes it fastest and proves the fix works.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise exposed a design gap: vague triggers that reasonable people read differently. Measurable thresholds for each severity, then a re-test to confirm they work, fix that specific gap quickly. A full rewrite would eventually address it, but it widens the scope, takes months and leaves the known weakness open in the meantime.

wrong_explanations.A: The participants followed the wording; the wording is the problem. Training on vague triggers cannot make them clear.
wrong_explanations.B: A full rewrite eventually covers the gap, but it takes months and leaves the known invocation weakness open while the project runs.
wrong_explanations.C: A 47-minute delay in invocation directly eats into recovery time objectives. It is a weakness to fix, not normal behaviour.

tips: Eliminate: A trains people on wording that is itself the problem, and C accepts a delay that threatens recovery objectives.
Final two: D beats B because a targeted fix closes the known gap now, while a full rewrite leaves it open for months.
Exam cue: when a test exposes one specific gap, fix that gap and re-test rather than starting a broad rewrite.

questions.question: An IT operations manager is setting up governance for a new configuration management database (CMDB). Which action should be performed FIRST?

options.A: Enable automated discovery to populate records in every environment
options.B: Define the in-scope item classes and their owners
options.C: Transfer data-model accountability to the ITSM tool vendor
options.D: Schedule monthly data-quality reviews of the populated records

questions.key_concept: CMDB governance starts with scope, a class model and named owners; discovery and quality checks only work against that defined baseline.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word FIRST. Ask what every later CMDB activity, including discovery and quality review, needs to exist beforehand.
questions.correct_explanation: Configuration management under COBIT BAI10 starts by defining which configuration items matter, how they are classified and who owns each class. Without that model, discovery and reviews have nothing to measure against. Automated discovery is valuable, but run first it floods the database with unowned, unclassified records that nobody is accountable for keeping accurate.

wrong_explanations.A: Discovery before scope floods the CMDB with unclassified, unowned records. It is a later step that feeds a defined configuration model.
wrong_explanations.C: Accountability for configuration data cannot be handed to a tool vendor. The organization must own its configuration model and data.
wrong_explanations.D: Quality reviews need a defined model and owners to measure against. Scheduled first, they review records nobody has agreed the standard for.

tips: Eliminate: C hands accountability to a vendor, and D reviews data quality before any standard for that data exists.
Final two: B beats A because scope and ownership must exist before discovery, or the tool fills the CMDB with unowned noise.
Exam cue: when setting up any repository FIRST, define scope and owners before automating collection.
