questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the asset inventory of a firm running workloads on three cloud providers. Which practice provides the MOST reliable inventory?

options.A: Quarterly spreadsheet updates kept by each platform's own team
options.B: Monthly billing reports reconciled to cost-center codes
options.C: A single account per business unit to simplify scope
options.D: Continuous API discovery checked against mandatory ownership tags

questions.key_concept: Cloud resources appear and vanish in minutes, so a reliable inventory needs continuous provider-API discovery tied to enforced ownership tags.
questions.pre_read: Think about how fast cloud resources change. Ask which source sees a new resource the moment it exists and knows who owns it.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloud resources are created and destroyed in minutes, so only continuous discovery through each provider's APIs keeps pace. Checking results against mandatory ownership tags turns a list of resources into an accountable inventory. Billing reports are tempting because they cover every paid service, but they lag, miss configuration detail and cannot say who owns or approved an untagged resource.

wrong_explanations.A: A quarterly spreadsheet is out of date within days in the cloud. Manual updates also miss resources teams forget to record.
wrong_explanations.B: Billing lags usage, omits configuration detail and cannot identify owners of untagged resources. It supports reconciliation but is not the authoritative inventory.
wrong_explanations.C: Account structure can simplify management, but it does not discover or record the resources inside each account.

tips: Eliminate: A is a stale manual snapshot, and C changes account structure without inventorying anything.
Final two: D beats B because continuous discovery with ownership tags is timely and accountable, while billing lags and cannot name owners.
Exam cue: for fast-changing environments, prefer continuous automated sources over periodic or financial proxies.

questions.question: A business continuity manager finds that only one engineer can restore the core payment platform. Which action BEST addresses this workforce risk?

options.A: Cross-train a second engineer and rehearse the restore
options.B: Document the restore steps in a detailed runbook for others
options.C: Buy key-person insurance covering the engineer's absence
options.D: Outsource the platform restore to a managed service vendor

questions.key_concept: Single-person dependency is resolved by building tested capability in another person, not by documents, insurance or outsourcing alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would actually happen on the day the engineer is unavailable. Which option proves someone else can do the restore?
questions.correct_explanation: The risk is that recovery depends on one person. Cross-training a second engineer and rehearsing the restore creates proven, alternate capability, which ISO 22301 expects plans and people to demonstrate through exercises. A runbook is useful, but an untested document read for the first time during an outage often fails; it supports cross-training rather than replacing it.

wrong_explanations.B: A runbook nobody has followed is untested. It helps, but it does not prove anyone else can perform the restore under pressure.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance compensates financially but restores nothing. The platform still cannot be recovered when the engineer is absent.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing moves the dependency to a vendor that does not yet know the platform, and the organization stays accountable for recovery.

tips: Eliminate: C only pays out money, and D shifts the dependency to an outsider who lacks platform knowledge.
Final two: A beats B because a rehearsed second person is tested capability, while a runbook alone is an untested plan.
Exam cue: in continuity questions, tested capability beats untested documentation every time.

questions.question: A business continuity manager is designing a quarterly dashboard for executive oversight of the BCM program. Which metric is MOST useful?

options.A: Number of exercises completed against the annual test plan
options.B: Total program spend compared with the approved budget
options.C: Recovery times achieved in exercises against each RTO
options.D: Maturity score compared with industry peer organizations

questions.key_concept: Executives need outcome metrics: whether recovery capability meets business-set RTOs, not merely whether activities happened or money was spent.
questions.pre_read: Separate metrics that show activity from those that show capability. Which one tells executives the business could actually recover in time?
questions.correct_explanation: Oversight should show whether the program delivers its purpose: recovering critical services within the RTOs the business impact analysis set. Comparing achieved recovery times with RTOs is an outcome measure under ISO 22301 performance evaluation. Counting completed exercises looks rigorous, but it shows activity only; every exercise could run on schedule and still miss its recovery targets.

wrong_explanations.A: Exercise counts measure activity. Exercises can all be completed while recovery still fails to meet the business's targets.
wrong_explanations.B: Spend against budget shows financial control, not whether critical services can be recovered in time.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer maturity scores describe relative process maturity, not whether this organization meets its own recovery objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B tracks money rather than resilience, and D compares process maturity with peers instead of with the firm's own targets.
Final two: C beats A because achieved recovery against RTOs measures outcomes, while exercise counts only measure activity.
Exam cue: for oversight metrics, choose the outcome tied to business objectives over activity or cost counts.

questions.question: Both cloud providers in a firm's failover design are degraded at once, and a third provider holds no production deployment. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Fail over to the third provider using improvised runbooks
options.B: Post hourly status updates while monitoring provider dashboards
options.C: Escalate to the CEO to lead the provider negotiations
options.D: Run in degraded mode with non-critical features disabled

questions.key_concept: When no tested failover path exists, controlled degraded operation protects service more safely than an improvised migration to an untested environment.
questions.pre_read: Note that the third provider has no production deployment. Ask which option keeps customers served without adding untested risk.
questions.correct_explanation: With both planned recovery paths degraded, the safest way to keep critical service running is controlled degraded-mode operation that sheds non-critical features. Failing over to a provider with no production deployment means building and cutting over under pressure with improvised runbooks, an untested change that can corrupt data or cause a second outage. The broken independence assumption should be reviewed after service is stable.

wrong_explanations.A: An improvised cutover to an environment with no production deployment is an untested plan executed in a crisis, risking a worse outage.
wrong_explanations.B: Status updates matter, but communication alone does nothing to keep critical services running for customers.
wrong_explanations.C: Executive escalation does not restore service, and provider negotiations cannot fix their outages faster.

tips: Eliminate: B only communicates, and C escalates without restoring any service.
Final two: D beats A because a controlled degraded mode is predictable, while an improvised failover to an empty environment is untested.
Exam cue: in an outage, prefer a known, controlled state over an untested recovery path built on the fly.

questions.question: An online retailer's autoscaling hits a soft cloud quota its provider can raise on request, and 28% of requests time out; no queueing exists. What should the IS auditor recommend the operations head do FIRST?

options.A: Raise an urgent quota-increase request with the cloud provider
options.B: Deploy the full site to a secondary region immediately
options.C: Take the discounted product offline to cut demand
options.D: Build request queueing so the site degrades gracefully

questions.key_concept: A soft cloud quota is an administrative limit; asking the provider to lift it is faster and safer than building new controls mid-incident.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of limit was hit and who can lift it fastest.
questions.correct_explanation: The binding constraint is a soft quota, an administrative limit the provider can lift quickly, so an urgent increase request is the fastest way to restore capacity. Building request queueing is sound resilience engineering, but with none in place, designing and deploying it during a live spike is a risky change that will not land sooner than the provider's response.

wrong_explanations.B: A full secondary-region deployment under load is a major, untested change. It takes hours and risks data inconsistency.
wrong_explanations.C: Pulling the promotion is a business decision that sacrifices revenue and reputation instead of managing the technical capacity problem.
wrong_explanations.D: Queueing helps future spikes, but building it mid-incident is an untested change that takes longer than lifting a soft quota.

tips: Eliminate: B attempts a risky regional rebuild under load, and C sacrifices the business to fix a technical constraint.
Final two: A beats D because the provider can lift a soft quota quickly, while building queueing mid-incident is slow and risky.
Exam cue: when the limit is administrative, remove it at the source before engineering around it mid-incident.

questions.question: Cloud spend ran at seven times normal for six days because cost-anomaly alerts went only to one engineer on leave. Which recommendation should the IS auditor make to BEST prevent recurrence?

options.A: Lower the anomaly thresholds so overruns are flagged sooner
options.B: Seek a service credit from the provider for the overrun
options.C: Route anomaly alerts to a monitored team queue with backup
options.D: Revoke developers' rights to provision new cloud resources

questions.key_concept: A detective control fails if its alerts reach no one; alert ownership needs a monitored queue and backup, not one individual.
questions.pre_read: Find the exact point where the control broke. Did the alert fail to fire, or did it fire and reach nobody?
questions.correct_explanation: The alerts worked; they reached a single person who was absent, so nobody acted. Routing them to a monitored team queue with a named backup removes that single point of failure in the response. Lowering thresholds is tempting, but it makes alerts fire earlier into the same unattended inbox, so the overrun would still go unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.A: Earlier alerts still land with an absent recipient. The control broke at delivery and response, not at detection sensitivity.
wrong_explanations.B: A credit may recover some cost, but it changes no control and the same gap remains for the next overrun.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking provisioning halts development work and is disproportionate. It ignores the real failure in alert ownership.

tips: Eliminate: B recovers money without fixing any control, and D blocks legitimate work instead of fixing alert ownership.
Final two: C beats A because the alert fired but reached nobody, so delivery, not sensitivity, must be fixed.
Exam cue: when a control fails, recommend the fix at the exact point it broke.

questions.question: A hospital network's EHR vendor proposes a 38% renewal increase; the offer expires in 21 days and migration would take three years. What should the IS auditor recommend the COO do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the renewal to avoid any clinical service disruption
options.B: Analyze total cost of ownership and benchmark market pricing
options.C: Issue an RFP and begin migration to a competing system
options.D: Refer the negotiation decision to the board for its direction

questions.key_concept: Vendor decisions need facts first: total cost of ownership and market benchmarks give the negotiating position and the basis for any governance decision.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word FIRST. Before anyone decides, ask what information the decision-makers still lack.
questions.correct_explanation: No decision-maker can judge a 38% increase without knowing total cost of ownership and what comparable contracts cost. That analysis, under COBIT APO10 vendor management, supports negotiation on specific elements and frames any board discussion. Referring the matter to the board is reasonable for a contract this size, but sending it up before the analysis exists asks the board to decide without evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting without analysis concedes the increase and gives up all leverage, when the deadline still allows a short review.
wrong_explanations.C: A three-year EHR migration carries major clinical risk. Committing to it before analysis turns a pricing dispute into an operational gamble.
wrong_explanations.D: Board engagement may follow, but escalating before cost and benchmark analysis exists asks the board to decide without evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A concedes without analysis, and C commits to a high-risk migration before the facts are known.
Final two: B beats D because the board needs cost and benchmark evidence before it can decide well.
Exam cue: when FIRST is asked about a major decision, gather and analyze the facts before escalating.

questions.subtopic: IAM Compromise via Stolen API Tokens
questions.question: Threat hunters find phished customer API tokens with read-write access being used from anomalous locations, and some data has already left. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Revoke the tokens and preserve evidence of their use
options.B: Keep the tokens live to gather more attacker intelligence
options.C: Notify affected customers and await their instructions first
options.D: Await law enforcement direction before taking technical action

questions.key_concept: When active misuse is exposing customer data, containment comes first; evidence is preserved alongside it, not by leaving the access open.
questions.pre_read: Notice that data is already leaving. Ask which option stops further loss while keeping what investigators will need.
questions.correct_explanation: Live tokens with read-write access are exposing customer data right now, so containment comes first under NIST incident handling: revoke them and preserve the logs of their use. Keeping the tokens active to study the attacker is a legitimate tactic in some hunts, but here it knowingly lets customer data keep leaving, putting intelligence ahead of protecting data.

wrong_explanations.B: Watching the attacker gives intelligence but lets exfiltration continue. Protecting customer data outranks studying the adversary.
wrong_explanations.C: Customers must be informed, but the provider controls the tokens and must contain first rather than wait for instructions.
wrong_explanations.D: Law enforcement rarely requires victims to leave active data loss unchecked. Containment with preserved evidence supports any later investigation.

tips: Eliminate: C waits on customers who cannot revoke the tokens, and D lets data loss continue pending outside direction.
Final two: A beats B because protecting customer data outranks gathering intelligence while exfiltration is active.
Exam cue: when data is actively leaving, contain first and preserve evidence as you do it.

questions.subtopic: Stakeholder Pressure to Skip BCP Exercise
questions.question: A CFO asks to defer a bank's quarterly failover exercise, committed to examiners, by six months because of acquisition workload. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the COO?

options.A: Approve the deferral with a signed risk-acceptance memo
options.B: Replace the failover with a walkthrough run by finance staff
options.C: Cancel the exercise and rely on last quarter's results
options.D: Run a scoped failover of remediated gaps on schedule

questions.key_concept: A regulatory test commitment can be right-sized to resource limits, but it should still be met; scope flexes before the commitment does.
questions.pre_read: Note that the exercise is a commitment to examiners. Ask how to honor it while respecting the real workload pressure.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise is a commitment to examiners and the way to prove last quarter's gaps were fixed. A scoped failover focused on the remediated gaps keeps that commitment on schedule while easing the load on staff busy with the acquisition. Formal risk acceptance is management's prerogative, but deferring six months breaks a regulatory commitment and leaves recovery capability unproven during a risky integration.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk acceptance is management's right, but a six-month deferral breaks an examiner commitment and leaves remediation unverified during integration.
wrong_explanations.B: A walkthrough by finance staff is a lower-rigour test owned by the wrong team. It cannot prove failover capability.
wrong_explanations.C: Last quarter's exercise found the gaps; it cannot show they are fixed. Relying on it gives false assurance.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps a technical test for a walkthrough by the wrong team, and C relies on results that exposed the gaps.
Final two: D beats A because right-sizing the scope keeps the regulatory commitment, while deferral breaks it.
Exam cue: when a required test clashes with workload, reduce scope before you reduce frequency.

questions.subtopic: Insider Threat Detected During DR Exercise
questions.question: Midway through a DR exercise, a DBA with authorized read rights queries customer tables outside the exercise scope, with no sign of data leaving. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Suspend the DBA's access and remove them from the exercise
options.B: Ask the DBA's manager to question the DBA during the exercise
options.C: Preserve the logs and engage HR and legal before any confrontation
options.D: Log the anomaly and review it after the exercise ends

questions.key_concept: With ambiguous but authorized insider activity, secure evidence and coordinate HR and legal before any visible action that could alert the person.
questions.pre_read: Note the access is authorized and nothing has left yet. Ask what must be in place before anyone acts visibly.
questions.correct_explanation: The access is technically authorized and nothing shows data leaving, so the evidence is ambiguous. Preserving the logs and engaging HR and legal first protects the investigation and the employee's rights, and the activity can be watched meanwhile. Immediate suspension is a reasonable containment step when harm is clear, but here it alerts the DBA, may destroy evidence and disrupts the exercise on unconfirmed suspicion.

wrong_explanations.A: Suspension alerts the DBA and disrupts the exercise before evidence is secured or the activity is understood.
wrong_explanations.B: An untrained manager questioning the DBA tips them off and risks evidence and legal process.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting until the exercise ends leaves the activity unexamined and logs at risk of being overwritten or altered.

tips: Eliminate: B tips off the DBA through an untrained interview, and D lets evidence age while activity continues unexamined.
Final two: C beats A because ambiguous, authorized access calls for securing evidence and coordination before visible action.
Exam cue: in suspected insider cases without active data loss, preserve evidence and involve HR and legal before confronting.

questions.question: After a failed Big Bang integration cutover, point-of-sale, inventory and payroll systems are broken, and the first rollback attempt failed. What should the IS auditor recommend the CEO do FIRST?

options.A: Retry the rollback with a larger vendor team
options.B: Appoint one incident commander to triage and set priorities
options.C: Give external consultants authority over the rollback decision
options.D: Force forward by fixing each broken function in turn

questions.key_concept: In a multi-front crisis, a single incident command structure must set priorities before teams commit to rollback or force-forward actions.
questions.pre_read: Count the broken systems and competing options. Ask what has to exist before anyone can choose between them sensibly.
questions.correct_explanation: Several critical functions are failing and the first recovery attempt already failed, so uncoordinated action is the main danger. A single incident commander can triage by business impact, put payroll ahead of lower priorities and decide between rollback and force-forward with facts. Retrying the rollback sounds like restoring a known state, but the method already failed once, and repeating it without diagnosis risks more damage.

wrong_explanations.A: Repeating a failed rollback with more people, before anyone understands why it failed, can deepen data damage.
wrong_explanations.C: Consultants can advise, but decision authority over the business's recovery must stay with management.
wrong_explanations.D: Fixing functions one by one ignores business impact. Payroll and sales may wait behind lower-priority repairs.

tips: Eliminate: C hands management's decision to outsiders, and D works through repairs without business-impact priorities.
Final two: B beats A because coordinated command and triage must come before repeating a recovery method that already failed.
Exam cue: when several systems fail at once, establish command and priorities before choosing technical fixes.

questions.question: At a hospital, an IS auditor finds 47 terminated users still hold clinical system access because HR emails leaver lists to IT weekly. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Disable the 47 accounts and check them for post-termination logins
options.B: Automate the leaver feed from the HR system into identity management
options.C: Ask managers to recertify team access at next quarter's review
options.D: Accept the risk since clinical areas also need badge entry

questions.key_concept: Deprovisioning must be timely; when orphaned accounts are found, disable them and check for misuse before re-engineering the leaver process.
questions.pre_read: Notice the accounts are still active today. Ask what removes the exposure fastest, then what prevents recurrence.
questions.correct_explanation: The 47 active accounts are a live exposure today, so the first step is to disable them and check whether any were used after termination, which may reveal an incident to handle. Automating the HR feed is the right root-cause fix and should follow, but building it takes weeks while the known orphaned accounts stay open to misuse.

wrong_explanations.B: Automation fixes future leavers but takes time to build, leaving the 47 known orphaned accounts usable in the meantime.
wrong_explanations.C: Quarterly recertification is a slow detective control; it leaves known orphaned accounts open for months.
wrong_explanations.D: Badge control does not stop remote or shared-workstation use of a valid account, so the logical exposure remains.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves known orphaned accounts open until a quarterly review, and D relies on physical access to cover a logical gap.
Final two: A beats B because known live exposure is removed first; the automated feed fixes the process afterward.
Exam cue: when a review finds active exposure, contain the known cases first, then fix the process that created them.

questions.question: At hour 18 of a 24-hour DR exercise, only 30% of recovery objectives are met, and the FDIC will receive the report. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the business continuity head?

options.A: Extend the window past 24 hours to raise the score
options.B: Restart from hour zero and report the rerun results instead
options.C: Stop the test, rank failures and notify the examiner proactively
options.D: Close the exercise record with an internal lessons-learned memo

questions.key_concept: A failed exercise is valuable evidence: stop it, analyze the failures for remediation and be transparent with the regulator.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the exercise is for. Does a failure need hiding or improving, or does it need analyzing and reporting honestly?
questions.correct_explanation: An exercise exists to find weaknesses, and this one has found several. Stopping it, ranking the failures by cause for remediation and informing the examiner proactively turns the result into an improvement plan and preserves regulatory trust. An internal lessons-learned memo records the failures, but it neither drives prioritized remediation nor tells the regulator, who will read the report anyway.

wrong_explanations.A: Stretching the window distorts the test conditions to improve the score, so the report no longer reflects real recovery capability.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting a clean rerun instead of the actual result misleads the regulator and hides the failures the exercise exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: A memo documents the failures but lacks prioritized remediation and leaves the examiner to discover the problems unprepared.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both manipulate the results the regulator will see, rather than learning from them.
Final two: C beats D because analyzed failures and proactive regulator contact drive remediation, while a memo only records.
Exam cue: a failed test is a finding to analyze and disclose, never a score to improve.

questions.subtopic: Data Corruption Recovery vs Business Deadline
questions.question: Storage corruption has damaged 8% of yesterday's trade records on settlement day; restoring the clean backup and replaying logs takes 6–8 hours. What should the IS auditor recommend the CFO do FIRST?

options.A: Settle using best-available data and correct the records afterward
options.B: Reconcile each affected trade manually before settling
options.C: Ask the clearing firm for an extension before taking action
options.D: Restore and replay from backup while notifying the regulator early

questions.key_concept: Integrity of settlement data comes first; the fastest verified recovery path plus early regulator contact beats settling on corrupt data.
questions.pre_read: Compare the recovery options against the deadline. Which one produces verified data in time, and who should hear early?
questions.correct_explanation: Settlement must rest on accurate records. Restoring the clean backup and replaying the transaction logs is the fastest route to verified data within the deadline, and telling the regulator early protects the firm if timing slips. Manual reconciliation is accurate in principle, but reworking thousands of trades by hand is far slower and more error-prone than a replay.

wrong_explanations.A: Settling on known-corrupt data harms customers and breaches books-and-records duties. Later correction does not undo that.
wrong_explanations.B: Manually reconciling thousands of trades takes far longer than a replay and introduces human error under deadline pressure.
wrong_explanations.C: Extensions are rarely granted, and waiting for an answer wastes hours that the restore needs.

tips: Eliminate: A knowingly settles on corrupt data, and C spends scarce hours waiting for an unlikely extension.
Final two: D beats B because a backup replay yields verified data far faster and more reliably than manual rework.
Exam cue: for corrupted data, choose the fastest verified recovery and engage regulators before deadlines, not after.

questions.subtopic: Help Desk Overwhelmed During Major Event
questions.question: During a campus email outage, help-desk tickets jump fivefold, mostly duplicates from users unaware the outage is universal. What should the IS auditor recommend the CIO do FIRST?

options.A: Reassign administrative staff to answer help-desk phone queues
options.B: Broadcast an outage notice with scheduled status updates
options.C: Contract a commercial call center for surge capacity
options.D: Redirect the help-desk line to the email vendor's support

questions.key_concept: When demand is driven by duplicate reports of a known incident, communication cuts demand faster than adding service desk capacity.
questions.pre_read: Look at why tickets are rising. Ask whether the problem is too few agents or too many avoidable contacts.
questions.correct_explanation: Most tickets are duplicates from users who do not know the outage is already known. A broadcast notice with scheduled status updates removes the reason to call, cutting demand at the source, as ITIL major-incident communication intends. Reassigning staff adds capacity, but untrained agents still answer the same avoidable calls, and queues stay long while users keep contacting the desk.

wrong_explanations.A: Extra untrained staff add some capacity but leave the cause, users not knowing, untouched, so avoidable contacts keep coming.
wrong_explanations.C: Onboarding a call center takes time and its agents lack local context. It also treats volume rather than its cause.
wrong_explanations.D: The institution keeps ownership of its users' incidents. Sending them to a vendor line abandons them and confuses the response.

tips: Eliminate: C is slow to onboard and lacks context, and D abandons ownership of the incident to a vendor.
Final two: B beats A because clear communication removes avoidable contacts, while extra staff only absorbs them.
Exam cue: when volume comes from duplicate reports, reduce demand with communication before adding capacity.
questions.framework_ref: ITIL 4 Service Desk practice; ITIL 4 Incident Management practice; COBIT 2019 DSS02 (Managed Service Requests and Incidents)
related_concepts: Mass communication to reduce duplicate tickets

questions.question: A key SaaS customer's acquisitions will raise its API traffic 3.4 times within four weeks, beyond current capacity. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Model the projected load and agree a phased onboarding plan
options.B: Accept the volume and accelerate scaling to meet the date
options.C: Refuse the extra volume under the existing contract terms
options.D: Negotiate a volume premium at the next contract renewal

questions.key_concept: Capacity management models demand before committing; phasing new load protects every tenant's service while capacity is proven.
questions.pre_read: Notice the four-week deadline and the size of the jump. Ask what must be known before promising anything.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity management starts by modelling the projected demand against current limits, then shaping how it arrives. A phased onboarding plan lets capacity be added and proven step by step without degrading other customers. Accepting the full volume and racing to scale meets the customer's date, but it commits to untested capacity and puts every tenant's service at risk if scaling falls short.

wrong_explanations.B: Committing to the full jump before modelling capacity bets every tenant's service on scaling that has not been tested.
wrong_explanations.C: Refusing a key customer's growth damages the relationship and revenue without exploring a safe way to support it.
wrong_explanations.D: Pricing at the next renewal ignores the four-week capacity problem; the load arrives long before the contract changes.

tips: Eliminate: C turns away a key customer, and D addresses price months after the load arrives.
Final two: A beats B because modelled, phased onboarding protects all tenants, while an untested scale-up risks everyone's service.
Exam cue: in capacity questions, model the demand first, then commit to a plan you can prove.

questions.question: A cloud vendor has missed its 99.95% SLA for 90 days despite an agreed remediation roadmap; credits cover about 8% of business impact. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the CTO?

options.A: Measure SLA performance against the remediation plan for another quarter
options.B: Migrate production to an alternative cloud vendor right away
options.C: Issue a formal cure notice demanding a remediation roadmap
options.D: Redesign critical services to tolerate the vendor's degradations

questions.key_concept: SLA credits do not transfer business impact; the organization stays accountable for resilience and must design critical services around vendor failures.
questions.pre_read: Compare the credits with the business impact. Ask who really bears the cost when the vendor falls short.
questions.correct_explanation: Credits cover a small fraction of the impact, which shows the firm, not the vendor, carries the risk. The firm remains accountable for its service, so the lasting fix is to design critical services to tolerate vendor degradation. A cure notice is a legitimate contractual step, but the vendor has already agreed a remediation roadmap and the pattern continues; more contract pressure changes little for customers.

wrong_explanations.A: The roadmap has already failed for 90 days. Another quarter of measurement leaves the business absorbing losses that credits barely cover.
wrong_explanations.B: An immediate migration is a large, risky change, and a new vendor can also degrade without resilient design.
wrong_explanations.C: A remediation roadmap is already agreed and still failing. A formal cure notice adds pressure but does not protect customers.

tips: Eliminate: A waits another quarter on a failing roadmap, and B makes a rushed, risky move that does not remove vendor dependence.
Final two: D beats C because the firm stays accountable for resilience, and an agreed roadmap has not changed the pattern.
Exam cue: SLA credits are not a risk response; when a vendor keeps failing, build resilience you control.

questions.question: Six hours into a clinical-trial database recovery, the only architect who knows the system is hospitalized for at least 24 hours. What should the IS auditor recommend the COO do FIRST?

options.A: Freeze the database and pause recovery until the architect returns
options.B: Let the two junior engineers continue without added oversight
options.C: Form an interim team of external specialists under one lead
options.D: Escalate the recovery decision to the board for direction

questions.key_concept: When a key person is lost mid-incident, establish alternate leadership and expertise quickly rather than halting recovery or proceeding unsupported.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the cost of a 24-hour pause against the risk of proceeding unsupported. Which option keeps recovery moving safely?
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery cannot depend on one unavailable person. An interim team under a named lead, strengthened by external specialists, restores leadership and expertise quickly while keeping decisions accountable. Freezing the database protects its current state, but pausing for at least a day prolongs the outage, threatens regulatory deadlines and only deepens the single-person dependency that caused the problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Freezing protects state but stalls recovery for a day or more and keeps the firm dependent on one person.
wrong_explanations.B: Engineers who have never led a major recovery, without oversight, risk compounding the data-integrity problem.
wrong_explanations.D: The board sets direction, not live recovery steps. Escalating the operational decision delays action and adds no expertise.

tips: Eliminate: B proceeds without the experience or oversight the recovery needs, and D sends an operational call to the board.
Final two: C beats A because rebuilding leadership keeps recovery moving, while waiting prolongs the outage and the dependency.
Exam cue: when a key person is lost, replace the capability rather than wait for the person.

questions.question: A remediation action to test the incident response plan, untested for 2.5 years, was closed after only a document revision. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Accept the closure because the plan document was revised
options.B: Reopen the action until a plan test evidences remediation
options.C: Close the finding since no major incident occurred this year
options.D: Obtain a signed attestation from the incident response lead

questions.key_concept: Remediation actions close only on evidence the control operates; for response plans, that evidence is a documented test.
questions.pre_read: Notice the item was closed without a test. Ask what proof would show a response plan actually works.
questions.correct_explanation: Remediation closes on evidence that the control now operates, and for a response plan that evidence is a test, such as a tabletop or simulation, with results and fixes recorded. Reopening the action keeps it tracked until that proof exists. A signed attestation looks formal, but it is the owner's own assertion, not evidence that the plan would work.

wrong_explanations.A: A revised document shows the plan was edited, not that it works; untested plans often fail on contacts, roles and tooling.
wrong_explanations.C: A quiet year says nothing about readiness; the plan exists for the incident that has not happened yet.
wrong_explanations.D: An attestation is the owner's own assertion; it does not show the plan would operate during a real incident.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an edited document as proof, and C treats a quiet year as evidence of readiness.
Final two: B beats D because closure needs test evidence that the plan works; an attestation is only the owner's assertion.
Exam cue: a remediation action closes on evidence the control operates, not on management's word.

questions.question: A resigning DBA with four days left downloaded 240MB of customer loan data, including SSNs, to a USB drive at 02:30. What should the IS auditor recommend the CISO do FIRST?

options.A: Revoke the DBA's access at Friday's scheduled off-boarding
options.B: Ask the DBA to return the drive and sign a declaration
options.C: Have the manager question the DBA at Monday's check-in
options.D: Suspend access now and secure the USB as evidence

questions.key_concept: Confirmed exfiltration by a departing privileged user calls for immediate containment, with evidence secured, rather than routine off-boarding timelines.
questions.pre_read: Note that data has already left the system and the person is leaving. Ask what the next four days of access could cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Sensitive customer data has already been copied by a departing privileged user, so containment cannot wait. Suspending access now and securing the drive under chain of custody stops further loss and keeps the evidence usable. Revoking at Friday's off-boarding follows normal process, but it leaves four more days of privileged access to data already being taken.

wrong_explanations.A: Routine off-boarding timing ignores confirmed exfiltration and leaves privileged access open for four more days.
wrong_explanations.B: A request alerts the DBA without securing access or evidence, and a declaration cannot prove no copies exist.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a check-in and confronting without securing the drive invites deletion of evidence and further loss.

tips: Eliminate: B alerts the DBA without securing access or evidence, and C confronts the DBA before evidence is secured.
Final two: D beats A because confirmed data theft overrides routine off-boarding timelines.
Exam cue: when a leaver's data theft is confirmed, contain now; process timelines are for normal departures.

questions.question: An attacker has forged Golden Tickets using a krbtgt account whose password has not changed in seven years. Which action should the IS auditor recommend the CISO prioritize FIRST?

options.A: Rotate the krbtgt password twice, with replication in between
options.B: Reset the krbtgt password once and force user password changes
options.C: Reimage every compromised workstation from a clean baseline
options.D: Hand incident command to the vendor's response team

questions.key_concept: Golden Tickets are signed with the krbtgt key; only a double rotation removes both current and previous keys that validate forged tickets.
questions.pre_read: Think about how domain controllers validate Kerberos tickets. Which keys still work after one password change?
questions.correct_explanation: Forged Golden Tickets are signed with the krbtgt key, and domain controllers accept tickets signed with the current or previous password. Rotating it twice, allowing replication between resets, invalidates both keys and every forged ticket. A single reset looks like it fixes the problem, but the old key survives as the previous password, so the attacker's tickets keep working.

wrong_explanations.B: After one reset the old key remains valid as the previous password, so forged tickets still work. User password changes do not affect them.
wrong_explanations.C: Reimaging workstations removes footholds but leaves forged tickets valid. The attacker can return with domain-wide access.
wrong_explanations.D: Outside responders may help, but management keeps incident command and accountability for the response.

tips: Eliminate: C cleans endpoints while forged tickets stay valid, and D gives away accountability for the incident.
Final two: A beats B because domain controllers still honor the previous krbtgt key after a single reset.
Exam cue: fix the root of trust an attacker forged before cleaning individual machines.

questions.question: An actively exploited flaw appears in an open-source library used by 340 services, and each safe rollout takes 4–6 hours. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Patch services in the standard change-board priority order
options.B: Patch internal microservices first, then customer-facing APIs
options.C: Patch exposed services first, shielded by interim WAF rules
options.D: Hand the rollout prioritization to an external IR firm

questions.key_concept: When patching cannot be instant, prioritize by exposure and use compensating controls to cover the window until each service is patched.
questions.pre_read: Note the rollout time per service. Ask which services attackers can reach first and how to protect them meanwhile.
questions.correct_explanation: With hundreds of services and hours per rollout, exposure decides the order: internet-facing services are reachable first, so they are patched first, while interim WAF rules shield them until the fix lands. This applies risk-based patch management under emergency change. The standard change-board order keeps governance, but routine priorities ignore which services an active exploit can reach today.

wrong_explanations.A: Change control still applies, but a routine priority order ignores exposure while attackers exploit reachable services.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal services are harder to reach. Patching them first leaves the most exposed, customer-facing surface open longest.
wrong_explanations.D: External responders can help, but prioritizing the firm's own services is a management decision it cannot hand off.

tips: Eliminate: B patches the least exposed services first, and D hands away a decision management owns.
Final two: C beats A because an active exploit demands exposure-based emergency priorities, not the routine change order.
Exam cue: when you cannot patch everything at once, patch by exposure and add a compensating control meanwhile.

questions.question: Eleven tenants on a shared SaaS platform report SLA breaches because one newly signed tenant runs six times the average workload. What should the IS auditor recommend the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Add shared capacity until the large tenant's load is absorbed
options.B: Enforce per-tenant resource quotas sized to each contract
options.C: Renegotiate the large tenant's contract to add volume pricing
options.D: Measure each tenant's load for a month, then review quotas

questions.key_concept: Multi-tenant service levels depend on isolation; per-tenant quotas stop one workload from consuming capacity contracted to others.
questions.pre_read: Ask why one tenant can hurt eleven others. Which option removes that ability rather than paying for its effects?
questions.correct_explanation: The breaches occur because nothing stops one tenant from consuming capacity sold to others. Per-tenant quotas sized to each contract restore isolation, so every customer gets what it pays for. Adding shared capacity eases pressure for now, but without isolation the large tenant's growth will absorb the new headroom and the breaches will return.

wrong_explanations.A: More shared capacity treats the symptom. Without isolation, the large tenant's growth consumes the headroom and breaches recur.
wrong_explanations.C: Pricing changes take time and do not stop the workload from degrading other tenants today.
wrong_explanations.D: The cause is already known. A month of measurement leaves eleven tenants in breach while isolation could be enforced now.

tips: Eliminate: C changes price without changing the load, and D delays a month although the cause is already known.
Final two: B beats A because isolation fixes the cause, while added shared capacity is absorbed by the same tenant.
Exam cue: in shared environments, fix isolation before adding capacity.

questions.question: A cyber insurer denies a $40M ransomware claim, citing inconsistent MFA and stale penetration tests, and offers $4M as goodwill. What should the IS auditor recommend the CFO do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the $4M goodwill offer and redirect effort to remediation
options.B: File suit against the carrier to recover the full claim
options.C: Lodge a complaint with the insurance regulator to press the carrier
options.D: Gather control evidence and obtain an independent coverage review

questions.key_concept: Disputed claims turn on evidence: documented control status and an independent reading of the policy come before settling, suing or complaining.
questions.pre_read: Look at the carrier's three reasons. Ask what the firm needs before it can judge whether any of them hold.
questions.correct_explanation: The denial rests on factual claims about MFA and penetration testing. Gathering contemporaneous control evidence and an independent coverage review shows whether the exclusions actually apply, and informs every later choice. A regulator complaint is a legitimate lever, but filed before the firm knows its own evidence, it relies on outside pressure instead of a documented position.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting a tenth of the claim before testing the exclusions may forfeit a valid recovery permanently.
wrong_explanations.B: Litigation before assessing the evidence is costly and premature, and may fail if an exclusion genuinely applies.
wrong_explanations.C: A regulator complaint can help, but without the firm's own evidence it rests on pressure rather than a documented position.

tips: Eliminate: A concedes before testing the exclusions, and B litigates before knowing whether the evidence supports it.
Final two: D beats C because the firm's documented evidence must come before any outside pressure on the carrier.
Exam cue: in any dispute, establish your own evidence first; it decides which response is worth pursuing.

questions.subtopic: Litigation Hold During Active BCP Exercise
questions.question: During a planned DR exercise, legal counsel issues a litigation hold covering data on systems the exercise will overwrite from backup. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Finish the exercise, then forensically image the affected systems afterward
options.B: Terminate the exercise and reschedule it once the hold is lifted
options.C: Pause the overwriting steps until counsel confirms the hold's scope
options.D: Continue the exercise and record the hold in the test log

questions.key_concept: A litigation hold overrides routine operations: pause the steps that would destroy covered data, and let counsel set the scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the restore would overwrite covered data. Ask which option stops the harm without abandoning the recovery test entirely.
questions.correct_explanation: A litigation hold is a legal duty to preserve data, and a restore from backup would destroy the very state the hold protects. Pausing only the overwriting steps preserves evidence while counsel defines scope, and unaffected parts of the test can resume. Terminating until the hold lifts also preserves data, but holds can last years, leaving the recovery plan untested far too long.

wrong_explanations.A: Imaging afterward is too late: the restore will already have overwritten the production state the hold requires the firm to preserve.
wrong_explanations.B: This preserves data but over-corrects. Holds can run for years, and the firm would be left with an untested recovery plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Logging the hold does nothing to stop the restore from destroying data that must be preserved, exposing the firm to spoliation claims.

tips: Eliminate: A preserves data only after it is overwritten, and D documents the hold without protecting anything.
Final two: C beats B because a targeted pause meets the legal duty without leaving the recovery plan untested for an open-ended period.
Exam cue: when a legal preservation duty collides with an operation, stop only the conflicting steps and let counsel define scope.

questions.question: An acquisition's IT integration is 40% complete with two months left, and the IT sponsor wants to declare it finished. What should the IS auditor recommend to the COO FIRST?

options.A: Add contractors to finish the integration inside the original window
options.B: Present an honest status with a go-forward cost-benefit analysis
options.C: Extend the integration window by twelve months with added budget
options.D: Declare completion and hand the open gaps to business-as-usual teams

questions.key_concept: For an off-track integration, give decision-makers an honest status and go-forward cost-benefit before committing to any recovery path.
questions.pre_read: Notice the gap between 40% done and two months left. Ask what management needs before it can choose any path.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaders cannot choose well between extending, restructuring or stopping without an accurate picture of where the integration stands and what each path costs from here. An honest status with go-forward cost-benefit analysis lets management decide on facts, ignoring sunk cost. Extending by twelve months may prove right, but it commits money to one option before anyone has compared the alternatives.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding people late to a complex migration rarely recovers 60% of the scope in two months, and it adds onboarding and coordination risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Extension may be a sound outcome, but choosing it before analysis commits budget without comparing restructuring or hybrid options.
wrong_explanations.D: Declaring success at 40% hides the true state from governance and shifts unfunded integration work onto operational teams.

tips: Eliminate: A expects late staffing to finish most of the scope in weeks, and D misreports progress to governance.
Final two: B beats C because management needs facts and options compared before committing another year of budget.
Exam cue: when a project is off track, the auditor's first recommendation is an accurate status and options analysis, not a chosen fix.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds the DR design replicates EU customer data nightly to a US region where local transfer rules prohibit it. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Suspend replication and accept the loss of DR coverage
options.B: Rely on the provider's contract for transfer compliance
options.C: Encrypt the replicated data in transit and at rest with customer-held keys
options.D: Move DR to a compliant region that still meets RTO and RPO

questions.key_concept: DR site selection must satisfy data residency rules and recovery objectives together; encryption does not change where data resides.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is prohibited: the location, not the exposure. Ask which option fixes the location without losing recovery capability.
questions.correct_explanation: Relocating the DR target to a compliant region removes the prohibited transfer while keeping recovery capability, provided the new site is tested against the agreed RTO and RPO. Encryption with customer-held keys is a strong safeguard, but it does not change where the copies reside; a transfer that local rules prohibit stays prohibited however well the data is protected.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping replication ends the transfer but leaves critical systems with no recovery path, trading a compliance breach for an unacceptable continuity gap.
wrong_explanations.B: A contract cannot make a prohibited transfer lawful, and the organization stays accountable for where its customer data is stored.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption protects confidentiality, but the replicated copies still sit in a region where local rules forbid the transfer.

tips: Eliminate: A gives up DR coverage, and B leans on a contract that cannot make the transfer lawful.
Final two: D beats C because the location itself is prohibited; encryption protects the copies but they still reside there.
Exam cue: when a DR design breaks a constraint, redesign the site and re-prove RTO and RPO rather than dropping recovery.

questions.subtopic: IoT Device Fleet Compromised in Field
questions.question: Threat hunters find 14,000 field IoT sensors beaconing to attacker infrastructure, and the firmware-update credentials were leaked publicly. What should the chief security officer do FIRST?

options.A: Block the command channel and revoke the leaked update credentials
options.B: Push an over-the-air firmware update to every deployed field sensor
options.C: Recall and physically replace each sensor at customer sites
options.D: Ask affected customers to remediate the sensors on their networks

questions.key_concept: Contain first: cut attacker command and control and revoke leaked credentials before remediating through any channel they could abuse.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the update credentials are public. Ask whether the remediation channel can be trusted yet.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment comes first: cutting the command channel stops the attacker steering compromised sensors, and revoking the leaked credentials closes the path used to tamper with firmware. A fleet-wide update is the right remediation later, but pushing it while the update credentials are still exposed risks the attacker using, or racing, that same channel.

wrong_explanations.B: Updating through a channel whose credentials are public is unsafe until those credentials are revoked and the attacker's control is cut.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacing a whole fleet takes months and costs far more than needed, while compromised sensors stay under attacker control in the meantime.
wrong_explanations.D: The manufacturer owns the firmware and the leak. Pushing remediation onto customers leaves the root cause untouched and response uneven.

tips: Eliminate: C is a slow, disproportionate recall, and D hands the manufacturer's problem to customers.
Final two: A beats B because the update channel itself is compromised; contain and revoke access before remediating through it.
Exam cue: in an active compromise, cut attacker control and revoke stolen credentials before rolling out fixes.

questions.question: The CFO orders a 50% cut in IT operations staff, leaving billing and financial reporting with single-person dependencies. What is the BEST recommendation from the IS auditor to the CIO?

options.A: Carry out the cuts and raise concerns informally with the CFO
options.B: Quantify the continuity risks and propose mitigations to senior management
options.C: Suspend the cuts until an independent risk analysis has been completed
options.D: Outsource IT operations to a managed provider to absorb the cuts

questions.key_concept: Management owns the staffing decision; the auditor quantifies continuity risk and proposes mitigations so the risk is accepted knowingly.
questions.pre_read: Notice who gave the order. Ask which option informs that decision without taking it away from management.
questions.correct_explanation: Staffing levels are management's decision, but leaders must decide with the continuity risk in view. Quantifying the single-person dependencies and proposing mitigations such as knowledge capture and cross-training gives senior management a documented basis for its choice. Suspending the cuts for an independent risk analysis sounds prudent, but it takes a business decision away from management.

wrong_explanations.A: Informal concerns leave no record and give decision-makers no quantified view of the risk they are accepting.
wrong_explanations.C: Halting management's staffing decision for an outside analysis oversteps the advisory role; the risk can be quantified alongside the decision.
wrong_explanations.D: A rushed outsourcing deal is a major strategic change with its own transition risk, and it does not address the dependencies before the cuts.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the risk undocumented, and D swaps one transition risk for a larger, unplanned one.
Final two: B beats C because management owns staffing decisions; the auditor's role is to make the risk visible, not to block the cut.
Exam cue: when management takes a risky decision, document and communicate the risk with options rather than halting the decision.

questions.question: A newly released version of a production credit-scoring model approves applicants from certain neighborhoods at markedly lower rates than the prior version. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Roll back to the prior validated version under emergency change
options.B: Keep the new version live and add a fairness dashboard
options.C: Drop the location field and push a hotfix release today
options.D: Route decisions to human review while the release is investigated

questions.key_concept: When a release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back out the release through emergency change before investigating root cause.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem began with the new release. Ask whether a known-good state exists and how fast it can be restored.
questions.correct_explanation: The harmful behaviour arrived with the new release and a validated prior version exists, so restoring it through emergency change removes the cause quickly and keeps an approval record. Root cause can then be found offline. Human review also contains decisions, but it is a workaround: the faulty release stays live, and reviewers must spot a subtle pattern across high volumes.

wrong_explanations.B: A dashboard measures the disparity but leaves the faulty release making the same skewed decisions for every new applicant.
wrong_explanations.C: Proxy features can carry the pattern without the field, and a same-day hotfix adds a second unvalidated change to production.
wrong_explanations.D: Manual review leaves the faulty release live and depends on reviewers catching a subtle pattern across high decision volumes.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the faulty release deciding, and C pushes an untested hotfix that proxy features may defeat.
Final two: A beats D because restoring the known-good version removes the cause, while human review only works around it.
Exam cue: when a new release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back it out first, then investigate.

questions.subtopic: Tax Authority IT Audit During Planned Outage
questions.question: A weekend database upgrade carries a patch for an actively exploited flaw, but tax auditors request uninterrupted system access starting during that window. What should the IS auditor recommend to the CFO FIRST?

options.A: Proceed with the upgrade without informing the tax authority
options.B: Defer the upgrade and accept the exploit risk until the audit ends
options.C: Ask the tax authority to start its fieldwork after the upgrade
options.D: Cancel the upgrade and keep the current version indefinitely

questions.key_concept: When a security patch and a regulator's request clash on timing, negotiate the sequence before accepting risk on either side.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the conflict is about timing, not substance. Ask whether one short delay could satisfy both parties.
questions.correct_explanation: Both obligations can usually be met by sequencing them. Asking the tax authority to start once the short upgrade window closes keeps the exploited flaw on track to be patched and gives the auditors full access soon after. Deferring the upgrade also avoids conflict, but it leaves an actively exploited vulnerability open for days to solve a timing issue a conversation may fix.

wrong_explanations.A: Silently proceeding denies access the authority requested and damages the relationship, when a simple timing request could avoid the clash.
wrong_explanations.B: Deferral leaves an actively exploited flaw open for the whole audit, accepting serious risk before trying to agree on timing.
wrong_explanations.D: Abandoning the patch leaves a known exploited vulnerability in place with no end date, which no compensating control fully justifies.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores the authority's request, and D leaves an exploited flaw open indefinitely.
Final two: C beats B because agreeing on sequence protects both the patch and the audit, while deferral accepts exploit risk first.
Exam cue: when two legitimate obligations clash on timing, try sequencing by agreement before sacrificing either one.

questions.question: A trigger bug silently corrupted 0.3% of invoices over 90 days, and backups older than 30 days have rotated out. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Notify every customer that past invoices may be inaccurate
options.B: Restore the latest backup and replay valid transactions
options.C: Fix the trigger and leave historical invoices as issued
options.D: Query the invoice data to identify every affected record

questions.key_concept: With no clean backup, analyze the data to identify and quantify the corruption before correcting records or notifying customers.
questions.pre_read: Compare the 90-day corruption with the 30-day backup retention. Ask whether any clean copy exists at all.
questions.correct_explanation: No clean backup exists, because every retained copy already contains corruption. The firm must therefore analyze the data to find which invoices are wrong and by how much. That scope drives correction, customer remediation, disclosure and financial reporting. Notifying every customer first is a transparent instinct, but without knowing who is affected it alarms the 99.7% with correct invoices.

wrong_explanations.A: Blanket notice before scoping alarms customers whose invoices are correct and gives affected customers no useful detail on the error.
wrong_explanations.B: Retained backups postdate the start of corruption, so restoring one brings back bad data and discards valid later work.
wrong_explanations.C: Fixing the cause is needed, but leaving known-wrong invoices in place keeps billing and financial records inaccurate.

tips: Eliminate: B overlooks that no clean backup exists, and C leaves known-wrong records uncorrected.
Final two: D beats A because you must know which records are wrong before telling customers anything useful.
Exam cue: when data integrity fails and no clean copy exists, scope the damage before remediating or notifying.

questions.subtopic: Log Retention. Preservation for Regulator Request
questions.question: A data protection authority requests 18 months of transfer logs, but the log platform keeps 90 days online and overwrites older archives monthly. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Answer using the 90 days of logs currently held online
options.B: Suspend archive rotation so requested logs are not overwritten
options.C: Ask counsel to seek an extension while the logs are rebuilt
options.D: Extend the log retention policy to 18 months for future requests

questions.key_concept: When logs are requested for an inquiry, preserve them by suspending scheduled deletion before retrieval or retention policy changes.
questions.pre_read: Notice the archives are overwritten monthly. Ask what will be lost if nothing changes today.
questions.correct_explanation: Monthly rotation is destroying records the authority has asked for, so preservation comes first; retrieval and review can follow once nothing more is lost. Extending retention to 18 months is a sound control fix, but it governs future logs only and does nothing to stop this month's rotation overwriting the archives already requested.

wrong_explanations.A: Ninety days covers a fraction of the requested period, and the older archives keep being overwritten while the reply is prepared.
wrong_explanations.C: Overwritten logs cannot be rebuilt, and extra time does nothing to stop the rotation that is destroying the requested records.
wrong_explanations.D: A longer policy fixes future retention but does not stop this month's rotation overwriting the logs already requested.

tips: Eliminate: A answers with a fraction of the period, and C seeks time while rotation keeps destroying records.
Final two: B beats D because the requested logs must be preserved now; a new policy only protects future records.
Exam cue: when records are requested, stop scheduled deletion first, then fix the retention policy.

questions.subtopic: SOC for Cybersecurity Report Audit Reliance
questions.question: The CISO presents a managed security provider's SOC for Cybersecurity report to the audit committee as evidence of the firm's own program. What is the BEST response from the IS auditor?

options.A: Accept it because the service auditor's opinion is unmodified
options.B: Defer to the CISO's judgment on the report's sufficiency
options.C: Accept it once the complementary user entity controls are confirmed
options.D: Use it for provider reliance and test the firm's controls

questions.key_concept: A service provider's report covers the provider's controls; the firm's own program still needs separate audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose controls the report actually covers. Then ask what the audit committee believes it covers.
questions.correct_explanation: The report covers the provider's cybersecurity program, not the firm's. It supports reliance on the provider, but the firm's own program needs separate evidence. Confirming complementary user entity controls is a good reliance step, yet those controls cover only the firm's side of the outsourced service, not its whole cybersecurity program.

wrong_explanations.A: An unmodified opinion speaks only to the provider's subject matter. It says nothing about controls the firm itself operates.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor must reach an independent conclusion on evidence sufficiency; deferring to the program owner impairs objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: User entity controls cover the firm's side of the outsourced service only, leaving the rest of the firm's program untested.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses a clean opinion with relevant scope, and B surrenders the auditor's independent judgment.
Final two: D beats C because user entity controls complete reliance on one service, not assurance over the whole program.
Exam cue: before relying on any third-party report, check whose controls it covers and whether that matches your audit objective.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a cluster's admission policies have run in audit-only mode for 11 months, and one violating pod is mining cryptocurrency. What should the CTO do FIRST?

options.A: Keep audit mode and analyze violations against policy for a month
options.B: Remove the admission controller and rely on runtime security tools
options.C: Isolate the compromised workload and hunt for further intrusion
options.D: Switch every policy to enforce mode across the cluster immediately

questions.key_concept: When a control gap has been exploited, contain the active compromise and hunt for spread before fixing the gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice that misuse is already happening. Separate actions that stop the attacker from those that prevent future deployments.
questions.correct_explanation: An attacker is already inside, so containing the known compromise and hunting for further foothold comes first. Enforcing the policies is essential, but it only governs new deployments; it does not evict an intruder already running, and flipping all policies at once may break the many existing workloads that violate them.

wrong_explanations.A: Analyzing violations for another month leaves the gap open and does nothing about the active intrusion already found in the cluster.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing preventive controls because they were misconfigured weakens defence further; the fix is correct configuration, not removal.
wrong_explanations.D: Enforcement is needed but governs only new deployments, so the running intruder is untouched and blanket enforcement may disrupt production.

tips: Eliminate: A tolerates the open gap for another month, and B removes a preventive control instead of fixing it.
Final two: C beats D because an active intrusion must be contained before hardening; enforcement does not evict a running attacker.
Exam cue: when a control gap has already been exploited, contain the incident first, then close the gap in phases.

questions.question: A firm moves to terminate its failing claims-processing vendor, which invokes an 18-month exit clause and a large penalty. What is the BEST recommendation from the IS auditor to the COO?

options.B: Pay the penalty and cut over to a new platform immediately
options.C: Sue for breach and withhold payments during the litigation
options.D: Accept the 18-month exit term and plan the full migration within it

questions.key_concept: In a contested vendor exit, protect continuity of the critical service while pursuing contractual remedies in parallel.
questions.pre_read: Notice that claims processing cannot stop. Ask which option keeps service running without giving up the firm's rights.
questions.correct_explanation: Claims processing cannot stop, so continuity must be secured through a transition services arrangement while counsel tests whether the repeated failures amount to material breach, which may void the penalty. Accepting the 18-month term keeps service running, but it waives the firm's strongest legal position and leaves it tied to a distressed, insecure vendor.

wrong_explanations.B: Paying immediately gives up the breach argument, and cutting over without migration and testing risks a gap in a critical service.
wrong_explanations.C: Withholding payment from the only processor of claims invites service suspension and puts continuity at risk during litigation.
wrong_explanations.D: This keeps service running but concedes the penalty and keeps a failing, breached vendor in place for 18 months.

tips: Eliminate: B cuts over without a tested migration, and C provokes a service stoppage mid-dispute.
Final two: A beats D because it protects continuity without conceding the firm's legal position against a failing vendor.

questions.subtopic: Active Malware in BCP Test Environment
questions.question: During a DR exercise, threat hunters find an active remote-access trojan on a recovery server connected to production. What should the chief security officer do FIRST?

options.A: Continue the exercise on the unaffected recovery servers
options.B: Remove the trojan with antivirus and then resume the exercise
options.C: Isolate the DR network and reimage servers from clean baselines
options.D: Isolate the DR network and preserve the server for forensics

questions.key_concept: Contain by isolation and preserve forensic evidence before eradication, so the incident's scope, including production exposure, can be determined.
questions.pre_read: Notice the link to production. Ask which option contains spread and still lets investigators find out what happened.
questions.correct_explanation: The DR site links to production, so it must be cut off to stop spread, and the infected server must be preserved so investigators can learn how the trojan entered and whether production is compromised. Reimaging also removes the malware, but it destroys the evidence needed to scope the incident.

wrong_explanations.A: Continuing keeps the DR site connected to production while an active trojan beacons, risking spread into live systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Antivirus cleanup may miss persistence, destroys evidence and resumes a test on an environment of unknown integrity.
wrong_explanations.C: Clean rebuilds come later; wiping now erases the evidence needed to determine entry point and production exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores an active threat linked to production, and B trusts a quick cleanup on a compromised host.
Final two: D beats C because evidence must be preserved before rebuilding, or the firm cannot tell whether production is affected.
Exam cue: contain and preserve evidence before you eradicate; wiping first destroys the investigation.

questions.question: A hotel chain's card processor has been down 12 hours with a 24-hour ETA; switching processors takes weeks. What is the BEST recommendation from the IS auditor to the CFO?

questions.key_concept: Incident priority reflects business impact and urgency; a misfiring severity rule is overridden for the live incident, then corrected.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the matrix measures and what was actually harmed. Ask what the live incident needs right now.
questions.correct_explanation: Priority should reflect business impact, and 340,000 exposed customer records is a major incident however few staff are affected. Fixing the matrix through change control is the right follow-up, but doing it first leaves the live breach misranked and under-resourced while the change is approved.

wrong_explanations.B: The matrix needs fixing, but changing it first leaves the live breach misranked and under-resourced while the change is approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Technical detail does not help directors, and briefing them before the incident is properly classified skips the escalation path.

tips: Eliminate: A waits on the wrong measure of impact, and D briefs directors on technical detail before classification.
Final two: C beats B because the live incident needs correct handling now; the matrix fix follows through change control.

questions.question: During ransomware recovery at a federal contractor, IT plans to restore systems in the order they failed, while the BIA ranks payroll and contract billing highest. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Restore systems in the same order they failed
options.B: Restore the most-used systems first to cut help desk calls
options.C: Restore payroll and billing, then directory and shared services
options.D: Restore directory and shared services, then payroll and billing

questions.key_concept: Restoration follows BIA criticality adjusted for technical dependencies: shared infrastructure is recovered first so critical applications can run.
questions.pre_read: Notice the BIA ranks payroll and billing highest. Ask what those applications need running before they can work.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery order follows the BIA's criticality tiers, but critical applications cannot run until the shared services beneath them, such as directory, DNS and databases, are restored and verified clean. Following the tiers with dependencies first gets payroll and billing working soonest. Restoring payroll and billing first matches the BIA ranking, yet without their dependencies they will not start or authenticate.

wrong_explanations.A: Failure order reflects how the attack spread, not business criticality, so critical services may wait behind minor ones.
wrong_explanations.B: Help desk volume is not a recovery criterion; the BIA ranks services by business impact and tolerable downtime.
wrong_explanations.C: The BIA priority is right, but payroll and billing cannot start or authenticate until directory and shared services are back.

tips: Eliminate: A follows the attack's path, and B ranks by help desk noise instead of business impact.
Final two: D beats C because critical applications depend on shared services that must be restored first.
Exam cue: recovery order is BIA priority plus the dependency map; restore foundations before the applications on them.

questions.question: A bug-bounty researcher publicly posts details of an unpatched API flaw on day 47 of the firm's 90-day fix window. What should the chief security officer do FIRST?

options.A: Deploy an emergency mitigation and fast-track the permanent fix
options.B: Notify customers and regulators that a data breach has occurred
options.C: Seek legal action against the researcher over the disclosure
options.D: Keep the 90-day schedule because the policy window is still open

questions.key_concept: Public disclosure turns a latent vulnerability into an imminent one: mitigate immediately, then assess impact before any breach notice.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed on day 47. Ask whether the original 90-day window still reflects the real risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Public technical details make exploitation likely within hours, so the risk has changed from latent to imminent. An emergency mitigation reduces exposure now, and fast-tracking the fix closes it. Notifying customers and regulators is transparent, but no breach has been confirmed yet; notice comes after assessing whether data was actually accessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Declaring a breach before evidence of access misstates the facts; the immediate need is to cut exposure, then assess and notify as required.
wrong_explanations.C: Legal action does not reduce exposure, and acting against a good-faith researcher damages the firm's disclosure program and reputation.
wrong_explanations.D: The internal window assumed the flaw was secret. Public disclosure changes the risk, so the original timeline no longer applies.

tips: Eliminate: C pursues the researcher instead of the risk, and D ignores that public disclosure makes exploitation imminent.
Final two: A beats B because the first priority is to reduce exposure; notification follows once access is actually assessed.
Exam cue: when a vulnerability becomes public, re-rate the risk and mitigate at once rather than holding to the old timeline.
