questions.subtopic: Sustained Vendor Outage Triggering BCP Invocation
questions.question: A bank's core-processing vendor has been down 26 hours, beyond the recovery time objective in the BIA, and now estimates another 12–24 hours. What is the BEST action for the chief operating officer?

options.A: Wait for restoration and reserve the BCP for a missed estimate
options.B: Invoke the BCP's alternate processing arrangement now
options.C: Extend manual branch procedures and escalate to the vendor's CEO
options.D: Suspend ACH and wire processing until the vendor recovers

questions.key_concept: An outage that passes the BIA's recovery time objective is the trigger to invoke the continuity plan's alternate arrangements.
questions.pre_read: Compare 26 hours with the recovery time objective. Ask what the plan says to do once that line is crossed.
questions.correct_explanation: The outage has already exceeded the recovery time objective set from business impact, which is the trigger for invoking the continuity plan. Activating the predefined alternate processing restores critical services on the bank's terms rather than the vendor's. Manual procedures and executive escalation help, but they cannot carry growing transaction volumes indefinitely and leave the bank dependent on an unreliable ETA.

wrong_explanations.A: The BIA threshold has already been crossed; waiting on an estimate that has already slipped extends harm beyond what the bank accepted.
wrong_explanations.C: Manual work and escalation are supporting steps, but they do not restore processing capacity once tolerance is exceeded.
wrong_explanations.D: Halting payments deepens customer and liquidity impact; it is the opposite of restoring critical services.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores that the RTO has passed, and D stops critical services instead of restoring them.
Final two: B beats C because exceeding the RTO triggers the planned alternate processing, while manual work cannot scale.
Exam cue: when an outage passes the BIA's recovery time objective, invoke the plan; do not keep waiting on vendor estimates.

questions.subtopic: Incident Records. Evidence Integrity and Custody
questions.question: During ransomware recovery, an IS auditor finds the incident log supporting a cyber-insurance claim was edited by a controller with ties to the forensic vendor. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Let the controller annotate each edit with its justification
options.B: Commission an independent claim review once recovery is complete
options.C: Preserve original log copies and move custody to another owner
options.D: Correct the claim figures and notify the insurer of the change

questions.key_concept: Incident documentation is evidence: preserve originals and keep chain of custody away from conflicted staff before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who edited the log and their link to the vendor. Ask what must be protected before anything is corrected.
questions.correct_explanation: The incident record is evidence for the claim, the recovery decisions and any later investigation, so its integrity comes first: preserve original copies from backups and system audit trails, and take custody away from the conflicted editor. Correcting the claim and notifying the insurer is the right destination, but figures drawn from an altered log may be wrong and need restating again.

wrong_explanations.A: The controller is the conflicted party; explaining their own edits leaves custody of the evidence in the wrong hands.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting until recovery ends lets originals age out of backups and logs, and the conflicted controller keeps custody meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.D: Figures rebuilt from an altered log may still be wrong; evidence integrity must be secured before the claim is restated.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the conflicted editor in charge of the record, and B delays while original evidence can be lost.
Final two: C beats D because a claim can only be corrected reliably from records whose integrity is secured.
Exam cue: when incident records may be tampered with, preserve originals and fix chain of custody before acting on them.

questions.subtopic: Monitoring Agent Rollout. Release Readiness Gate
questions.question: Management plans to release a keystroke-monitoring agent to 2,400 laptops in the US, EU and India before its 50-laptop pilot finishes. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Hold the release until pilot results and change approval are in
options.B: Release to one region now and expand as issues are fixed
options.C: Deploy everywhere and roll back any laptops that report problems
options.D: Deploy globally once counsel approves jurisdiction-specific privacy notices

questions.key_concept: A release reaches production only after pilot or test evidence is reviewed and change approval is granted, with a tested backout plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice the pilot has not finished. Ask what a pilot is for and what should gate the release.
questions.correct_explanation: An endpoint agent on every laptop is a high-impact change, so release management requires pilot evidence, formal change approval and a tested backout before deployment. Holding the release secures all three. A regional rollout sounds controlled, but it still pushes an unvalidated build to hundreds of users and makes production staff the test group the pilot was meant to replace.

wrong_explanations.B: Phasing limits blast radius but still deploys a build whose pilot has not finished, so production users become the test group.
wrong_explanations.C: Fleet-wide deployment with reactive rollback assumes a tested backout exists and accepts widespread disruption before problems are known.
wrong_explanations.D: Privacy notices address transparency, not release readiness; the agent would still ship without pilot results or change approval.

tips: Eliminate: C deploys fleet-wide on untested rollback, and D treats privacy notices as release readiness.
Final two: A beats B because a regional rollout still releases an unvalidated build; pilot evidence and approval come first.
Exam cue: a pilot exists to gate the release, so do not release before its results are reviewed and approved.

questions.subtopic: Major Data Center Physical Security Breach
questions.question: A colocation provider reports intruders spent 40 minutes near the firm's racks; remote diagnostics show no tampering. What is the BEST next step for the chief security officer?

options.A: Accept the remote diagnostics as evidence of no tampering
options.B: Arrange an independent on-site inspection of the firm's equipment
options.C: Await an independent analysis of the provider's access logs
options.D: Relocate the equipment to a new colocation provider immediately

questions.key_concept: Physical access breaches need independent physical inspection; remote diagnostics and access logs cannot show whether hardware was altered.
questions.pre_read: Ask what remote diagnostics and access logs can and cannot see. Then ask who is independent of the control that failed.
questions.correct_explanation: Remote diagnostics cannot detect physical implants or added hardware, so only a hands-on inspection can confirm the equipment's integrity. Making it independent ensures the finding does not depend on the party whose controls failed. An independent review of the provider's access logs sounds rigorous, but logs show who entered and when, not whether anyone altered the firm's hardware.

wrong_explanations.A: Remote diagnostics cannot see hardware implants or physical changes, so they cannot prove the equipment is untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Access logs show who entered, not whether hardware was altered, and waiting delays the hands-on check that can.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving equipment before inspection may destroy evidence and moves possibly tampered hardware into a new site.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts tools that cannot see physical tampering, and D relocates hardware before checking it.
Final two: B beats C because only a physical inspection can reveal tampering; access logs show entry, not changes to hardware.
Exam cue: after a physical breach, verify with independent physical evidence; remote checks and the breached party's word are not enough.

questions.subtopic: Generative AI Inadvertently Exposing Customer Data
questions.question: An internal generative AI tool trained on support tickets reveals customer contact details when prompted, once during a vendor demo. What should the chief technology officer do FIRST?

options.A: Restrict the tool to senior staff and continue using it
options.B: Add an output filter that masks personal data in responses
options.C: Suspend the tool until the training data is remediated
options.D: Notify every customer in the corpus of a confirmed breach

questions.key_concept: When a system exposes personal data by design, suspend the processing before assessing impact and remediating the root cause.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the personal data lives: in the model itself. Ask which option actually stops it being disclosed.
questions.correct_explanation: The personal data is embedded in the model itself, so every prompt can expose it. Suspending the tool stops further disclosure while the data is assessed and the model retrained on redacted data. An output filter reduces exposure, but filters are routinely bypassed by rephrased prompts, and the data remains in the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Fewer users lowers volume, but anyone with access can still extract customer data from the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Filters can be bypassed by rephrased prompts, and the personal data stays embedded in the model regardless.
wrong_explanations.D: Notification may be required after assessment, but declaring a confirmed breach to everyone before scoping is premature and does not stop exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the exposure live for fewer users, and D notifies before scoping and does not stop the leak.
Final two: C beats B because the data sits inside the model; a bypassable filter is a half-measure while exposure continues.
Exam cue: when personal data is exposed by design, stop the processing first, then assess, remediate and notify.

questions.question: A credential-stuffing attack from rotating proxy IPs has pushed an e-commerce login service to 95% capacity, slowing checkout for real customers. What should operations management do FIRST?

options.A: Block each attacking IP address at the web application firewall
options.B: Scale out the login tier to absorb the added traffic
options.C: Analyze the attack traffic before changing login policy
options.D: Filter bot logins and step up MFA on risky attempts

questions.key_concept: When hostile traffic consumes capacity, contain the attack traffic first; adding capacity treats the symptom and can amplify the attack.
questions.pre_read: Notice why capacity is near its limit. Ask whether more resources would help customers or the attacker.
questions.correct_explanation: The attack is both a security incident and a capacity drain, so the first step is to stop hostile attempts consuming the login tier: behavioural bot filtering sheds attack traffic, and step-up MFA blocks stolen passwords. Scaling out restores headroom, but it also lets the attacker try credentials faster, raising takeovers and cost without removing the cause of the load.

wrong_explanations.A: Rotating residential proxies supply new addresses faster than they can be blocked, so the load and takeovers continue.
wrong_explanations.B: Extra capacity absorbs the load but lets the attacker test credentials faster, increasing takeovers and cost.
wrong_explanations.C: Analysis can run alongside containment. Delaying controls lets takeovers and checkout slowdowns continue in the meantime.

tips: Eliminate: A fails against rotating proxies, and C delays containment for analysis while takeovers continue.
Final two: D beats B because removing attack traffic fixes the cause; scaling out gives the attacker more capacity.
Exam cue: when an attack drives a capacity problem, shed the hostile load before adding resources.

questions.question: A hospital's HSM has failed and its untested key escrow cannot be decrypted, leaving seven years of encrypted backup archives unreadable. What should the chief technology officer do FIRST?

options.A: Preserve the failed HSM and engage its vendor on recovery
options.B: Declare the archives permanently unrecoverable to the regulator
options.C: Destroy the unreadable tapes since the data is now erased
options.D: Procure a replacement HSM and generate new backup keys

questions.key_concept: After a key-management failure, preserve the failed device and pursue recovery before declaring loss or taking irreversible steps.
questions.pre_read: Notice that nothing has been tried yet. Ask which option keeps every recovery path open.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery may still be possible, because HSM vendors and specialists can sometimes extract key material from failed hardware. Preserving the device and every related artifact keeps that option open before any irreversible step. Procuring a new HSM is needed for future backups, but it does nothing for the archive and may lead to the failed unit being returned or wiped.

wrong_explanations.B: Declaring permanent loss before recovery has been attempted is premature and may misstate the position to the regulator.
wrong_explanations.C: Destroying tapes removes any chance of recovery and may breach record-retention duties for patient and financial data.
wrong_explanations.D: New keys protect future backups, but this abandons the archive and risks the failed device being swapped out and wiped.

tips: Eliminate: B gives up before trying recovery, and C makes the loss irreversible and breaches retention duties.
Final two: A beats D because recovery of the archive must be attempted first; the forward fix can follow without destroying options.
Exam cue: when data may be lost, preserve every artifact and attempt recovery before any irreversible action.

questions.subtopic: Year-End Close. Job Scheduling Control Bypass
questions.question: An IS auditor confirms a whistleblower's claim that, during the ongoing year-end close, operators are running ad hoc batch jobs that post journal entries outside the scheduler's approval workflow. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have operators document each ad hoc run and its purpose after close
options.B: Block job submission outside the scheduler's approved queue now
options.C: Review the ad hoc runs for unauthorized entries before close
options.D: Rely on the external auditors' year-end testing to cover it

questions.key_concept: Production jobs run only through the scheduler's approved path; when a bypass is active, close it before assessing its impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the bypass is still happening during close. Ask which step stops the problem growing.
questions.correct_explanation: While the bypass stays open, every new ad hoc run adds unapproved entries to the close, so the first step is to force all job submissions through the scheduler's approval path. Any review then works on a fixed population. Reviewing runs before close is essential, but doing it while operators keep bypassing the workflow means new unapproved entries arrive faster than they are checked.

wrong_explanations.A: After-the-fact notes do not stop the bypass, and operators documenting their own unapproved runs give weak evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Review is needed, but with the bypass still open, new unapproved runs keep adding entries faster than they can be checked.
wrong_explanations.D: External testing is not the organization's control; relying on it lets unapproved postings continue through close and into the statements.

tips: Eliminate: A documents the bypass without stopping it, and D hands the organization's control duty to external auditors.
Final two: B beats C because closing the bypass fixes the population; reviewing first lets new unapproved runs keep arriving.
Exam cue: when a control bypass is still happening, stop the bypass first, then assess what already got through.

questions.subtopic: Geographic Data Sovereignty. Russia Exit Sanctions
questions.question: A firm must exit Russia within 90 days under new sanctions, while customer data sits in local data centers under a localization law. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to the chief privacy officer?

options.A: Delete Russian-hosted customer data once local operations cease
options.B: Migrate the customer data to EU data centers before the deadline
options.C: Map each data set to its sanctions and localization obligations
options.D: Freeze the data in place until the sanctions are lifted

questions.key_concept: In a sanctions-driven exit, inventory the data and map each set's legal obligations before choosing to delete, transfer or retain it.
questions.pre_read: Notice two legal regimes pull in opposite directions. Ask what must be known before any data can safely move or be destroyed.
questions.correct_explanation: Sanctions rules and the localization law impose conflicting duties, and the right action differs by data set: some must be returned to customers, some retained, some cannot leave the country. Mapping each set to its obligations, with counsel, is the basis for every later decision. Migrating to the EU is decisive but may itself breach the export rules the map would reveal.

wrong_explanations.A: Blanket deletion may breach retention duties and customer contracts, and destroys data customers may be entitled to extract.
wrong_explanations.B: Cross-border transfer out of Russia is restricted by the localization and export rules. Moving data before mapping those obligations creates new legal exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for sanctions to lift ignores the 90-day exit deadline and keeps the firm exposed to sanctions risk.

tips: Eliminate: A destroys data without checking retention or customer rights, and D ignores both the deadline and the sanctions exposure.
Final two: C beats B because the obligations must be known before data moves; a transfer may itself breach export rules.
Exam cue: when laws conflict, the FIRST step is to understand obligations, not to pick a physical action.

questions.subtopic: DR Site Located in Active-War-Zone Region
questions.question: A bank's DR site lies in a region now suffering attacks on power and telecoms, and switching providers takes six months. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation to the chief operating officer?

options.A: Keep the current site until the contract renewal date
options.B: Defer exit and add interim recovery capacity while migrating
options.C: Terminate the DR contract and begin migrating immediately
options.D: Rely on the vendor's assurance that operations continue

questions.key_concept: When a recovery site's risk rises but replacement takes months, a staged exit with interim safeguards keeps recovery capability in place.
questions.pre_read: Notice the six-month switching time. Ask what happens to recovery capability while the bank moves.
questions.correct_explanation: The current site is degraded but remains the bank's only recovery capability, and a replacement takes six months. Keeping it while adding interim recovery capacity elsewhere, then moving in stages, holds risk within the BIA objectives until the new site is proven. Terminating at once sounds decisive, but it leaves the bank with no DR capability for the whole six-month switch.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting for renewal adds no safeguards against a material change in risk. Contract timing should not drive a resilience decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Ending the contract before an alternate site is ready removes all recovery capability during the six-month switch.
wrong_explanations.D: The vendor's self-report is not independent evidence that the site can still meet the BIA recovery objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the contract date drive a resilience decision, and D accepts an interested party's word as evidence.
Final two: B beats C because a staged exit with interim capacity keeps recovery capability; terminating first leaves none for six months.
Exam cue: when the only recovery option is degraded, keep it under compensating safeguards until its replacement is proven.

questions.question: Customer card data has appeared on the dark web, and the outsourced MDR provider's logs show events that should have raised alerts. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to the CISO?

options.B: Rely on the MDR provider's own review of the missed alerts

questions.key_concept: A confirmed cardholder data breach triggers the incident response plan first; vendor accountability is addressed after containment and independent evidence.

questions.correct_explanation: Card data is already exposed, so the incident response plan required by PCI DSS must start now: contain, preserve evidence and engage independent forensics, which also supports brand and QSA notification. The MDR provider cannot investigate its own failure. Reviewing the detection rules is a sound step, but it explains why alerts were missed rather than containing the live breach, so it comes later.

wrong_explanations.D: Pursuing damages is a commercial remedy. It does not contain the breach and is premature before forensics establish the facts.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the vendor investigate itself, and D jumps to a commercial claim before the facts are known.
Final two: A beats C because a live breach needs response and evidence first; the detection-rule review waits.

questions.question: A post-implementation review finds an acquired firm's legacy ERP still running 11 months after integration because three interfaces depend on it, delaying promised IT savings. What is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Shut down the legacy ERP now to realize the savings
options.B: Defer decommissioning until the next annual budget cycle is approved
options.C: Retain the legacy ERP as a warm standby for the new platform
options.D: Migrate the three interfaces, then retire it under change control

questions.key_concept: After implementation, legacy systems are retired through change control once dependent interfaces are migrated; untested leftovers are not resilience.
questions.pre_read: Notice what keeps the legacy ERP alive. Ask which option removes that blocker safely.
questions.correct_explanation: The savings depend on retiring the legacy ERP, and the blocker is three live interfaces. Migrating them, then decommissioning through change control with data archived and access removed, delivers the benefit without breaking operations. Keeping the old ERP as a warm standby sounds prudent, but it was never designed or tested for recovery, so it adds cost and stale-data risk rather than real resilience.

wrong_explanations.A: Shutting down now breaks the three interfaces that still depend on the legacy ERP, disrupting order processing to hit a savings date.
wrong_explanations.B: Deferring without a migration plan leaves the dependencies in place, so parallel running and its costs simply continue.
wrong_explanations.C: An untested parallel system is not a recovery capability; it keeps cost and duplicate-data risk without meeting any RTO.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks live interfaces to hit a savings date, and B defers without removing the dependencies.
Final two: D beats C because a legacy system needs a planned exit, and an untested standby gives no real recovery capability.
Exam cue: retire legacy systems only after their dependencies are migrated, and do it through change control.

questions.subtopic: System Running Unsupported OS for Legacy Reasons
questions.question: A production system runs on an unsupported OS behind network isolation and compensating controls; replacing it costs $8M and 18 months. What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the CTO?

options.A: Compress validation so the system is replaced within six months
options.B: Obtain formal management risk acceptance with a funded exit plan
options.C: Continue operating the system under its existing compensating controls
options.D: Leave the system off the insurer's renewal risk questionnaire

questions.key_concept: Residual risk from an end-of-support system must be formally accepted by the accountable risk owner and tied to a dated replacement plan.
questions.pre_read: Notice the controls already exist. Ask what is still missing: who owns the residual risk, and when does it end?
questions.correct_explanation: Isolation and compensating controls reduce but do not remove the risk of an unpatchable OS. Management, as risk owner, should formally accept the residual risk and commit funding and dates to replace the system, which also gives regulators and the insurer an accurate position. Continuing under existing controls keeps the system safe today but leaves the risk unowned and with no end date.

wrong_explanations.A: Compressing validation of the replacement risks errors and compliance failures in production. Speed does not justify skipping testing.
wrong_explanations.C: The controls help, but without formal acceptance and an exit plan the risk has no accountable owner and no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Omitting a known risk from an insurance application is misrepresentation and could void cover when it is needed.

tips: Eliminate: A sacrifices required validation for speed, and D misrepresents the risk to the insurer.
Final two: B beats C because compensating controls need an accountable owner and an end date, not just continuation.
Exam cue: for unsupported systems, look for formal risk acceptance by management plus a replacement plan.

questions.question: A researcher reports a publicly readable cloud bucket holding customer emails and source code, and asks for a bounty before deleting their copy. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to the CTO?

options.A: Block public bucket access and preserve its access logs
options.B: Pay the requested bounty in return for a deletion confirmation
options.C: Analyze which data was exposed and who accessed it
options.D: Send the researcher a legal warning under computer misuse law

questions.key_concept: When exposure is confirmed, contain it first while preserving the evidence needed for impact analysis and notification decisions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the bucket is still open. Ask what stops further exposure while keeping the evidence you will need next.
questions.correct_explanation: The data remains publicly readable, so containment comes first: remove public access and preserve access logs, which the impact analysis will rely on. Every minute open is new exposure. Analyzing what was exposed and who accessed it is essential for notification decisions, but it can proceed once the door is closed, and it needs the logs that containment preserves.

wrong_explanations.B: Paying on request does not contain the exposure and sets a bounty precedent outside any disclosure program.
wrong_explanations.C: Impact analysis is necessary, but doing it while the bucket stays public allows exposure to continue.
wrong_explanations.D: A hostile legal response discourages good-faith disclosure and does nothing to close the exposed bucket.

tips: Eliminate: B pays before containing anything, and D treats a reporter as an attacker while the data stays open.
Final two: A beats C because exposure is ongoing; contain first, then analyze using the logs you preserved.
Exam cue: when data is still exposed, the FIRST step is containment that also preserves evidence.

questions.question: During a Sev-1 outage, each decision waits 30 minutes for a satellite call to executives, though the incident plan names an incident commander. What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the COO?

options.A: Keep routing each decision to executives by satellite call
options.B: Pause major recovery actions until executives can reconvene
options.C: Let the VP decide alone and brief executives after closure
options.D: Let the incident commander decide, with hourly executive updates

questions.key_concept: Incident plans pre-delegate decision rights to an incident commander so response is fast, while regular updates keep executive oversight.
questions.pre_read: Notice the plan already names someone. Ask how to restore speed without losing oversight of the decisions being made.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan already pre-delegates authority to an incident commander, so invoking it removes the 30-minute delay while hourly updates keep executives informed and able to intervene. That is how ITIL incident practice and incident command are meant to work. Letting the VP decide alone also restores speed, but it bypasses the defined role and leaves executives blind until the incident closes.

wrong_explanations.A: Per-decision approval by satellite is the cause of the delay. Continuing it extends the outage and the revenue loss.
wrong_explanations.B: Pausing recovery during a customer-facing outage maximizes business impact. Restoration should continue under delegated authority.
wrong_explanations.C: Speed returns, but decisions bypass the plan's defined role and executives get no visibility until after closure.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the bottleneck causing the delay, and B halts recovery while customers are down.
Final two: D beats C because pre-delegated authority keeps both speed and oversight; ad hoc autonomy loses oversight.
Exam cue: in an incident, use the decision rights the plan already defines rather than inventing new ones.

questions.subtopic: DBA Deleted Production Data. Mistake or Malice
questions.question: A DBA on call but not assigned any change deleted 2.4M production records at 03:00, claiming a typo, while restoration from backup proceeds. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST to the CISO?

options.A: Accept the typo account and start an HR corrective process
options.B: Terminate the DBA for cause and revoke database access
options.C: Suspend the DBA's access pending an independent investigation
options.D: Defer any investigation until the backup restoration completes

questions.key_concept: When intent is unclear, suspend access and investigate independently in parallel with recovery; neither prejudge guilt nor delay evidence collection.
questions.pre_read: Notice the change was unassigned and off-hours, yet intent is unknown. Ask what protects the systems and the evidence without prejudging.
questions.correct_explanation: An unassigned off-hours deletion could be error or malice, and the facts are not yet known. Suspending access removes further risk without prejudging, and an independent investigation preserves logs while they are fresh, alongside the restore. Deferring the investigation until recovery ends follows restore-first logic, but recovery is already under way and waiting lets volatile evidence and session data age out.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting the explanation before investigating ignores red flags: no assigned change and off-hours timing.
wrong_explanations.B: Termination prejudges intent before the facts are known and exposes the firm to employment claims if it was an error.
wrong_explanations.D: Restoration is already running. Waiting lets logs and session evidence age out, and nothing stops the investigation running in parallel.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the story despite red flags, and B punishes before the facts are known.
Final two: C beats D because recovery is already under way; investigation runs in parallel, before evidence ages out.
Exam cue: restore before root cause, but never at the cost of the evidence the root cause depends on.

questions.subtopic: SLA Dispute Escalates to Arbitration Mid-Recovery
questions.question: During a 78-hour core-banking vendor outage, the vendor files for arbitration over a separate payment dispute, with 30 days to respond. What is the BEST recommendation the IS auditor should give the CFO?

options.A: Prioritize recovery and run arbitration on a separate legal track
options.B: Settle the dispute on the vendor's terms to secure cooperation
options.C: Postpone the arbitration response until core service is fully restored
options.D: Terminate the contract for cause, citing the outage as breach

questions.key_concept: Keep service recovery and legal disputes on separate tracks so neither compromises the other; recovery takes priority without forfeiting legal deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Notice two clocks running: the outage and a 30-day deadline. Ask which option protects both without trading one for the other.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers are affected now, so recovery stays the priority, but the arbitration has its own deadline and must not be ignored. Assigning it to a separate legal track keeps operational teams focused while counsel protects the bank's position. Postponing the response feels like sensible prioritization, but an outage of unknown length could eat into the 30-day window and forfeit legal rights.

wrong_explanations.B: Settling on the vendor's terms under pressure concedes the dispute and does not guarantee faster recovery.
wrong_explanations.C: Recovery length is unknown, so postponing risks missing the 30-day deadline. Legal work does not need the operations team.
wrong_explanations.D: Terminating mid-outage cuts off the only core-banking provider while recovery and the dispute are both unresolved.

tips: Eliminate: B concedes under pressure without securing recovery, and D cuts off the only provider mid-outage.
Final two: A beats C because a parallel legal track protects the deadline without distracting recovery teams.
Exam cue: when operational and legal pressures collide, separate the tracks rather than sacrificing either one.

questions.question: After a year-long operations audit with 38 findings across five areas, each team tracks remediation in its own spreadsheet. With an examination due in six months, what is the IS auditor's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep separate team trackers and consolidate them before the exam
options.B: Close each item once its owner confirms the fix is done
options.C: Remediate items in the examination's scope before the others
options.D: Use one risk-ranked register with owners, dates and retesting

questions.key_concept: Remediation is tracked in one risk-ranked register with owners, target dates and retesting before closure, not by examination scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice the trackers are scattered and an examination is coming. Ask what should set the order of the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Scattered trackers hide overdue and duplicated actions, so one register ranked by risk, with named owners, target dates and retesting before closure, lets management and audit see real progress across all five areas. Remediating examination-scope items first is tempting, but it lets the examiner's agenda override risk and leaves higher-risk issues outside that scope open.

wrong_explanations.A: Consolidating only before the exam keeps progress invisible for months, so slipped or duplicated actions surface too late to fix.
wrong_explanations.B: Owner confirmation is an assertion, not evidence; items need retesting before closure or they may reopen at examination.
wrong_explanations.C: Ordering work by the examiner's scope rather than by risk leaves higher-risk items outside that scope unremediated.

tips: Eliminate: A hides progress until just before the exam, and B closes items on the owner's word without retesting.
Final two: D beats C because remediation is ordered by risk, not by what examiners plan to look at.
Exam cue: sound remediation tracking means one register, risk ranking, owners, due dates and retesting before closure.

questions.question: During a BIA review, an IS auditor sees management set 24 hours to restore payroll, well inside the 72 hours the business could survive. Which measure does the 24-hour figure MOST directly represent?

options.A: Recovery point objective
options.B: Recovery time objective
options.C: Maximum tolerable period of disruption
options.D: Mean time to repair

questions.key_concept: RTO is the target time to restore a process after disruption; it must sit inside the maximum tolerable period of disruption.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem gives two times. Ask which one is the target management set, and which is the survival limit.
questions.correct_explanation: The recovery time objective is the target elapsed time to restore a process after disruption, set by management through the BIA. Here that is 24 hours. The maximum tolerable period of disruption is the 72-hour survival limit; the RTO must sit inside it to leave a safety margin. Confusing the two would set recovery targets at the edge of business failure.

wrong_explanations.A: RPO measures acceptable data loss, expressed as time before the disruption. It says nothing about how quickly payroll must run again.
wrong_explanations.C: The maximum tolerable period is the 72-hour survival limit in the stem, not the 24-hour restoration target.
wrong_explanations.D: Mean time to repair is a component reliability metric, not a business recovery objective set in a BIA.

tips: Eliminate: A measures data loss, not restoration time, and D is an equipment reliability metric, not a BIA objective.
Final two: B beats C because 24 hours is the restoration target; 72 hours is the survival limit it must sit within.
Exam cue: RTO is the target, MTPD is the cliff edge; the RTO must always be shorter.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a customer database has a 15-minute RPO, but its backups run only nightly. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: The RPO should be relaxed to match the nightly backup cycle
options.B: The backups suffice provided the media are stored offsite
options.C: Potential data loss exceeds what the business has accepted
options.D: Restoration will take longer than the agreed time objective

questions.key_concept: RPO sets the maximum tolerable data loss; backup or replication frequency must be at least as frequent as the RPO.
questions.pre_read: Notice the two time figures. Ask what a gap between them puts at risk: data, or recovery speed?
questions.correct_explanation: A 15-minute RPO means the business accepts losing at most 15 minutes of data. Nightly backups could lose up to a full day, so potential data loss far exceeds the accepted level and the gap should be reported. The concern about restoration taking longer confuses RPO with RTO: backup frequency sets how much data is lost, not how long recovery takes.

wrong_explanations.A: The RPO is a business decision from the BIA. The auditor reports the gap; relaxing the objective is management's call, not the auditor's conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Offsite storage protects backups from site loss but does nothing about the nightly frequency that causes the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: This confuses RPO with RTO. Backup frequency drives potential data loss, not the time needed to restore.

tips: Eliminate: A has the auditor change a business objective, and B fixes media location, not backup frequency.
Final two: C beats D because RPO measures data loss; restoration time belongs to the RTO.
Exam cue: RPO points backward to data lost, RTO points forward to downtime; match the gap to the right one.

questions.question: A business continuity manager must choose recovery strategies for a new payments platform. Which activity should be completed FIRST?

options.A: A business impact analysis of the supported processes
options.B: Drafting step-by-step recovery procedures for staff
options.C: Setting the platform's RTO and RPO with IT operations
options.D: Choosing between a hot site and a warm site

questions.key_concept: The BIA comes before strategy: it identifies critical processes and impact over time, which then set the recovery objectives.
questions.pre_read: Notice the manager wants to choose strategies. Ask what input those strategies and their recovery targets depend on.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery strategies must be driven by business impact, so the BIA comes first: it identifies the critical processes the platform supports and how impact grows over time. Recovery objectives are outputs of that analysis. Setting the RTO and RPO with IT operations sounds like the right first move, but without the BIA the targets reflect technical preference rather than business need.

wrong_explanations.B: Procedures implement a chosen strategy. Drafting them first means documenting a recovery approach that has not yet been justified.
wrong_explanations.C: RTO and RPO come out of the BIA. Setting them with IT alone bases targets on technical preference, not business impact.
wrong_explanations.D: Site selection is itself a strategy choice and depends on recovery objectives that have not been set.

tips: Eliminate: B documents procedures for an undecided strategy, and D picks the strategy before knowing the need.
Final two: A beats C because recovery objectives come from the BIA; setting them with IT first skips business impact.
Exam cue: in continuity planning, BIA before objectives, objectives before strategy, strategy before procedures.

questions.question: A business continuity manager needs an alternate site for a trading system whose BIA sets a four-hour RTO and near-zero data loss. Which option is MOST appropriate?

options.A: A reciprocal agreement with a peer firm
options.B: A cold site with power and floor space
options.C: A warm site with preinstalled hardware
options.D: A hot site with current replicated data

questions.key_concept: Alternate site type follows the recovery objectives: short RTO and near-zero RPO need a hot site with current data.
questions.pre_read: Notice both the RTO and the data-loss tolerance. Ask which site meets both, not just one.
questions.correct_explanation: A four-hour RTO with near-zero data loss requires equipment ready to run and data already current, which is what a hot site with replication provides. A warm site has hardware in place, so it looks close, but data must be restored from backups, which takes longer than four hours and loses everything since the last backup.

wrong_explanations.A: Reciprocal agreements are hard to enforce and test, and a peer rarely has spare capacity for a trading load within four hours.
wrong_explanations.B: A cold site needs equipment delivered and installed, which takes days or weeks, far beyond a four-hour RTO.
wrong_explanations.C: Hardware is ready, but data must be restored from backups, breaking both the four-hour RTO and near-zero data loss.

tips: Eliminate: A depends on a peer's unenforceable spare capacity, and B needs equipment installed, taking days or weeks.
Final two: D beats C because only current replicated data meets near-zero data loss; a warm site restores from backup.
Exam cue: match site type to both objectives; short RTO plus tiny RPO means hot.

questions.question: An incident manager restores a failed payment service with a workaround, but the root cause is still unknown. What is the BEST next step under ITIL 4?

options.A: Raise an emergency change to replace the suspect component
options.B: Ask the service owner to renegotiate the SLA target
options.C: Close the incident and raise a problem record
options.D: Keep the incident open until the root cause is confirmed

questions.key_concept: Incident management restores service; root-cause work moves to problem management so it is tracked, not skipped.
questions.pre_read: Notice that service is already restored. Ask which practice owns the unanswered question that remains.
questions.correct_explanation: In ITIL 4, incident management aims to restore normal service quickly, and that is done. The unknown cause is handed to problem management through a problem record, so investigation is tracked rather than lost. Keeping the incident open looks thorough, but it mixes the two practices, distorts incident metrics and leaves root-cause work without the owner and method problem management provides.

wrong_explanations.A: Replacing a component without a confirmed cause is guesswork, and an emergency change is unjustified once service is restored.
wrong_explanations.B: Renegotiating the SLA does nothing about the cause of the failure and is unrelated to closing out this incident.
wrong_explanations.D: Root-cause analysis belongs to problem management. Holding the incident open blurs the practices and skews incident metrics.

tips: Eliminate: A changes a component on a guess, and B changes the target instead of addressing the failure.
Final two: C beats D because root cause moves to problem management; the incident closes once service is restored.
Exam cue: restore service before root cause, but never skip root cause; hand it to problem management.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a critical database server's two disks are mirrored using RAID 1. Which risk does this control MOST directly address?

options.A: Fire destroying the server room
options.B: Failure of a single disk
options.C: Logical corruption of database tables
options.D: Slow writes under heavy transaction load

questions.key_concept: RAID 1 mirrors data across disks so one disk can fail without data loss; it is not a backup and copies logical errors instantly.
questions.pre_read: Notice that mirroring copies every write. Ask what failure that survives, and what it copies straight to the second disk.
questions.correct_explanation: RAID 1 writes identical data to both disks, so the server keeps running if one disk fails, which is the risk it directly addresses. Logical corruption looks covered because data exists twice, but mirroring copies every write, including corrupted ones, to both disks at once. Protecting against corruption needs backups or point-in-time copies, not mirroring.

wrong_explanations.A: Both mirrored disks sit in the same server, so a fire destroys both. Site-level loss needs offsite backups or an alternate site.
wrong_explanations.C: Mirroring copies corrupted writes to both disks immediately. Logical corruption requires backups or snapshots to recover.
wrong_explanations.D: RAID 1 can speed reads, but every write goes to both disks, so it does not address write performance.

tips: Eliminate: A is a site-level loss that destroys both disks, and D is a performance concern RAID 1 does not solve.
Final two: B beats C because mirroring copies corruption to both disks instantly; it protects only against hardware failure.
Exam cue: RAID is availability, not backup; it protects against disk failure, never against bad data.
